parole.significato: someone associated with something
parole.testo: From Latin -asta, from Ancient Greek -αστής (-astḗs), from -άζω (-ázō, verbal suffix) + -τής (-tḗs, agent-noun suffix).

parole.significato: A cavity.
parole.testo: Via Latin, from Ancient Greek κοῖλος (koîlos, “hollow”).

parole.significato: Used to form cell names and classifications for mature cells.
parole.testo: From Latin cyta, from Ancient Greek κύτος (kútos, “vessel, jar”). Compare cyte.

parole.significato: Forms adjectives, usually from proper nouns.
parole.testo: From Latin -ānus, following Latin stems ending in -ae(us) (many from Ancient Greek -αῖος (-aîos)), -e(us) or -ē(us) (many from Ancient Greek -εῖος (-eîos)).

parole.significato: Forms adjectives relating to places and nouns for their inhabitants.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -ēnus, from Ancient Greek -ηνός (-ēnós), forming adjectives from place names.

parole.significato: Used to form nouns denoting condition, action, or process.
parole.testo: From Latin -ēsis, from Ancient Greek -ησις (-ēsis), from -σις (-sis).

parole.significato: Noun-forming suffix found in words of Greek origin meaning “place or building associated with a specific purpose or per…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -ēum, from Ancient Greek -εῖον (-eîon), originating in the substantivized neuter of -εῖος (-eîos, adjective suffix).

parole.significato: origin
parole.testo: Via Latin, from Ancient Greek γένεσις (génesis). The simplex genesis is in use as a common noun (as opposed to Genesis, the name of the biblical book) since the late 16th century, as a suffix since the mid 17th century (attested in epigenesis and palingenesis). Influenced by French -génésie and Germ

parole.significato: Used in forming plurals of nouns in -ium and -ion.
parole.testo: From the endings of corresponding Latin and Ancient Greek plural nouns.

parole.significato: A pathological condition or process.
parole.testo: A Latin word-forming element meaning "process" or "morbid condition". Originally from Ancient Greek ἴασις (íasis). By surface analysis, -i- + -asis.

parole.significato: Divination.
parole.testo: From Latin -mantīa, ultimately from Ancient Greek μᾰντείᾱ (mănteíā, “divination”).

parole.significato: A linking vowel inserted interconsonantally between two morphemes, to ease pronunciation, without contributing to the m…
parole.testo: Adopted from Latin -o-, originating ultimately from Ancient Greek -ο- (-o-). In English, the connective is found from the Middle English period in direct borrowings from Latin. Direct formations of English terms with the connective, always combining Greek or Latin roots, appear from the 16th or 17th

parole.significato: Indicating an oily substance
parole.testo: From Latin oleum (“oil, olive oil”), from Ancient Greek ἔλαιον (élaion, “olive oil”).

parole.significato: eater; something that eats, or consumes.
parole.testo: From Latin -phagus, from Ancient Greek φάγος (phágos, “glutton”), from φαγεῖν (phageîn, “to eat”), aorist active infinitive of ἔφαγον (éphagon, “I ate, devoured”). Stem φαγ- (phag-) may also derive from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂g- (“to divide, distribute”) thus ultimately doublet of bhakti (via San

parole.significato: Used to form adjectives meaning "eating" or "feeding on".
parole.testo: From Latin -phagus, from Ancient Greek -φάγος (-phágos, “-eating”), from φαγεῖν (phageîn, “to eat”).

parole.significato: Forming nouns and adjectives meaning "loving", "friendly", or "friend".
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin -phila, from Ancient Greek φίλος (phílos, “dear, beloved”).

parole.significato: Used to form nouns that denote the making or creating of something.
parole.testo: From Latin -poeia, from Ancient Greek ποιέω (poiéō, “I make”).

parole.significato: Forms names of cities or kinds of cities.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin -polis, from Ancient Greek πόλις (pólis, “city”).

parole.significato: Forms nouns indicating excessive discharge or haemorrhage from an organ.
parole.testo: From Latin -rrhagia, from Ancient Greek -ραγία (-ragía), from the stem of ῥήγνυμι (rhḗgnumi, “to break, burst”).

parole.significato: Describes the cleavage of minerals.
parole.testo: From Latin -tomus, introduced by James Dwight Dana, from Ancient Greek τόμος (tómos, “slice, something cut”). Perhaps modelled on Ancient Greek ἀκρότομος (akrótomos, “cut off sharply”, adjective).

parole.significato: place
parole.testo: From Latin topica, from Ancient Greek τοπικός (topikós, “pertaining to a place, local, pertaining to a common place, or topic, topical”), from τόπος (tópos, “a place”); equivalent to -topia + -ic.

parole.significato: something that turns, affects, changes, responds, moves.
parole.testo: From Latin tropus, from Ancient Greek τρόπος (trópos, “a turn, way, manner, style, a trope or figure of speech, a mode in music, a mode or mood in logic”), from τροπή (tropḗ, “turn; solstice; trope”). See trope.

parole.significato: movement, turning.
parole.testo: From Latin tropus (English trope) + -ism, from Ancient Greek τρόπος (trópos, “a turn, way, manner, style, a trope or figure of speech, a mode in music, a mode or mood in logic”), from τροπή (tropḗ, “turn; solstice; trope”). Early use in botany as geotropism and heliotropism.

parole.significato: Forming nouns indicating individual members of taxonomic groups whose names end in -zoa.
parole.testo: From Latin -zoon, from Ancient Greek ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”).

parole.significato: The leader of a group of thieves.
parole.testo: From Latin Aaron, from Ancient Greek Ἀαρών (Aarṓn), from Hebrew אַהֲרֹן (ʾAhărōn), of unknown meaning, possibly meaning “bearer of martyrs”, or perhaps also, or instead, related to the Ancient Egyptian ꜥḥꜣ rw (“warrior lion”), though it has been suggested to also mean “elevated”, “exalted” or “high

parole.significato: An inscribed stone square.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin abacus.

parole.significato: A table or tray scattered with sand which was used for calculating or drawing.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English abacus, abagus, agabus (“abacus; art of counting with an abacus”), from Latin abacus, abax (“sideboard or table with a slab at the top; slab at the top of a column; counting board, sand table; board for playing games”) (compare Late Latin abacus (“art of arithmetic”)), from

parole.significato: Father, an honorific title given to God in the New Testament, especially used in prayers.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Latin abba, from Ancient Greek ἀββα (abba), from Aramaic אבא/ܐܒܐ (ʼabbāʼ, “father”).

parole.significato: Father; religious superior; in the Syriac, Coptic, and Ethiopic churches, a title given to the bishops, and by the bish…
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Latin, from Ancient Greek, from Aramaic אבא/ܐܒܐ (ʼaḇā, “father”); see abbot, Abraham for more.

parole.significato: The superior or head of an abbey or monastery.
parole.testo: From Middle English abbot, abbod, abbed, from Old English abbat, abbad, abbod, from Latin abbās (“father”), from Ancient Greek ἀββᾶς (abbâs), from Aramaic אבא (’abbā, “father”). Doublet of abba, abbé, and bwana.

parole.significato: An inhabitant or native of Abdera, in Thrace.
parole.testo: From Latin Abderita, Abderites, from Ancient Greek Ἀβδηρίτης (Abdērítēs).

parole.significato: Relating to organs outside of the intestine.
parole.testo: From Latin ab- (“away from”) + Ancient Greek ἔντερον (énteron, “intestine”) + -ic.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Abila
parole.testo: From Latin Abilēnus, from Ancient Greek Ἀβιληνός (Abilēnós). By surface analysis, Abila + -ene.

parole.significato: A person who fears bathing.
parole.testo: From Latin ablutio (“a washing”) + Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos, “fear”).

parole.significato: A pathological fear of washing or bathing.
parole.testo: From Latin ablutio (“a washing”) + Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos, “fear”) (equivalent to -phobia).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to or suffering from ablutophobia.
parole.testo: From Latin ablutio (“a washing”) + Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos, “fear”).

parole.significato: A shop selling cheap and low-quality clothes, especially in the East End of London.
parole.testo: From Middle English Abraham, from Old English Abraham, from Late Latin Ābrahām, from Ancient Greek Ἀβρᾱᾱ́μ (Abrāā́m), from Hebrew אַבְרָהָם ('aḇrāhām, “Abraham”). Thomas L. Thompson suggests that the meaning of the name in Genesis was forgotten due to its age and that its original meaning was "Fathe

parole.significato: Denoting the effect that irradiation of a tissue has on remote nonirradiated tissue.
parole.testo: From Latin ab (“away from”) and Ancient Greek σκοπός (skopós, “target, aim”). Term first described by Dr. R. J. Mole in 1953 in the British Journal of Radiology, "Whole body irradiation- radiobiology or medicine?" . Br. J. Radiol., 26: 234-241, 1953.

parole.significato: Common wormwood (Artemisia absinthium), an intensely bitter herb used in the production of absinthe and vermouth, and a…
parole.testo: From Middle English absinthium, from Latin absinthium, from Ancient Greek ἀψίνθιον (apsínthion). Doublet of absinthe.

parole.significato: A shrub or tree of the tribe Acacieae.
parole.testo: From Latin acacia, from Ancient Greek ἀκακία (akakía, “shittah tree”), either from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp”) (compare ἀκή (akḗ, “point”)) or more likely a Pre-Greek word. First attested before 1398. Doublet of cassie.

parole.significato: A member of the former Acalephae group, now a part of the Cnidaria phylum.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin acalephe, from Ancient Greek ἀκαλήφη (akalḗphē, “stinging nettle”).

parole.significato: A member of the genus Acanthus of herbaceous prickly plants with toothed leaves, (family Acanthaceae, order Lamiales (f…
parole.testo: From Latin acanthus, from Ancient Greek ἄκανθος (ákanthos, “thorn”), from ἀκή (akḗ, “point”) + ἄνθος (ánthos, “flower”).

parole.significato: Incapable of being comprehended; incomprehensible; inconceivable.
parole.testo: From Latin acatalēpticus, from Ancient Greek ἀκατάληπτος (akatálēptos, “incomprehensible”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + καταλαμβάνω (katalambánō, “to seize”), from κατά (katá, “against”) + λαμβάνω (lambánō, “to take”).

parole.significato: A member of a group of 4th century penitants who wore coarse clothing and used water for the Eucharist instead of wine.…
parole.testo: From a misreading of Saccaophori; from Latin saccus (“sack”) and Ancient Greek σᾰ́κκος (sắkkos, “sack, bag”) + φέρω (phérō, “bearer, carrier”).

parole.significato: The feigning of disinterest in something while actually desiring it.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin accismus, from Ancient Greek ακκισμός (akkismós, “prudery”).

parole.significato: Spiritual or mental sloth and the feeling it provokes; apathy or indifference; a lack of care or interest and the resul…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin acēdia, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀκηδίᾱ (akēdíā), from ἀκηδής (akēdḗs, “careless”) + -ίᾱ (-íā). Doublet of accidie.

parole.significato: The univalent radical CH₃CO- derived from acetic acid.
parole.testo: aceto- + -yl. From Latin acētum (“vinegar”) + Ancient Greek ὕλη (húlē, “substance”).

parole.significato: An inhabitant or resident of Achaea, especially a member of an ancient Hellenic tribe that inhabited the region of Acha…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin achaeus, from Ancient Greek Ἀχαιός (Akhaiós), + -an.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the dynasty which ruled the Persian empire c. 550–330 BCE (the Achaemenid Empire), founded by Achaeme…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Achaemenidēs, from Ancient Greek Ἀχαιμενίδης (Akhaimenídēs), from Ancient Greek Ἀχαιμένης (Akhaiménēs) + Ancient Greek -ίδης (-ídēs, patronymic suffix). By surface analysis, Achaemenes + -id.

parole.significato: Any dry indehiscent fruit.
parole.testo: From Latin achenium, from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not”) + χαίνω (khaínō, “to gape”), + Ancient Greek καρπός (karpós, “fruit”).

parole.significato: A short sword or saber.
parole.testo: From Latin acīnacēs, from Ancient Greek ἀκινάκης (akinákēs, “the short sabre of the Persians, Medes, and Scythians; a scimitar”).

parole.significato: Referring to a sound that has no visually identifiable cause.
parole.testo: From Latin acousmaticus, from Ancient Greek ἀκουσματικός (akousmatikós), from ἀκούω (akoúō, “to hear”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to hearing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin acroamaticus, acroaticus (“esoteric”), at first chiefly in reference to the “esoteric” and originally oral teachings of Aristotle, from Ancient Greek ἀκροαματικός (akroamatikós, “for hearing only; esoteric”), from ἀκροάομαι (akroáomai, “to listen”).

parole.significato: An oral discourse.
parole.testo: From Latin acroāsis, from Ancient Greek ἀκρόᾱσις (akróāsis, “a hearing or lecture”), from ἀκροάομαι (akroáomai, “listen”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Ceraunian Mountains.
parole.testo: From Latin Acroceraunius, from Ancient Greek ἄκρος (ákros, “high, heights”) + κεραυνός (keraunós, “thunderbolt”).

parole.significato: acromion
parole.testo: From Latin acromion, from Ancient Greek ἀκρώμιον (akrṓmion). By surface analysis, acromi(on) + -o-.

parole.significato: One of the small pedestals, for statues or other ornaments, placed on the apex and at the basal angles of a pediment, o…
parole.testo: From Latin acrōtērium, from Ancient Greek ἀκρωτήριον (akrōtḗrion); related to ἄκρος (ákros, “highest, at the extremity”). By surface analysis, acro- + Latin -tērium. Fully Latinized form. Doublet of acroter.

parole.significato: A cuckold.
parole.testo: From Latin Actaeōn, from Ancient Greek Ἀκταίων (Aktaíōn). In Greek mythology, Artemis transformed Actaeon into a stag with horns on his head. In European folklore, horns were considered the sign of a cuckold, whence the noun sense of Actaeon, "cuckold", and the verb sense "to cuckold", are derived.

parole.significato: Any sea slug of the family Actaeonidae.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin Actæon, borrowed from Ancient Greek Ἀκταίων (Aktaíōn) (Acteon).

parole.significato: A diacritical mark ( ´ ) that can be placed above a number of letters in many languages of the Latin, Greek and Cyrilli…
parole.testo: From Latin accentus (“accent”) acūtus (“sharp”), a calque of Ancient Greek προσῳδία (prosōidía, “accent”) ὀξύς (oxús, “sharp”). Cognate to French accent aigu.

parole.significato: inexact, inappropriate or improper use of a word
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek ἀκυρολογία (akurología), ἀ- (a-, “not”) + κύριος (kúrios, “having authority”) + -λογία (-logía, “speech”).

parole.significato: Firm; unshakeable; unyielding; determined.
parole.testo: From Middle English adamant, adamaunt, from Latin adamantem, accusative singular form of adamās (“hard as steel”), from Ancient Greek ἀδάμαντ- (adámant-, “invincible”), oblique stem of ἀδάμας (adámas). Doublet of diamond.

parole.significato: A salty concretion found on reeds and grasses in marshy grounds. Soft and porous, it was formerly used for cleansing th…
parole.testo: From Latin adarcē, adarca, from Ancient Greek ἀδάρκη (adárkē).

parole.significato: Bad, rotten; inviable, containing a dead embryo.
parole.testo: From Middle English addled, adyld, equivalent to addle (“urine, liquid filth”) + -ed. Addle derives from Old English adel, adela (“mud, mire, liquid manure”), cognate with Old Swedish adel (“urine”), Middle Low German adel, Dutch aal (“manure”). Used in noun phrase addle egg (mid-13c.) “egg that doe

parole.significato: neither harmful nor beneficial
parole.testo: From Latin adiaphorus or Ancient Greek ἀδιάφορος (adiáphoros).

parole.significato: The innermost sanctuary or shrine in a temple, from where oracles were given.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin adytum, from Ancient Greek ἄδυτον (áduton, “innermost sanctuary; shrine”), inflected form of ἄδυτος (ádutos, “not to be entered”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Aegean Sea or the regions bordering it.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin aegaeus (from Ancient Greek Αἰγαῖος (Aigaîos, “Aegean”)) + English -an. The name might be connected to αἶγες (aîges, “waves”).

parole.significato: An ulcer or fistula in the inner angle of the eye.
parole.testo: From Latin aegilōps, from Ancient Greek αἰγίλωψ (aigílōps, “haver-grass (Aegilops neglecta)”).

parole.significato: A goat-like creature resembling a satyr, sometimes portrayed as having a fish's tail.
parole.testo: From Latin Aegipān, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek Αἰγίπαν (Aigípan), from αἴξ (aíx, “goat”) + Πάν (Pán, “Pan”).

parole.significato: A mythological shield associated with the Greek deities Zeus and Athena (and their Roman counterparts Jupiter and Miner…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aegis, from Ancient Greek αἰγίς (aigís, “goatskin; shield of Athena”), probably from αἴξ (aíx, “goat”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eyǵ- (“goat”). The plural form aegides (/ˈiːd͡ʒɪdiːz/) is borrowed from Latin aegides, from Ancient Greek αἰγῐ́δες (aigĭ́des).

parole.significato: Of the Anatolian region Aeolis, Aeolia.
parole.testo: From Latin aeolicus, from Ancient Greek Αἰολικός (Aiolikós, “like the Aeolians”).

parole.significato: Commonwealth standard spelling of eon.
parole.testo: From Latin aeon, from Ancient Greek αἰών (aiṓn, “age, era”).

parole.significato: Related to or concerning the Greek fabulist Aesop.
parole.testo: From Latin Aesopius (“Aesopian”), from Ancient Greek Αἴσωπος (Aísōpos, “the famous Greek fabulist Aesop”).

parole.significato: Attributing a cause for a statement or claim made, often as a simple relative clause of explanation.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin aetiologia, from Ancient Greek αἰτιολογία (aitiología). Doublet of aetiology.

parole.significato: The establishment of a cause, origin, or reason for something.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aetiologia. By surface analysis, aetio- + -logy. Doublet of aetiologia.

parole.significato: Synonym of agalloch.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin agallochum, from Ancient Greek ἀγάλοχον (agálokhon).

parole.significato: Any of various fungi, principally of the order Agaricales, having fruiting bodies consisting of umbrella-like caps, on…
parole.testo: From Latin agaricum, from Ancient Greek ἀγαρικόν (agarikón, “a tree fungus (Phellinus pomaceus”)), from the country of Agaria, in Sarmatia.

parole.significato: A tribe of Sarmatia
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Agathyrsī, from Ancient Greek Ἀγάθυρσοι (Agáthursoi).

parole.significato: A struggle or contest; conflict; especially between the protagonist and antagonist in a literary work.
parole.testo: From Latin agōn, from Ancient Greek ἀγών (agṓn, “contest”).

parole.significato: Competitive struggle (especially political).
parole.testo: From agon + -ism, from Latin agōn, from Ancient Greek ἀγών (agṓn, “contest”).

parole.significato: Someone involved in a contest or battle (as in an agon), protagonist.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin agōnista, from Ancient Greek ἀγωνιστής (agōnistḗs, “combatant, champion”). By surface analysis, agon or agony + -ist.

parole.significato: One who trained persons to compete in public games and contests.
parole.testo: From Latin agonistarcha, from Ancient Greek *ἀγωνιστάρχης (*agōnistárkhēs), from ἀγωνιστής (agōnistḗs, “contestant”) + ἀρχός (arkhós, “leader”).

parole.significato: The fear of wide open spaces, crowds, or uncontrolled social conditions.
parole.testo: From Latin agoraphobia, from Ancient Greek ἀγορά (agorá, “assembly”) + φοβία (phobía, “fear”). By surface analysis, agora + -phobia. Coined by Karl Friedrich Otto Westphal in 1871.

parole.significato: The title of the governor or chief magistrate of the Jews in Alexandria under the Ptolemies and Roman emperors.
parole.testo: From Latin alabarches, more correctly arabarches, from Ancient Greek Ἀλαβάρχης (Alabárkhēs), more correctly Ἀραβάρχης (Arabárkhēs, “the prefect of the Arabian nome in Egypt, in Josephus appar. as in def.”), from Ἄραψ (Áraps) pl. Ἄρᾰβες (Árăbes, “Arabs”) + ἀρχός (arkhós, “leader”).

parole.significato: A member of a group of Sarmatian tribes, nomadic pastoralists of the 1st millennium AD who spoke an Eastern Iranian lan…
parole.testo: From Latin Alānī, from Ancient Greek Ἀλανοί (Alanoí), from Proto-Sarmatian *Āllān.

parole.significato: Pertaining to Alcaeus, a Greek lyric poet of around 600 BC; especially, of a verse meter in a four-line stanza which he…
parole.testo: From Latin Alcaicus, from Ancient Greek Ἀλκαϊκός (Alkaïkós), from Ἀλκαῖος (Alkaîos, “Alcaeus”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic”). By surface analysis, Alcaeus + -ic.

parole.significato: A magical stone said to be found in the gizzard of cocks.
parole.testo: From Latin alectoria, formed from Ancient Greek ἀλέκτωρ (aléktōr, “cock”).

parole.significato: A form of divination in which the diviner observes a bird or birds (preferably a white rooster or cockerel) pecking at…
parole.testo: From Latin alectryomantia, from Ancient Greek ἀλεκτρυών (alektruṓn, “rooster”) + Latin -mantia.

parole.significato: Something which protects against, or cures, a poison; an antidote.
parole.testo: From Latin alexipharmacum, from Ancient Greek ἀλεξιφάρμακον (alexiphármakon).

parole.significato: An official responsible for training and anointing athletes for the games.
parole.testo: From Latin alipta (“trainer of wrestlers or gymnasts”), from Ancient Greek ἀλείπτης (aleíptēs).

parole.significato: A liturgical or variant form of hallelujah.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin allēlūia, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀλληλούϊα (allēloúïa), borrowed from Biblical Hebrew הַלְּלוּיָהּ (halləlūyɔh, “praise the Lord”), from הַלְּלוּ (halləlū, “praise!”) + יָהּ (yɔh, “Lord, Jah”).

parole.significato: The resins of the tree Aquilaria malaccensis (syn. Aquilaria agallocha), known for their fragrant aroma, produced after…
parole.testo: From Old English alwe (“fragrant resin of an East Indian tree”), from Latin aloē, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓λόη (ălóē), from Hebrew אָהָל (ʾāhāl) or related Aramaic forms, ultimately from Tamil அகில் (akil); reinforced in Middle English by Old French aloes.

parole.significato: unreasonableness, absurdity
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin alogia, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Baldness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin alōpecia, from the Ancient Greek ἀλωπεκία (alōpekía, “fox-mange”), from ἀλώπηξ (alṓpēx, “fox”) + -ία (-ía, a formative ending used in Ancient Greek, especially used in naming diseases).

parole.significato: The prefix a- (or an- when prefixing a root which begins with a vowel) found in some English words of Greek derivation.…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin alpha prīvātīvum, from Ancient Greek ἄλφα στερητικόν (álpha sterētikón).

parole.significato: Any disease causing dull white or silvery spots on the skin, including non-contagious forms of leprosy and psoriasis.
parole.testo: From Latin alphos, from Ancient Greek ἀλφός (alphós, “dull white, used for some leprosy, psoriasis, etc.”).

parole.significato: The absence of one or both of the mammary glands, with the nipple and areola present.
parole.testo: From Modern Latin [Term?]. If so, from the hypothetical Ancient Greek *ἀμαζία (*amazía), ultimately from ἀ- (a-) + μαζός (mazós) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā).

parole.significato: A member of a mythical race of female warriors inhabiting the Black Sea area.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Latin, from Ancient Greek Ἀμαζών (Amazṓn); perhaps Ionian Greek pronunciation of Old Persian *hamazan- (“warrior”), as the Amazon women were known warriors. A popular folk etymology, of Ancient Greek provenance, claims that the word derives from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + μαζός (mazó

parole.significato: Having equally bad ability in both hands; clumsy; butterfingered.
parole.testo: First attested in English in 1646: from Latin ambilaevus (ambi- (“both”) + laevus (“left”)), a calque of Ancient Greek ἀμφαρίστερος (ampharísteros, “with two left hands, awkward, clumsy”) from ἀμφί (amphí, “on both sides”) + ἀριστερός (aristerós, “left”).

parole.significato: abortion (termination of pregnancy)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin amblosis, from Ancient Greek ἄμβλωσις (ámblōsis).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the city of Ambracia; Ambracian.
parole.testo: An adaptation of the Latin Ambraciōtēs and the Ancient Greek Ἀμβρᾰκῐώτης (Ambrăkĭṓtēs).

parole.significato: The food of the gods, thought to confer immortality.
parole.testo: From Latin ambrosia (“food of the gods”), from Ancient Greek ἀμβροσία (ambrosía, “immortality”), from ἄμβροτος (ámbrotos, “immortal”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + βροτός (brotós, “mortal”).

parole.significato: One of the genus Ammodytes of fishes; the sand eel.
parole.testo: From Latin ammodytes, from Ancient Greek "sand burrower, a kind of serpent".

parole.significato: A gaseous, toxic compound of hydrogen and nitrogen, NH₃, with a pungent smell and taste.
parole.testo: From Latin sal ammoniacus (“salt of Amun, ammonium chloride”), named so because it was found near the temple of (Jupiter) Ammon in Egypt. Ammon derives from Ancient Greek Ἄμμων (Ámmōn), from Egyptian jmn (i-mn:n-A4).

parole.significato: Loss of memory; forgetfulness.
parole.testo: From modified Latin amnesia, from Ancient Greek ἀμνησία (amnēsía, “forgetfulness”), a noun derivation from μιμνήσκω (mimnḗskō, “to remind, to remember”) prefixed with the alpha privative.

parole.significato: The innermost membrane of the fetal membranes of reptiles, birds, and mammals; the sac in which the embryo is suspended.
parole.testo: From Latin amnion (“membrane around a fetus”), from Ancient Greek ἀμνίον (amníon).

parole.significato: A poem in which people are represented speaking alternately.
parole.testo: From the neuter of Latin amoebaeus, from Ancient Greek ἀμοιβαῖος (amoibaîos, “alternate”).

parole.significato: Describing a form of prosody (amoebaeum) featuring alternating responses.
parole.testo: From Latin amoebaeus, from Ancient Greek ἀμοιβαῖος (amoibaîos, “reciprocal”), from ἀμοιβή (amoibḗ, “change; alternation”).

parole.significato: An earth abounding in pyrites, used by the Ancients Greeks as a pesticide on vines.
parole.testo: From Latin ampelitis, from Ancient Greek ἀμπελῖτις (ampelîtis, “of or for vines”), from ἄμπελος (ámpelos, “vine”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the class Amphibia.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin amphibius [from Ancient Greek ἀμφίβιος (amphíbios), from ἀμφίς (amphís, “of both kinds”) + βίος (bíos, “life”)] + -an.

parole.significato: Ambiguous; doubtful or unclear.
parole.testo: From Latin amphibolus, Ancient Greek ἀμφίβολος (amphíbolos, “thrown about, doubtful”). See amphibole.

parole.significato: A metrical foot in ancient Greek or Latin consisting of two short syllables surrounding one long one (e.g. amāta).
parole.testo: From Latin amphibrachys, from Ancient Greek ἀμφίβραχυς (amphíbrakhus, “short at both ends”), from ἀμφί (amphí) + βραχύς (brakhús, “short”).

parole.significato: One of the deputies from the confederated states of Ancient Greece to a congress or council. They considered both polit…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Amphictyones, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek Ἀμφικτύονες (Amphiktúones), both of which are only attested in the plural. Probably the word originally meant "dwellers around, neighbours".

parole.significato: A metrical foot consisting of an unaccented or light syllable between two accented or heavy syllables; a cretic.
parole.testo: From Latin amphimacrus, from Ancient Greek ἀμφίμακρος (amphímakros, “long at both ends”); see amphi-, macro-.

parole.significato: Having columns at either end but not along the sides.
parole.testo: From Latin amphiprostȳlos, from Ancient Greek ἀμφι- (amphi-) + πρόστῡλος (próstūlos, “having pillars”).

parole.significato: A mythical serpent having a head at each end of its body, able to move in either direction.
parole.testo: From Latin amphisbaena, from Ancient Greek ἀμφίσβαινα (amphísbaina, from ἀμφίς (amphís, “both ways”) + βαίνω (baínō, “to go”)).

parole.significato: An open, outdoor theatre (which may be a theatre in the round, or have a stage with seating on only one side), especial…
parole.testo: From Latin amphitheatrum, from Ancient Greek ἀμφιθέατρον (amphithéatron) from ἀμφί (amphí, “on both sides”) + θέᾱτρον (théātron, “theatre”).

parole.significato: A large, two-handled vessel, especially a thin-necked clay vat used in ancient Greece and Rome for storing and transpor…
parole.testo: From Latin amphora (“large wine vessel, Roman unit of liquid measure”), from Ancient Greek ἀμφορεύς (amphoreús, “two-handled pitcher, Greek units of liquid measure”), ultimately from Mycenaean Greek 𐀀𐀠𐀡𐀩𐀸 (a-pi-po-re-we, “carried on both sides”).

parole.significato: Tonsil.
parole.testo: From Latin amygdala, from Ancient Greek ἀμυγδάλη (amugdálē, “almond”), named for the almond shape.

parole.significato: tonsillitis
parole.testo: From amygdala, amygdale (“tonsils”) + -itis, from Latin amygdala, from Ancient Greek ἀμυγδάλη (amugdálē, “almond”), named for the almond-shape.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to starch
parole.testo: From Latin amylum (“starch”), from Ancient Greek ἄμυλον (ámulon, “starch”) from ἀ- (a-, “privative”) + μύλη (múlē, “mill”).

parole.significato: starch
parole.testo: From Latin amylum, from Ancient Greek ἄμυλον (ámulon), from ἀ- (a-, “privative”) + μύλη (múlē, “mill”).

parole.significato: A raised seat, chair or platform; a pulpit.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin anabathrum, from Ancient Greek ἀνάβαθρον (anábathron, “raised seat or chair”).

parole.significato: A headband, especially a garland of flowers.
parole.testo: From Latin anadēma, from Ancient Greek ἀνάδημα (anádēma, “head-band”).

parole.significato: A figure of speech in which a word or phrase used at the end of a clause or expression is repeated near the beginning o…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin anadiplōsis, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀναδίπλωσις (anadíplōsis).

parole.significato: The spiritual or mystical interpretation of a word or passage beyond the literal, allegorical or moral sense (especiall…
parole.testo: From Latin anagōgē, from Ancient Greek ἀναγωγή (anagōgḗ, “elevation”).

parole.significato: Having analogy, the status of an analogue; corresponding to something else; bearing some resemblance or similar proport…
parole.testo: From Latin analogus, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓νᾰ́λογος (ănắlogos); Its English equivalent is analogue + -ous. The application to similar features of organisms is nearly as old as the general sense. Recognizably modern uses of the second sense, distinguishing analogous from homologous, appear in the mid-

parole.significato: A relationship of resemblance or equivalence between two situations, people, or objects, especially when used as a basi…
parole.testo: From Latin analogia, from Ancient Greek ἀναλογίᾱ (analogíā), from ἀνα- (ana-) + λόγος (lógos, “speech, reckoning”).

parole.significato: A metrical foot of three syllables of the shape | ⏖ – |:
parole.testo: From Latin anapaestus, from Ancient Greek ἀνάπαιστος (anápaistos, “struck back, reversed [relative to dactyl]”), from ἀνά (aná, “back”) + παίω (paíō, “to strike”).

parole.significato: retraction of the edges of a wound
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin anastolē, from Ancient Greek ἀναστολή (anastolḗ).

parole.significato: One who lives in isolation or seclusion, especially for religious reasons; hermit.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀναχωρητής (anakhōrētḗs, “anchorite”), from ἀναχωρέω (anakhōréō, “to withdraw, retire”), via Latin anchōrēta, a variant of anachōrēta (“anchorite”), see -ite.

parole.significato: The corner of a wall or rafter.
parole.testo: From Latin ancōn, from Ancient Greek ἀγκών (ankṓn, “bend, elbow, cranny”).

parole.significato: Possessing the sex organs of both sexes.
parole.testo: From Latin androgynus (“man-woman, hermaphrodite”), from Ancient Greek ἀνδρόγῠνος (andrógŭnos), from ἀνήρ (anḗr, “man”) + γῠνή (gŭnḗ, “woman”) + -ος (-os, “-ous”, adjectival suffix), equivalent to andro- + gyno- + -ous.

parole.significato: the room reserved for males and their activities, often in the lower part of the house.
parole.testo: Latin andron, from Ancient Greek ἀνδρών (andrṓn).

parole.significato: An ancient nation of anthropophagi (cannibals) north of Scythia, recorded by Herodotus
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Androphagī, from Ancient Greek Ἀνδροφάγοι (Androphágoi).

parole.significato: Soothing; helping to relieve a malady.
parole.testo: From Latin aneticus, from Ancient Greek ἀνετικός (anetikós, “relaxing, remitting”), from ἄνεσις (ánesis, “relaxation, abatement”).

parole.significato: coercion
parole.testo: From Latin angariatio, from Latin angaria (“service to a lord, villenage”), from Ancient Greek (a Persian word) for a courier for carrying royal dispatches.

parole.significato: A Christian devotion in memory of the Incarnation.
parole.testo: * (given name): From Latin Angelus and its etymon Ancient Greek ἄγγελος (ángelos, “angel”). * (common noun): From the first word (angelus) of its Latin incipit, "Angelus Domini nuntiavit Mariæ": "the Angel of the Lord declared unto Mary". Doublet of angel.

parole.significato: A deviation from a rule or from what is regarded as normal; an outlier.
parole.testo: From Latin anomalia, from Ancient Greek ἀνωμαλία (anōmalía, “irregularity, anomaly”), from ἀνώμαλος (anṓmalos, “irregular, uneven”), negating the meaning of ὁμαλός (homalós, “even”), from ὁμός (homós, “same”).

parole.significato: The quality or state of being anonymous (nameless or unidentified).
parole.testo: From Latin anonymus or its etymon Ancient Greek ἀνώνυμος (anṓnumos, “anonymous”) + -ity. Compare French anonymité.

parole.significato: An opponent or enemy.
parole.testo: From Latin antagonista, from Ancient Greek ἀνταγωνιστής (antagōnistḗs, “opponent”) (ἀντί (antí, “against”) + ἀγωνιστής (agōnistḗs, “a combatant, pleader, actor”)), from ἀνταγωνίζομαι (antagōnízomai, “to antagonize”).

parole.significato: A form of carbonized ancient plants; the hardest and cleanest-burning of all the coals.
parole.testo: Via Latin from Ancient Greek ἀνθρακῖτις (anthrakîtis, “a kind of coal”), from ἄνθραξ (ánthrax, “charcoal”). By surface analysis, anthrac- + -ite.

parole.significato: A remedy to counteract the effects of poison.
parole.testo: From Latin antidotum, from Ancient Greek ἀντίδοτον (antídoton, “antidote, remedy”), Clipping of ἀντίδοτον φάρμακον (antídoton phármakon, “drug given against”), from ἀντιδίδωμι (antidídōmi, “to give in return, repay”), from ἀντί (antí, “against”) + δίδωμι (dídōmi, “to give”). Compare French antidote.

parole.significato: A manuscript from which a copy (apograph) is made.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin antigraphum, from Ancient Greek ἀντίγραφον (antígraphon, “a transcribing”); compare French antigraphe.

parole.significato: A contradiction within a law, or between different laws; also, a contradiction between authorities.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin antinomia, from Ancient Greek ἀντινομία (antinomía), from ἀντι- (anti-, prefix meaning ‘against’) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ent- (“face; forehead; front”)) + νόμος (nómos, “custom, usage; law, ordinance”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, suffix forming feminine abstract nouns

parole.significato: A handsome young man.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Antinous, from Ancient Greek Ἀντίνοος (Antínoos).

parole.significato: In Greek choruses and dances, the returning of the chorus, exactly answering to a previous strophe or movement from rig…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin antistrophe, from Ancient Greek ἀντιστροφή (antistrophḗ, “turning about”).

parole.significato: A proposition that is the diametric opposite of some other proposition.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin antithesis, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀντίθεσις (antíthesis). By surface analysis, anti- + thesis.

parole.significato: An antithetical or contrasted statement; a statement containing antithesis
parole.testo: From Latin antithetum, antitheton, from Ancient Greek ἀντίθετον (antítheton), substantivization of the neuter form of ἀντίθετος (antíthetos, “opposing, contrasting”).

parole.significato: The spiral tubular proboscis of butterflies.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin antlia (“pump”), from Ancient Greek ἀντλία (antlía).

parole.significato: The inhabitants at two points on the globe that share a longitude and for which the sum of their degrees of latitude eq…
parole.testo: From the Latin antoecī, from the Ancient Greek ἄντοικοι (ántoikoi, “dwellers opposite”), from ἀντί (antí, “opposite”) + οἶκος (oîkos, “dwelling”).

parole.significato: The substitution of an epithet or title in place of a proper noun.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin antonomasia, Ancient Greek ἀντονομασία (antonomasía, “antonomasia”).

parole.significato: Relating to, or characterized by, antonomasia.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin antonomasticus, Ancient Greek ἀντονομασία (antonomasía, “antonomasia”).

parole.significato: A bodily cavity, especially one having bony walls, especially one in the sinuses.
parole.testo: From Latin antrum, from Ancient Greek ἄντρον (ántron, “cave”). Doublet of antre.

parole.significato: Synonym of Apamean.
parole.testo: From Latin Apamēnus, from Ancient Greek Ἀπαμηνός (Apamēnós).

parole.significato: A master artist.
parole.testo: From the Latin Apellēs, from the Ancient Greek Ἀπελλῆς (Apellês) (Apellēs, Apelles of Kos, a renowned painter in the time of Alexander the Great).

parole.significato: Elision, suppression, or complete loss of a letter or sound (syllable) from the beginning of a word, such as the develo…
parole.testo: From Latin aphaeresis, from Ancient Greek ἀφαίρεσις (aphaíresis, “a taking away”), from ἀφαιρέω (aphairéō) (from ἀφ- (aph-), variant of ἀπό (apó, “off, away from”) before an aspirated vowel) + αἱρέω (hairéō, “to take; to snatch”)) + -σις (-sis, suffix forming nouns of action); the grammatical sense

parole.significato: A revealing, especially a prophecy of, or the unfolding of, supernatural events.
parole.testo: From Middle English apocalips, from Latin apocalypsis, from Ancient Greek ἀποκάλυψις (apokálupsis, “revelation”, literally “uncovering”), from ἀποκαλύπτω (apokalúptō, “to reveal”), from ἀπό (apó, “back, away from”) + καλύπτω (kalúptō, “to cover”), + -σις (-sis, suffix forming nouns). The sense evolu

parole.significato: Of or relating to an apocalypse:
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin apocalypticus, from Ancient Greek ἀποκαλυπτικός (apokaluptikós, “revelatory”), from ἀποκάλυψις (apokálupsis, “revelation”), from ἀποκαλύπτω (apokalúptō, “to reveal, uncover”).

parole.significato: Restoration, renovation, reestablishment
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin apocatastasis, itself from Ancient Greek ἀποκατάστασις (apokatástasis, “restoration, reëstablishment”), from ἀποκαθίστημι (apokathístēmi, “to stand up again”), from ἀπό- (apó-, “back again”) + καθίστημι (kathístēmi, “to set, place, constitute, appoint”), from κατά- (katá

parole.significato: Shortened by apocope; lacking a final sound or syllable
parole.testo: From Latin apocopātus (“cut off”), from Ancient Greek ἀποκόπτω (apokóptō, “cut off”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to apocope; lacking a final sound or syllable.
parole.testo: From apocope, from Latin, from Ancient Greek ἀποκοπή (apokopḗ, “a cutting off, termination, apocope”).

parole.significato: A high diplomatic representative, approximately equivalent to a papal nuncio.
parole.testo: From Latin apocrisiarius, apocrisarius, from Ancient Greek ἀπόκρισις (apókrisis, “separation, answer, embassy or commission”).

parole.significato: Incontrovertible; demonstrably true or certain.
parole.testo: From the Latin apodīcticus (“proving clearly”, “demonstrative”), from the Ancient Greek ἀποδεικτικός (apodeiktikós, “affording proof”, “demonstrative”), from ἀποδείκνυμι (apodeíknumi, “to demonstrate”). In turn, from ἀπο- (apo-, “separate, without”), and δεικτικός (deiktikós, “capable of proof”).

parole.significato: Emphatic rejection or dismissal of an opponent or an opposing proposition.
parole.testo: From Latin, from ἀποδίωξις (apodíōxis), from Ancient Greek ἀποδιώκειν (apodiṓkein, “to drive away”).

parole.significato: The apartment at the entrance of the baths, or in the palestra, for getting undressed.
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek ἀποδυτήριον (apodutḗrion), from ἀποδύω (apodúō, “strip oneself”).

parole.significato: Any of several papilionid butterflies of the genus Parnassius, especially Parnassius apollo of Eurasia (also known as t…
parole.testo: From Latin Apollō, from Ancient Greek Ἀπόλλων (Apóllōn).

parole.significato: An expression of deliberation with oneself regarding uncertainty or doubt as to how to proceed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aporia, from Ancient Greek ἀπορία (aporía), from ἄπορος (áporos, “impassable”), from ἀ- (a-, “a-”) + πόρος (póros, “passage”). By surface analysis, a- + pore + -ia.

parole.significato: An abrupt breaking-off in speech, often indicated in print using an ellipsis (…) or an em dash (—).
parole.testo: From Latin aposiopesis, from Ancient Greek ἀποσιώπησις (aposiṓpēsis), from ἀποσιωπάω (aposiōpáō, “be silent”), from ἀπό (apó, “off, from”) + σιωπάω (siōpáō, “to be silent”).

parole.significato: The renunciation of a belief or set of beliefs.
parole.testo: From Latin apostasia, from Ancient Greek ἀποστασία (apostasía, “defection, revolt”), from ἀφίστημι (aphístēmi, “to withdraw, revolt”), from ἀπό (apó, “from”) + ἵστημι (hístēmi, “to stand”).

parole.significato: Apostate.
parole.testo: Latin apostaticus, Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Pertaining to apostles or their practice or teaching; pertaining to the apostles (of early Christianity) or their teach…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin apostolicus (“apostolic”), from Ancient Greek ἀποστολικός (apostolikós, “apostolic”).

parole.significato: A sudden exclamatory piece of dialogue addressed to someone or something, especially absent.
parole.testo: From Latin apostrophe, from Ancient Greek ἀποστροφή (apostrophḗ), from ἀποστρέφω (apostréphō, “to turn away”), from ἀπό (apó) + στρέφω (stréphō, “to turn”).

parole.significato: The fact or action of becoming or making into a god; deification.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin apotheōsis, from Ancient Greek ἀποθέωσις (apothéōsis), from verb ἀποθεόω (apotheóō, “deify”) (factitive verb formed from θεός (theós, “God”) with intensive prefix ἀπο- (apo-)) + -σις (-sis, “forms noun of action”). By surface analysis, apo- + theo- + -sis.

parole.significato: A decoction or infusion.
parole.testo: From Latin apozema, from Ancient Greek ἀπόζεμα (apózema, “to extract by boiling”), from the root ζέω (zéō, “to boil, seethe”), q. v.

parole.significato: A recess or projection, with a dome or vault, at the east end of a church.
parole.testo: From Latin apsis, hapsis, from Ancient Greek ἁψίς (hapsís, “arch, vault”). See also apse.

parole.significato: Any subsequence of nucleic acid, selected from a large random sequence-pool, used to bind to a specific target molecule.
parole.testo: From Latin aptus (“apt, proper”) + -mer (from Ancient Greek μέρος (méros, “part, portion”); compare mero-).

parole.significato: A noun (broadly speaking) which has no distinction of cases; an indeclinable noun.
parole.testo: From Latin aptotum, from Ancient Greek ἄπτωτος (áptōtos, “without cases”).

parole.significato: A sexual attraction to general imagery of people in water, sexual acts in water, or watery environments.
parole.testo: From aqua- + -philia, from Latin aqua (“water”) + Ancient Greek φιλία (philía, “love, affection”). Literally: “love of water”.

parole.significato: Related to the Arabic language.
parole.testo: From Latin arabicus, from Ancient Greek Ἀραβικός (Arabikós), from Ἄραψ (Áraps, “Arab”) [from Arabic عَرَب (ʕarab)] + -ικός (-ikós, adjective suffix). By surface analysis, Arab + -ic.

parole.significato: A type of intercolumniation
parole.testo: From Latin araeostylos, from Ancient Greek ἀραιόστυλος (araióstulos). By surface analysis, Ancient Greek ἀραιός (araiós, “widely spaced”) + -style.

parole.significato: An arrangement of columns that alternates between araeostyle and systyle.
parole.testo: From Latin araeostylos, from Ancient Greek ἀραιόστυλος (araióstulos). By surface analysis, Ancient Greek ἀραιός (araiós, “widely spaced”) + sy- + -style.

parole.significato: Referring to the Aramaic language, alphabet, culture or poetry.
parole.testo: From Latin Aramaicus, from Ancient Greek Ἀραμαϊκός (Aramaïkós), itself a calque of Aramaic ܐܪܡܝܐ / אָרָמָיָא (ʾārāmāyā, “Aramean”) using Ἀράμ f (Arám, “Aram”, the name of a land originally covering central regions of what is now Syria) (from Aramaic ܐܪܡ / ארם (ʾarām)) + -ικός (-ikós, adjective suffi

parole.significato: An ideal region of rural and idyllic contentment; a pastoral utopia.
parole.testo: From Latin Arcadia, from Ancient Greek Ἀρκαδία (Arkadía). Not related to arcade.

parole.significato: A title in a hierarchy which indicates a higher degree of rank than its root word.
parole.testo: From Middle English arch-, arche-, from Old English arċe-, ærċe-, erċe- (“arch-”), borrowed from Latin archi-, this stemming from Ancient Greek ἀρχι- (arkhi-).

parole.significato: A primitive alimentary cavity
parole.testo: arch- from Latin archi- from Ancient Greek ἀρχι- (arkhi-) + enteron from Ancient Greek ἔντερον (énteron, “gut”).

parole.significato: Relating to or characteristic of architecture, design and construction.
parole.testo: From Latin architectonicus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχιτεκτονικός (arkhitektonikós), from ἀρχιτέκτων (arkhitéktōn, “architect”).

parole.significato: The study of historical offices and the people who held them.
parole.testo: From Latin archontologia, equivalent to Ancient Greek ἄρχων (árkhōn, “ruler”) + -λογία (-logía, “study of”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to sandstone.
parole.testo: Latin arena (“sand”) + Ancient Greek λίθος (líthos, “stone”).

parole.significato: A member of the ancient-Athenian conciliary court of the Areopagus.
parole.testo: From the Middle English Ariopagite, Ariopagyte, from the Latin arēopagītes, from the Ancient Greek Ἀρεοπαγίτης (Areopagítēs); equivalent to Areopagus + -ite.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Areopagus (council of ancient Athens).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Areopagiticus, from Ancient Greek Ἀρεοπᾰγῑτῐκός (Areopăgītĭkós).

parole.significato: Pertaining to clay; made of, containing, or resembling clay; clayey.
parole.testo: From Latin argillaceus, from argilla (“clay”), from Ancient Greek ἄργιλλος (árgillos, “white clay, potter's earth”), from ἀργός (argós, “white”).

parole.significato: Of, from or pertaining to Argos.
parole.testo: From Latin Argīvus, from Ancient Greek Ἀργεῖος (Argeîos).

parole.significato: Relating to Argolis (various subdivisions which such name) in the Peloponnesus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Argolicus, from Ancient Greek Ἀργολικός (Argolikós).

parole.significato: Someone with an Aries star sign.
parole.testo: From Latin Aries, from aries (“ram”), calque of Ancient Greek Κριός (Kriós), calque of Akkadian 𒅈𒌺𒊑𒈨 (immeru, “sheep”).

parole.significato: A severe critic.
parole.testo: From the Latin Aristarchus, from the Ancient Greek Ἀρίσταρχος (Arístarkhos) (Aristarkhos; “Aristarchus of Samothrace”, a severe critic of Homeric poetry).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Parthian dynasty established by Arsaces I which ruled the Parthian Empire during 247 BC – 224 A…
parole.testo: From Latin Arsacidēs, from Ancient Greek Ἀρσακίδης (Arsakídēs), from Ancient Greek Ἀρσάκης (Arsákēs, “Arsaces”) [from Old Persian 𐎠𐎼𐏁𐎣 (a-r-š-k /⁠aršaka-⁠/); see there for more] + -ίδης (-ídēs, patronymic suffix). By surface analysis, Arsaces + -id.

parole.significato: Raising of the voice in prosody, accented part of a metrical foot
parole.testo: From Latin Arsis, from Ancient Greek ἄρσις (ársis, “elevation”).

parole.significato: Synonym of artery.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin artēria (“a windpipe; an artery”), from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓ρτηρῐ́ᾱ (ărtērĭ́ā). Doublet of artery.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the arteries; arterial.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin arteriacus, from Ancient Greek ἀρτηριακός (artēriakós). By surface analysis, artery + -ac.

parole.significato: Of, or affected by arthritis.
parole.testo: From Latin arthriticus (“gouty, arthritic”), from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Inflammation of a joint or joints causing pain and/or disability, swelling and stiffness, and due to various causes suc…
parole.testo: From Latin arthrītis, from Ancient Greek ἀρθρῖτις (arthrîtis, “joint-disease, gout”), from ἄρθρον (árthron, “a joint”). By surface analysis, arthr- + -itis.

parole.significato: A flower or plant in the genus Arum
parole.testo: From the botanical name Arum, from Latin arum, from Ancient Greek ἄρον (áron).

parole.significato: ascians
parole.testo: From Latin asciī, plural of ascius, from Ancient Greek ἄσκῐος (áskĭos, “shadowless”).

parole.significato: An accumulation of fluid in the peritoneal cavity, frequently symptomatic of liver disease.
parole.testo: From Latin ascītēs, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀσκίτης (askítēs), from ἀσκός (askós, “wineskin”).

parole.significato: Any one of the children of Asclepius and Epione (or Aristodama).
parole.testo: From Latin Asclēpiadēs, from Ancient Greek Ἀσκληπιάδης (Asklēpiádēs).

parole.significato: A choriambic verse consisting of four metrical feet: a spondee, two choriambi, and an iambus. First used by the ancient…
parole.testo: From Latin Asclēpiadēus, from Ancient Greek Ἀσκληπιάδειος (Asklēpiádeios), from Ἀσκληπιάδης (Asklēpiádēs) + -ειος (-eios).

parole.significato: One of the chiefs or pontiffs of the Roman province of Asia, who had the superintendence of the public games and religi…
parole.testo: From Latin Asiarcha, from Ancient Greek Ἀσιάρχης (Asiárkhēs).

parole.significato: Asian, specifically, relating to the parts of Asia east of Egypt, i.e the Middle East or West Asia.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin āsiāticus; equivalent to Asia + -atic.

parole.significato: Without a material body; incorporeal.
parole.testo: Latin asomatus, Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Any member of the genus Aspalathus of flowering plants.
parole.testo: From Latin aspalathus, from Ancient Greek ἀσπάλαθος (aspálathos).

parole.significato: Any of the flowering plants of the family Asphodelaceae, especially Asphodelus ramosus and Asphodelus albus; the flower…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin asphodelus, from Ancient Greek ἀσφόδελος (asphódelos). Doublet of daffodil.

parole.significato: Synonym of Assyrian
parole.testo: From Latin Assyriacus, from Ancient Greek Ἀσσυριακός (Assuriakós).

parole.significato: Witty dialog or response.
parole.testo: From Latin astĕïsmŏs (“the more refined style of speaking”), from Ancient Greek ἀστείσμός (asteísmós).

parole.significato: Any of several plants of the genus Aster; one of its flowers.
parole.testo: From Latin astēr, from Ancient Greek ἀστήρ (astḗr). Doublet of star; related to estoile, étoile, stella, and stelo.

parole.significato: Relating to stars.
parole.testo: From Latin aster, from Ancient Greek ἀστήρ (astḗr).

parole.significato: Pertaining to the astragalus, the anklebone
parole.testo: By surface analysis, astragal(us) + -o-, ultimately from Latin astragalus, from Ancient Greek ἀστράγαλος (astrágalos).

parole.significato: Synonym of anklebone.
parole.testo: From Latin astragalus, from Ancient Greek ἀστράγαλος (astrágalos). Doublet of astragal.

parole.significato: Divination by the stars; astrology in its modern prophetic aspect.
parole.testo: From astro- + -mancy. From Latin astromantīa, from Ancient Greek ἀστρομαντεία (astromanteía), from ἄστρον (ástron, “star”) + μαντεία (manteía, “divination”).

parole.significato: A place of safety or refuge.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin asȳlum, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἄσυλον (ásulon).

parole.significato: A pattern of spoken or written discourse demonstrating inability or diminished capacity to connect ideas.
parole.testo: From Latin asyndesis, from Ancient Greek ἀσύνδεσις (asúndesis), from ἀ- (a-, “a-, un-: without”) + σύνδεσις (súndesis, “binding, joining”), from συνδεῖν (sundeîn, “to join, to bind”) + -σῐς (-sĭs, “-sis: forming nouns”), from σῠν- (sŭn-, “together”) + δεῖν (deîn, “to bind, to tie”). Equivalent to a-

parole.significato: Omission of conjunctions, especially for rhetorical effect.
parole.testo: From Latin asyndeton, from Ancient Greek ἀσύνδετον (asúndeton), from ἀ- (a-, “a-, un-, non-”) and the neuter substantive of σῠ́νδετος (sŭ́ndetos, “bound, joined”), from συνδεῖν (sundeîn, “to join, to bind”), from σῠν- (sŭn-, “together”) + δεῖν (deîn, “to bind, to tie”). Equivalent to a- + syndeton.

parole.significato: imperturbability, ataraxia
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin athambia, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀθαμβία (athambía), from θάμβος (thámbos).

parole.significato: A woman who colludes with the patriarchy rather than actively opposing it.
parole.testo: From Middle English Athena, from Latin Athēna, from Ancient Greek Ἀθηνᾶ (Athēnâ). Doublet of Athina.

parole.significato: An abnormal fatty deposit which develops within the walls of arteries.
parole.testo: From Latin athērōma (“tumor/mass full of gruel-like matter”), from Ancient Greek ἀθήρωμα (athḗrōma). By surface analysis, ather- + -oma.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the Atlantic Ocean.
parole.testo: From Middle English Atlantyke, from Latin Ā̆tlanticus, from Ancient Greek Ἀτλαντικός (Atlantikós, “Atlantean, of Atlas”), from Ancient Greek Ἄτλᾱς (Átlās), either from ἁ- (ha-, copulative prefix) + Proto-Indo-European *telh₂- (“bear, undergo, endure”) or of Pre-Greek origin.

parole.significato: A bound collection of maps often including tables, illustrations or other text.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Atlas, from the name of the Ancient Greek mythological figure Ἄτλας (Átlas, “Bearer (of the Heavens)”), from τλῆναι (tlênai, “to suffer”, “to endure”, “to bear”). The sense referring to books of maps comes from the Atlas of Mercator, which he named thus in honor of Atlas, who was

parole.significato: Synonym of atom.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin atomus, from Ancient Greek ἄτομος (átomos). Doublet of atom.

parole.significato: A tiny particle; an atom, a mote, a speck.
parole.testo: A variant of atomi, the plural of atomus (“hypothetical particle posited as an ultimate and indivisible component of matter; mote of dust in a sunbeam”) treated as a singular form. Atomus is derived from Latin atomus, from Ancient Greek ἄτομος (átomos, “indivisible”, adjective), from ᾰ̓- (ă-, prefix

parole.significato: A condition in which a body orifice or passage in the body is abnormally closed or absent.
parole.testo: From Latin atresia, from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not, without”) and τρῆσις (trêsis, “perforation”).

parole.significato: Synonym of Atropatian
parole.testo: From Latin Atropatēnus, from Ancient Greek Ἀτροπατηνός (Atropatēnós), from Ἀτροπάτης (Atropátēs, “Atropates”) + -ηνός (-ēnós). By surface analysis, Atropates + -ene.

parole.significato: Of or related to Attica, ancient Athens and its hinterland
parole.testo: From Latin Atticus, from Ancient Greek Ἀττικός (Attikós), from some Pre-Greek demonym or toponym for Athens and its hinterland of Attica + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic: forming adjectives”). Equivalent to a modified and clipped Athens + -ic. Doublet of Atticus.

parole.significato: Epitympanic recess or the uppermost part of the middle ear cavity located above the tympanic membrane and containing th…
parole.testo: From Latin atticus, from Ancient Greek Ἀττικός (Attikós) + -o-. By surface analysis, attic + -o-.

parole.significato: A court or hall.
parole.testo: From Latin aula (“forecourt”), from Ancient Greek αὐλά (aulá), the form of αὐλή (aulḗ, “forecourt”) in dialects other than Ionic and Attic.

parole.significato: A tail-like longitudinally differentiated appendage found in mitrates and cornutes, originally believed to be used for…
parole.testo: From Latin aulax (“furrow”) or its etymon Ancient Greek αὖλαξ (aûlax, “furrow”) + -phore (“bearer, carrier”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to a musical pipe or piper.
parole.testo: Latin auleticus, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a royal court; courtly.
parole.testo: From Latin aulicus (“of a prince's court”), from aula (“royal court”), from Ancient Greek αὐλή (aulḗ, “courtyard”).

parole.significato: A subtle emanation or exhalation of any substance, such as an aroma or odour.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin aura (“a breeze, a breath of air, the air”), from Ancient Greek αὔρα (aúra, “breeze, soft wind”), from ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”). Doublet of east, auster, air, and aria. Sense 4 originated in the early 2020s and was popularized on TikTok around May 2024.

parole.significato: Of ancient Ausonia or the Ausonians.
parole.testo: From Latin Ausonia (“Lower Italy”), extended poetically to “Italy”, from Ancient Greek Αὐσονία (Ausonía), from Αὔσων (Aúsōn), a son of Ulysses, who is said to have settled there.

parole.significato: Divination by saws or axes.
parole.testo: Latin axinomantia, from Ancient Greek ἀξινομαντεία (axinomanteía), from ἀξίνη (axínē, “axe”) and μαντεία (manteía, “prophecy”)

parole.significato: An axiom.
parole.testo: From the Latin axiōma, from the Ancient Greek ἀξίωμα (axíōma): see axiom.

parole.significato: One who administers the Eucharist with unleavened bread, in particular a member of the Latin Church or Roman Catholic C…
parole.testo: From Latin azȳmita, from Ancient Greek ἀζῡμίτης (azūmítēs), from ἄζῡμος (ázūmos) + -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs, suffix forming masculine nouns meaning being connected to or a member of something, or coming from a particular place). ἄζῡμος is derived from ᾰ̓- (ă-, the alpha privativum, a prefix forming words havi

parole.significato: Pertaining to the city of Babylon, or the Babylonian Empire.
parole.testo: From Latin Babylōnius (“of Babylon, Babylonian”) (from Ancient Greek Βαβυλώνιος (Babulṓnios)) + -an. By surface analysis, Babylon + -ian. Piecewise doublet of Babelian.

parole.significato: A priest of Bacchus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bacchantem, present active participle of bacchor (“to celebrate rites of Bacchus; to revel”), from Bacchus (“the god of wine”), from Ancient Greek Βάκχος (Bákkhos).

parole.significato: A meteorite or similar-looking rough stone thought to be of divine origin and worshipped as sacred.
parole.testo: From Latin baetulus, from Ancient Greek βαίτυλος (baítulos, “a meteoric stone”).

parole.significato: Relating to the glans.
parole.testo: From Latin balanus, from Ancient Greek βάλανος (bálanos). By surface analysis, balan(us) + -o-.

parole.significato: The glans
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin balanus, from Ancient Greek βάλανος (bálanos, “acorn”).

parole.significato: An ancient military engine, in the form of a crossbow, used for hurling large missiles.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ballista, from Ancient Greek βαλλίστρα (ballístra), from βάλλω (bállō, “to throw”).

parole.significato: A room for bathing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin balnearium, from balneum (“bath”), from Ancient Greek βαλανεῖον (balaneîon).

parole.significato: A sweet-smelling oil or resin derived from various plants.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin balsamum, from Ancient Greek βάλσαμον (bálsamon, “balsam”), of Semitic origin (Hebrew בושם (“spice, perfume”)); compare Old English balsam, balsamum (“balsam, balm”), Doublet of balm and desman. Not related to balsa.

parole.significato: A very large wine bottle with the capacity of about 12 liters, equivalent to 16 standard bottles.
parole.testo: From Middle English Balthasar, from Latin Baltassar, from Ancient Greek Βαλτάσαρ (Baltásar), from Hebrew בֵּלְשַׁאצַּר (bēlšaṣṣar), attested in the Tanakh and the Old Testament (Daniel 5:1), from Akkadian 𒁹𒀭𒂗𒈗𒋀 (Bēl-šarra-uṣṣur, literally “May Bel protect the king”). Doublet of Belshazzar.

parole.significato: A pit, especially one at Athens into which criminals were thrown.
parole.testo: From Latin barathrum, from Ancient Greek βάραθρον (bárathron).

parole.significato: Rule by barbarians.
parole.testo: From Latin barbarus (“foreigner, savage”), from Ancient Greek βάρβαρος (bárbaros, “foreign, strange”) + -cracy.

parole.significato: Not classical or pure.
parole.testo: Late Middle English, from Latin barbarus (“foreigner, savage”), from Ancient Greek βάρβαρος (bárbaros, “foreign, strange”).

parole.significato: an ancient stringed musical instrument, apparently a type of lute or lyre
parole.testo: From Latin barbiton, from Ancient Greek βάρβιτον (bárbiton).

parole.significato: An ancient stringed musical instrument from Greece, apparently a type of lute or lyre.
parole.testo: From Latin barbitos, from Ancient Greek βάρβιτος (bárbitos).

parole.significato: Positioned at the base; forming a base
parole.testo: From Latin basis.

parole.significato: A Christian church building having a nave with a semicircular apse, side aisles, a narthex and a clerestory.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin basilica, from Ancient Greek βᾰσῐλῐκή (băsĭlĭkḗ), from βᾰσῐλῐκὴ στοά (băsĭlĭkḕ stoá, “royal hall”), ultimately from βασιλικός (basilikós, “royal”), from βασιλεύς (basileús, “king, chief”). Doublet of basoche.

parole.significato: A physical base or foundation.
parole.testo: From Latin basis, from Ancient Greek βάσις (básis), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷémtis, derived from Proto-Indo-European *gʷem- (whence also come). Doublet of base.

parole.significato: A gelatinous substance found in mud dredged from the Atlantic and once supposed to be a free living protoplasm, later f…
parole.testo: Latin, from Ancient Greek. See bathy-. Coined by Thomas Henry Huxley.

parole.significato: A pale greenish-grey variety of montmorillonite.
parole.testo: From Latin batrachītēs, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: To engage in the logical fallacy of begging the question (petitio principii).
parole.testo: Translating Latin petītiō prīncipiī, itself translating Ancient Greek τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ αἰτεῖσθαι (tò en arkhēî aiteîsthai, “to assume from the beginning”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Berytus (“the ancient city of Beirut”).
parole.testo: From Berytus + -ian (suffix meaning ‘from, related to, or like’; or ‘one from, belonging to, relating to, or like’). Berytus is derived from Latin Bērȳtus, from Ancient Greek Βηρῡτός (Bērūtós), from a Semitic source.

parole.significato: A bookseller.
parole.testo: From Latin bibliopōla, from Ancient Greek βιβλίον (biblíon, “paper, document, tablet”) + πωλέω (pōléō, “to barter, sell”) — (compare with the etymology of monopoly).

parole.significato: Bookselling.
parole.testo: From bibliopole (“bookseller”) + -poly (suffix denoting sellers in a market). Bibliopole is derived from Latin bibliopōla (“bookseller”), from Ancient Greek βῐβλῐοπώλης (bĭblĭopṓlēs, “bookseller”), from βῐβλῐ́ον (bĭblĭ́on), βυβλίον (bublíon, “book; letter; tablet; strip of papyrus; writing”) (from β

parole.significato: A library.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin bibliothēca, borrowed from Ancient Greek βιβλιοθήκη (bibliothḗkē, “library”). Equivalent to biblio- + -theca. Doublet of bibliotheque.

parole.significato: A librarian.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin bibliothēcārius (“librarian”), from bibliothēca (“library”) + -ārius, from Ancient Greek βῐβλῐοθήκη (bĭblĭothḗkē, “library”), from βῐβλῐ́ον (bĭblĭ́on) + θήκη (thḗkē). Compare French bibliothécaire and Italian and Spanish bibliotecario. By surface analysis, bibliotheca +

parole.significato: A horizontally bedded stratum of fossilized remains of sedentary organisms
parole.testo: bio- (“life”) + Latin stroma (“coverlet”), from Ancient Greek στρῶμα (strôma, “bed, mattress”).

parole.significato: A member of the Bistons or Bistones
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Bistōn, from Ancient Greek Βίστων (Bístōn).

parole.significato: One of the four humours of ancient and mediaeval physiology, that was believed to be secreted by the kidneys and spleen…
parole.testo: Calque of Latin ātra bīlis, itself a calque of Ancient Greek μελαγχολία (melankholía).

parole.significato: Lacking piety or respect for the sacred; resembling blasphemy.
parole.testo: From Latin blasphēmus (“blaspheming”), from Ancient Greek βλάσφημος (blásphēmos, “uttering ill-omened words”), equivalent to blaspheme + -ous.

parole.significato: A true blenny, any of various marine fishes from the suborder Blennioidei or order Blenniiformes that are generally sma…
parole.testo: From Latin blennius, blendius, from Ancient Greek βλέννα (blénna, “mucus, slime”) (whence Modern Greek βλέννα (vlénna)), because of its slimy coating. From Proto-Indo-European *mel- (“soft”).

parole.significato: A type of fruiting body produced by certain fungus species in the order Boletales, especially those of genus Boletus, m…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bōlētus (“edible mushroom”), from Ancient Greek βωλίτης (bōlítēs).

parole.significato: A bolide or fireball (type of meteor)
parole.testo: From Latin bolis, from Ancient Greek βολίς (bolís, “missile, arrow, javelin”). Doublet of bolide.

parole.significato: A buzzing or humming.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bombus.

parole.significato: A bonnacon.
parole.testo: From Latin bonāsus, from Ancient Greek βόνᾱσος (bónāsos).

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or coming from the north.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin boreālis (“northern”), from Boreās, from Ancient Greek Βορέᾱς (Boréās, “personification of the north wind”).

parole.significato: A Mediterranean food fish of the genus Boops, which is a variety of sea bream; a bogue or oxeye.
parole.testo: From Latin bōx, from Ancient Greek βῶξ (bôx, “box (marine fish)”), from βοῦς (boûs, “ox”) + ὤψ (ṓps, “eye, view”), a reference to the large size of the fish's eyes relative to its body.

parole.significato: brachyural
parole.testo: From Latin brachyūrus, from Ancient Greek βραχύουρος (brakhúouros, “short-tailed”), from βραχύς (brakhús, “short”) + οὐρά (ourá, “tail”).

parole.significato: A gill or other organ having the same function.
parole.testo: From Latin branchia, from Ancient Greek βράγχια (bránkhia, “gills”).

parole.significato: A perennial herb of the genus Bryonia, especially the common wild subspecies Bryonia cretica dioica (syn. Bryonia dioic…
parole.testo: From Middle English brionie, from Latin bryōnia (“bryony”), from Ancient Greek βρυωνία (bruōnía, “bryony”), from βρύω (brúō).

parole.significato: Any of several North African antelopes of the genus Alcelaphus.
parole.testo: PIE word  *gʷṓws From Latin būbalus, from Ancient Greek βούβαλος (boúbalos). Doublet of buffalo and buffle.

parole.significato: Any horse used for riding.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Būcephalus, from Ancient Greek Βουκέφαλος, Βουκεφάλας (Bouképhalos, Boukephálas), from βοῦς (boûs, “ox”) + κεφᾰλή (kephălḗ, “head”) + -ᾱς (-ās).

parole.significato: Rustic, pastoral, country-styled.
parole.testo: PIE word  *gʷṓws Borrowed from Latin būcolicus, from Ancient Greek βουκολικός (boukolikós, “rustic, pastoral; meter used by pastoral poets”, literally “pertaining to cowherds”).

parole.significato: The depiction of the head of an ox, as ornamental flourishes in architectural works.
parole.testo: From Latin būcrānium, from Ancient Greek βουκράνιον (boukránion).

parole.significato: The bulb-shaped underground portion of a plant such as a tulip, consisting of a shortened stem and many fleshy scale le…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English bulb, bolbe, from Latin bulbus (“bulb, onion”), from Ancient Greek βολβός (bolbós, “plant with round swelling on underground stem”).

parole.significato: An eating disorder characterized by a binge-and-purge cycle: extreme overeating followed by self-induced vomiting.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin būlīmia, from Ancient Greek βουλῑμῐ́ᾱ (boulīmĭ́ā, “ravenous hunger”), from βοῦς (boûs, “ox”) + λῑμός (līmós, “hunger, famine”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, “-ia”), and Latin nervōsa (“nervous”).

parole.significato: Any of a number of jewel beetles of the family Buprestidae, usually with shiny metallic colours.
parole.testo: Latin buprestis, Ancient Greek a poisonous beetle, which, being eaten by cattle in the grass, caused them to swell up and die; ox, cow + to blow up, swell out.

parole.significato: Made of, or resembling, silk; silken.
parole.testo: From Latin byssinus (“made of byssus”), from Ancient Greek βύσσινος (bússinos, “made of byssus”). See byssus.

parole.significato: The long fine silky filaments excreted by several mollusks (particularly Pinna nobilis) by which they attach themselves…
parole.testo: From Latin byssus, from Ancient Greek βύσσος (bússos, “flax; flax cotton”), from a Semitic source cognate to Hebrew בּוּץ (būṣ, “byssus”) and Aramaic בּוּצָא (būṣā, “byssus”)

parole.significato: A dark shade of purple, close to Tyrian purple and palatinate purple.
parole.testo: From Latin Bȳzantium, from Ancient Greek Βῡζᾰ́ντῐον (Būzắntĭon), named after its legendary founder, Byzas.

parole.significato: Having cachexia; wasting away from a disease or chronic illness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cachecticus.

parole.significato: Compulsion; mania.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cacoēthes, from Ancient Greek κακοήθης (kakoḗthēs, “ill-disposed”) from κακός (kakós, “bad”) + ἦθος (êthos, “disposition, nature”).

parole.significato: Ill-conditioned, malignant; cacoethical.
parole.testo: Latin, from Ancient Greek κακοήθης (kakoḗthēs, “ill-disposed”) (κακός (kakós, “bad”) + ἦθος (êthos, “disposition, nature”)) + -ic

parole.significato: A stylistic affectation of diction, such as throwing in foreign words to appear learned.
parole.testo: From Latin cacozēlia (“a bad, faulty, awkward imitation”), from Ancient Greek κᾰκοζηλία (kăkozēlía, “unhappy imitation, affectation”).

parole.significato: Synonym of calamine, a pink form of zinc oxide.
parole.testo: From Latin cadmia, ultimately from Ancient Greek Καδμεία (Kadmeía), from Κάδμος (Kádmos, “Cadmus”) + -εια (-eia, “-ia: forming related substances”). Doublet of calamine, calaminaris, and lapis calaminaris.

parole.significato: The official wand carried by a herald in ancient Greece and Rome, specifically the one carried in mythology by Hermes,…
parole.testo: Via Latin cādūceus, cādūceum, adaptation of Doric Ancient Greek καρύκειον (karúkeion, “herald’s wand or staff”). This and Attic Greek κηρύκειον (kērúkeion) are derived from κῆρυξ (kêrux, “herald, public messenger”). Related to κηρύσσω (kērússō, “to announce”).

parole.significato: A cavity open at one end (such as the blind end of a duct), especially a blind pouch connected to the large intestine b…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin caecum (“invisible, hidden”), clipping of intestīnum caecum (“blind gut”), translation of Ancient Greek τῠφλὸν ἔντερον (tŭphlòn énteron).

parole.significato: A vase-shaped basket made from reeds or twigs, used in Ancient Greece.
parole.testo: From Latin calathus, from Ancient Greek κάλαθος (kálathos).

parole.significato: An African primate.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin callithrix. First attested in 1572.

parole.significato: Any secondary calcareous deposit, created by the action of water outside the natural cave environment. They are typical…
parole.testo: From Latin calx (“lime”) + Latin < Ancient Greek θέμα (théma, “what is laid down”), (also Mediaeval Latin thema, "deposit") and the Latin -īta < Ancient Greek -ίτης (-ítēs) – used as a suffix indicating a rock or mineral.

parole.significato: Calyx, bud, or cup of a flower or nut.
parole.testo: From Latin calycis, genitive of calyx, from Ancient Greek κάλυξ (kálux, “case of a bud, husk”). By surface analysis, calyc- + -i-.

parole.significato: A bulbous bog orchid of the genus Calypso, Calypso bulbosa
parole.testo: From Latin, itself from Ancient Greek Καλυψώ (Kalupsṓ, “name of a sea nymph”)

parole.significato: The outermost whorl of flower parts, comprising the sepals, which covers and protects the petals as they develop.
parole.testo: From Latin calyx, from Ancient Greek κάλυξ (kálux, “case of a bud, husk”). Doublet of chalice and kelch.

parole.significato: Synonym of giraffe.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin camēlopardus, variant of camēlopardalis, from Ancient Greek καμηλοπάρδαλις (kamēlopárdalis, “giraffe”).

parole.significato: A device for taking still or moving pictures or photographs.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin camera (“chamber or bedchamber”), from Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára, “anything with an arched cover, a covered carriage or boat, a vaulted chamber, a vault”), of Old Iranian origin, from Proto-Iranian *kamarā- (“something curved”), from *kamárati, from Proto-Indo-Iranian

parole.significato: Any of many small canals or ducts in the body, such as in the bone, or in some plants.
parole.testo: From Latin canāliculus (“small channel, pipe or gutter”), diminutive of canālis (“channel; pipe, gutter”), from canna (“cane, reed”), from Ancient Greek κάννα (kánna, “reed”).

parole.significato: Someone with a Cancer star sign.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cancer (“crab”), calque of Ancient Greek Καρκίνος (Karkínos, “crab”), calque of Akkadian 𒀀𒇻𒌅 (allutu, “crab”), from Sumerian 𒀯𒀠𒈜 (ᵐᵘˡAL.LUL, “crab; name of constellation”).

parole.significato: A disease in which the cells of a tissue undergo uncontrolled (often rapid) proliferation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cancer (“crab”), a calque of Ancient Greek καρκίνος (karkínos, “crab; ulcer; cancer”), possibly cognate, applied to cancerous tumors because of a supposed resemblence between their enlarged veins and the legs of a crab. Doublet of canker and chancre.

parole.significato: Synonym of dog days.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin diēs caniculārēs (literally “puppy days”), from Canīcula (“the Puppy”), a semantic loan of Ancient Greek Κῠ́ων (Kŭ́ōn, “the Dog”) in reference to Sirius, which appears in Epic Greek as κῠ́ων Ὠρίωνος (kŭ́ōn Ōríōnos, literally “Orion’s dog”) in its elided accusative form κύν’ Ὠρίωνος (

parole.significato: A tall annual dioecious plant (Cannabis, especially Cannabis sativa), native to central Asia and having alternate, palm…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cannabis (“hemp”), borrowed from Ancient Greek κάνναβις (kánnabis). See there for more. Further reading at Etymology of cannabis on Wikipedia. Doublet of canvas and hemp.

parole.significato: A large drinking cup with two handles.
parole.testo: From Latin cantharus, from Ancient Greek κάνθαρος (kántharos).

parole.significato: Canthus, corner of the eye where the upper and lower lids meet.
parole.testo: From canthus, from Latin canthus (“corner of the eye”), from Ancient Greek κανθός (kanthós, “corner of the eye”). By surface analysis, canth- + -o-.

parole.significato: Either corner of the eye, where the eyelids meet.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin canthus (“corner of the eye”), from Ancient Greek κανθός (kanthós, “corner of the eye”).

parole.significato: The pungent grayish green flower bud of the European and Oriental caper (Capparis spinosa), which is pickled and eaten.
parole.testo: From Latin capparis, from Ancient Greek κάππαρις (kápparis).

parole.significato: Accumulation of wasteful elements of carbon or mere carbon inside blood.
parole.testo: From carbo- + -hæmia, conjunction: Latin carbo (“charcol”) and Ancient Greek αἷμα (haîma, “blood”).

parole.significato: An excessive amount of carbon, particularity carbon dioxide, in the blood.
parole.testo: From carbon + -aemia, conjunction: Latin carbo (“charcol”) and Ancient Greek αἷμα (haîma, “blood”).

parole.significato: An invasive malignant tumour derived from epithelial tissue that tends to metastasize to other areas of the body.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin carcinōma (“tumour; ulcer; carcinoma”), from Ancient Greek κᾰρκῐ́νωμᾰ (kărkĭ́nōmă, “sore, ulcer; cancer”), from καρκινόω (karkinóō, “to make (something) resemble a crab”, in the mediopassive "to become cancerous; to suffer from cancer") + -μᾰ (-mă, action noun suffix). Κ

parole.significato: A piece of body armour—originally a metal breastplate or pair of plates—worn in classical antiquity to protect the regi…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cardiophylax, derived from Ancient Greek καρδία (kardía) + φύλαξ (phúlax).

parole.significato: Synonym of carenum (“reduction of must or sweet wine in ancient European cuisine”).
parole.testo: From Latin carēnum or caroenum, from Ancient Greek κάροινον (károinon), q.v.

parole.significato: A reduction of must or sweet wine produced by boiling it in large kettles until it was reduced by half or two-thirds in…
parole.testo: From Latin carēnum or caroenum, from Ancient Greek κάροινον (károinon), q.v.

parole.significato: The spice made from the bark of members of the genus Cinnamomum other than true cinnamon (C. verum), when they are dist…
parole.testo: From Latin cassia (“cinnamon”), from Ancient Greek κασσία, κασία, κάσια (kassía, kasía, kásia), from Hebrew קְצִיעָה (qəṣīʿā), from Aramaic קְצִיעֲתָא (qəṣīʿătā), from קְצַע (qṣaʿ, “to cut off”). Compare Kezia.

parole.significato: The study of castles.
parole.testo: Based on Latin castellum (“castle, fortress”) and Ancient Greek λόγος (lógos, “word”)

parole.significato: The bitter exudate of the castor sacs of mature beavers, used as a scent mark, and as a tincture in some perfumes.
parole.testo: From Latin castoreum, from Ancient Greek καστόριον (kastórion).

parole.significato: Either of two types of misuse of a word or misapplication of a concept.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin catachrēsis, borrowed from Ancient Greek κατάχρησις (katákhrēsis, “misuse (of a word)”).

parole.significato: A rhetorical device in which a series is arranged in "proper order", particularly
parole.testo: From the Latin form of the Ancient Greek κατακόσμησις (katakósmēsis, “arrangement”).

parole.significato: (said of a line with incomplete meter) lacking a syllable at the end or ending with an incomplete foot.
parole.testo: From Latin catalecticus, from Ancient Greek καταληκτικός (katalēktikós, “leaving off, incomplete”) from κατάληξις (katálēxis).

parole.significato: Semicoma.
parole.testo: From Latin cataphora (“a coma”), from Ancient Greek καταφορά (kataphorá, “a bringing down, a lethargic attack”).

parole.significato: Defensive armour covering the entire body of a soldier and often the soldier's horse as well, especially the linked mai…
parole.testo: From Latin cataphractes (“suit of armour”), from Ancient Greek κατάφρακτος (katáphraktos, “suit of armour”), from κατα- (kata-, prefix indicating a great degree or intensity) + φρακτός (phraktós, “protected; fenced in”) (from φράσσω (phrássō, “to fortify, secure; to fence in”)) + -της (-tēs, suffix

parole.significato: A plaster or poultice, spread over one's skin as medical treatment.
parole.testo: From Latin cataplasma, from Ancient Greek κατάπλασμα (katáplasma).

parole.significato: Religious instruction given orally to catechumens.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin catēchēsis, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek κατήχησις (katḗkhēsis), from κατηχέω (katēkhéō, “sound through, instruct orally, catechise”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to catechesis.
parole.testo: From the Latin catēchēticus, from the Ancient Greek κᾰτηχητῐκός (kătēkhētĭkós), from κᾰτηχητής (kătēkhētḗs, “oral instructor”).

parole.significato: Religious teaching, especially that given to children before confirmation.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin catēchēticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek κατηχητικός (katēkhētikós), from κατηχέω (katēkhéō, “catechize”).
