parole.significato: To give oral instruction, especially of religion; (specifically) by the formal question-and-answer method; in the Churc…
parole.testo: Derived from Latin catēchizāre, from Ancient Greek κατηχίζω (katēkhízō), from κατηχέω (katēkhéō, “to teach (orally)”), from κατά (katá, “down”) + ἠχέω (ēkhéō, “to sound, to resound”).

parole.significato: The chair or throne of a bishop.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cathedra (“seat”), from Ancient Greek καθέδρα (kathédra, “chair of a teacher, throne”), from κατά (katá, “down”) + ἕδρα (hédra, “seat”). Doublet of chair and chaise.

parole.significato: A line perpendicular to a surface (or line); in particular, either of the sides of a right triangle other than its hypo…
parole.testo: From Latin cathetus, from Ancient Greek κάθετος (káthetos, “perpendicular”).

parole.significato: A legendary creature from Ethiopia, said to have the body of a Cape buffalo, scales on its back, and the head of a wild…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin catōblepās, from Ancient Greek κᾰτῶβλεψ (kătôbleps), κᾰτωβλέπων (kătōblépōn), κᾰτώβλεπον (kătṓblepon, “down-looker”), from κᾰτᾰβλέπω (kătăblépō, “to look downwards”, from κᾰτᾰ́ (kătắ) + βλέπω (blépō)).

parole.significato: Great heat, as of the body in fever.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cauma (“heat”), from Ancient Greek καῦμα (kaûma, “heat, especially of the sun”). Probably a doublet of calm.

parole.significato: Capable of burning, corroding or destroying organic tissue.
parole.testo: From the Latin causticus (“burning”), from Ancient Greek καυστικός (kaustikós, “burning”), from καυστός (kaustós, “burnt”) + -ικός (-ikós).

parole.significato: cedar
parole.testo: From the Latin cedrus (“cedar”), from the Ancient Greek κέδρος (kédros, “cedar”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to or located within the abdomen or abdominal cavity.
parole.testo: From Latin coeliacus, from Ancient Greek κοιλιακός (koiliakós), from κοιλία (koilía, “belly”). Cognate with coelom.

parole.significato: A member of one of the ancient peoples of Western Europe called Celtae by the Romans.
parole.testo: From Latin Celtae (singular Celta) from Ancient Greek Κελτοί (Keltoí). English Celts is from the 17th century. Until the mid 19th century, /sɛlt/ is the only recorded pronunciation. A consciously archaizing pronunciation /kɛlt/ was advocated during Irish and Welsh nationalism beginning in the 1850s.

parole.significato: A mythical beast having a horse's body with a man's head and torso in place of the head and neck of the horse.
parole.testo: From Latin centaurus, from Ancient Greek κένταυρος (kéntauros), from Κένταυρος (Kéntauros, “a member of a savage race from Thessaly”).

parole.significato: Synonym of Hecatoncheires.
parole.testo: From Latin centimanus, a calque of Ancient Greek Ἑκατόγχειρες (Hekatónkheires, “the Hundred-Handed”) from centi- (“100”) + manus (“hand”).

parole.significato: central, especially of mass nouns
parole.testo: From centre + -o-, from from Latin centrum, from Ancient Greek κέντρον (kéntron).

parole.significato: Relating to, or affected with, headache.
parole.testo: Latin cephalalgicus, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: A Cepheid variable.
parole.testo: From Latin Cephei + -id, from Latin Cepheus, from Ancient Greek Κηφεύς (Kēpheús).

parole.significato: A white amorphous substance, the insoluble part of cherry gum; meta-arabinic acid.
parole.testo: From Latin cerasus, from Ancient Greek κέρασος (kérasos, “cherry tree”) + -in.

parole.significato: An orchid (Eria compressa).
parole.testo: From Latin cerātium (“carob”), from Ancient Greek κερᾱ́τῐον (kerā́tĭon, “little horn, carob”), diminutive of κέρᾰς (kérăs, “horn”). Doublet of carat, karat, and quilate.

parole.significato: A form of fine-grained quartz that is nearly transparent or has a milky translucence; it fractures conchoidally.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin chalcēdōnius, from Ancient Greek χαλκηδόνιος (khalkēdónios), from Ancient Greek χαλκηδών (khalkēdṓn), cognate to Arabic كَرْكَنْد (karkand).

parole.significato: Synonym of Chalcidian
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Chalcidicus, from Ancient Greek Χαλκιδικός (Khalkidikós).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Chaldea specifically, or ancient Babylonia in general.
parole.testo: From Latin chaldaeus [from Ancient Greek Χαλδαῖος (Khaldaîos)] + -an.

parole.significato: Any ferryman.
parole.testo: From Latin Charōn, from Ancient Greek Χάρων (Khárōn). The name of the moon was coined by American astronomer James W. Christy in 1978, in reference to a fictional moon of Pluto in a novel by Edmond Hamilton but also influenced by its similarity to Char, a pet name for Charlene, his wife's name — hen

parole.significato: A deep, steep-sided rift, gap or fissure; a gorge or abyss.
parole.testo: From Latin chasma, from Ancient Greek χάσμα (khásma, “abyss, cleft”). Doublet of chasma. Compare schism. Displaced native Old English swelh and Old English elh.

parole.significato: A pincer-like claw of a crustacean or arachnid.
parole.testo: From Latin chele, from Ancient Greek χηλή (khēlḗ).

parole.significato: pseudoscorpion
parole.testo: From Latin chēlē (“claw”) (from Ancient Greek χηλή (khēlḗ, “claw”)) + -fer.

parole.significato: A hyrax.
parole.testo: From Latin choerogryllus, from Ancient Greek χοιρογρύλλιος (khoirogrúllios), a compound of χοῖρος (khoîros) and γρῦλος (grûlos), both meaning “pig”. The Greek word was used in the Septuagint to render Hebrew שפן (“hyrax”).

parole.significato: A peninsula.
parole.testo: From Latin Chersonēsus, from Ancient Greek χερσόνησος (khersónēsos, “originally, the Gallipoli peninsula; later, any peninsula”), from χέρσος (khérsos, “dry land”) + νῆσος (nêsos, “island”).

parole.significato: A winged creature attending God and guarding his throne described as a being with four faces (man, lion, ox, and eagle)…
parole.testo: From Middle English cherub, cherube, cherubin, cherubine, cherubym, cherubyn, cherybin, gerubin, jerubin (“angel of the second highest order; depiction of such an angel”), from Old English cerubin, cerubim, ceruphin, cherubin, from Latin cherūbīm, cherūbīn, from Ancient Greek χερουβῑ́μ (kheroubī́m),

parole.significato: A cherub.
parole.testo: From Middle English cherubin, cherubine, cherubym, cherubyn, cherybin, gerubin, jerubin, from Old English cerubin, cerubim, ceruphin, cherubin, from Latin cherūbīn, cherūbīm, from Ancient Greek χερουβίν (kheroubín), χερουβείν (kheroubeín), χερουβίμ (kheroubím), from Hebrew כְּרוּבִים (k'ruvím), from

parole.significato: The twenty-second letter of the Classical and Modern Greek alphabets.
parole.testo: From Latin chī, from Ancient Greek χεῖ (kheî).

parole.significato: An inversion of the relationship between the elements of phrases.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin chiasmus, borrowed from Ancient Greek χιασμός (khiasmós), from χῑᾰ́ζω (khīắzō, “to mark with an X”) + -μός (-mós).

parole.significato: thousand; thousandfold.
parole.testo: From Latin chilias, itself from Ancient Greek χίλιοι (khílioi, “thousand”). Doublet of kilo-.

parole.significato: A regiment of 1000 soldiers, typically commanded by a chiliarch.
parole.testo: From Latin chiliarchia, from Ancient Greek χιλιαρχία (khiliarkhía), from χῑ́λιοι (khī́lioi, “1000”) + -αρχία (-arkhía, “-archy: rule by”). Equivalent to chilia- + -archy.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a chimera.
parole.testo: From chimera, from Latin chimaera, from Ancient Greek χίμαιρα (khímaira, “she-goat”). This term entered English in or around 1638.

parole.significato: Gout in the hand.
parole.testo: From Latin chīragra, from Ancient Greek χειράγρα (kheirágra).

parole.significato: Chironomy.
parole.testo: From Latin chīronomia, from Ancient Greek χειρονομία (kheironomía, “gesticulation”).

parole.significato: An ancient dry measure of two pints or greater.
parole.testo: From Latin choenix, from Ancient Greek χοῖνῐξ (khoînĭx).

parole.significato: Any of several acute infectious diseases of humans and domestic animals, caused by certain strains of the Vibrio choler…
parole.testo: From Latin cholera (“bilious disease”), from Ancient Greek χολέρα (kholéra, “cholera”). Doublet of choler.

parole.significato: A limping iamb.
parole.testo: From Latin choliambus, from Ancient Greek χωλίαμβος (khōlíambos).

parole.significato: A country or suffragan bishop, appointed in the ancient church by a diocesan bishop to exercise episcopal jurisdiction…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin chōrepiscopus, from Ancient Greek χωρεπίσκοπος (khōrepískopos); χώρα (khṓra, “place, country”) + ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos, “overseer, bishop”) (from ἐπί (epí, “on, upon, over”) + σκοπός (skopós, “watcher”)). Compare bishop.

parole.significato: A trochee.
parole.testo: From Latin choreus, from Ancient Greek χορεῖος (khoreîos), related to χορός (khorós, “choir, chorus”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to a choriamb.
parole.testo: Latin choriambicus, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: A metrical foot consisting of four syllables, of which the first and last are long, and the others short; a choreus, or…
parole.testo: From Latin choriambus, from Ancient Greek. Equivalent to choreus + iambus.

parole.significato: Someone who describes a particular region or country.
parole.testo: From Latin chōrographus, from Ancient Greek χωρογράφος (khōrográphos, “describing countries”), from χώρα (khṓra), χῶρος (khôros, “region, country”).

parole.significato: A figure or other artistic depiction of Jesus Christ.
parole.testo: From Middle English Crist, from Old English Crist, from Latin Chrīst(us), from Ancient Greek Χρῑστός (Khrīstós), proper noun use of χρῑστός (khrīstós, “[the] anointed [one]”), a semantic loan of Hebrew מָשִׁיחַ (māšīaḥ, “anointed”) or the Aramaic equivalent (whence ultimately also English messiah, a

parole.significato: A butterfly pupa or the pupal stage of the butterfly lifestyle; (originally) any pupal stage of any insect wherein the…
parole.testo: From Latin chrysalis, variant of chrȳsallis, from Ancient Greek χρυσαλλίς (khrusallís), usually derived from χρυσός (khrusós, “gold, golden”) + -αλλ- + -ις (-is, “-id: forming feminine nouns”) but compare θρυαλλίς (thruallís) and ἀρυβαλλίς (aruballís), both believed to come from a Pre-Greek substrat

parole.significato: A vitreous mineral, often pale green, a mixed oxide of aluminium and beryllium with the chemical formula BeAl₂O₄, used…
parole.testo: From Latin chrysoberyllus, from Ancient Greek χρῡσοβήρυλλος (khrūsobḗrullos, “gold beryl”), from χρυσός (khrusós, “gold”) after its color, and βήρυλλος (bḗrullos, “beryl”), equivalent to chryso- + beryl.

parole.significato: Myrrhis odorata, a plant in the genus Myrrhis, in the family Apiaceae.
parole.testo: From Latin seselis, from Ancient Greek σέσελις (séselis).

parole.significato: A superintendent or keeper of a church's valuables; a churchwarden.
parole.testo: Latin cimeliarcha, from Ancient Greek treasurer.

parole.significato: Any of the mythical people supposed to inhabit a land of perpetual darkness.
parole.testo: From the Latin Cimmerius, from Ancient Greek Κιμμέριος (Kimmérios, “pertaining to the Cimmerii”) + -an.

parole.significato: A soft clayey mineral of whitish or greyish colour.
parole.testo: First attested in 1801; formed as Latin Cimōlia (from the Ancient Greek Κιμωλία γῆ (Kimōlía gê, “earth of Kimolos”) — Cimōlus being the former name of Argentiera) + English -ite.

parole.significato: Synonym of around, about, approximately, particularly used with historical dating.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin circā.

parole.significato: around, surrounding
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin circum-, from circum, from circus. See also circle and circus.

parole.significato: A roundabout or indirect way of speaking; thus
parole.testo: From Latin circumlocūtiō (“the act of speaking around; circumlocution, periphrasis”). By surface analysis, circum- (“around”) + locution (“talk”), thus "getting around (a problem) in speaking or writing". Probably a calque of Ancient Greek περίφρασις (períphrasis, “periphrasis”).

parole.significato: A traveling company of performers that may include acrobats, clowns, trained animals, and other novelty acts, that give…
parole.testo: From Middle English circus, circo, from Latin circus (“ring, circle”), from Ancient Greek κρίκος (kríkos), κίρκος (kírkos, “ring”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to bend, turn”). Doublet of cirque. Cognate with Old English hring (whence English ring) and Old English hringsetl (“circus”, litera

parole.significato: A small receptacle for sacred utensils carried in festivals in Ancient Greece.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cista, from Ancient Greek κίστη (kístē). Doublet of chest.

parole.significato: An ancient Greek stringed instrument, which could be considered a forerunner of the guitar.
parole.testo: From Latin cithara, from Ancient Greek κιθάρα (kithára). Doublet of cither, guitar, kithara, kissar, and zither.

parole.significato: Relating to a cithara or a citharist.
parole.testo: From Latin citharoedicus, from Ancient Greek κιθαρῳδικός (kitharōidikós), from κιθάρα (kithára, “cithara”) + ἀοιδός (aoidós, “singer”).

parole.significato: A woman of great seductive beauty.
parole.testo: From Middle English Cleopatra, from Latin Cleopatra, from Ancient Greek Κλεοπάτρα (Kleopátra), meaning "glory of her father", from κλέος (kléos, “glory”) + πατήρ (patḗr, “father”).

parole.significato: Synonym of water clock, especially (historical) ancient Greek and Roman forms.
parole.testo: From Latin clepsydra, from Ancient Greek κλεψύδρα (klepsúdra), from κλέπτειν (kléptein, “to steal”) + ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”).

parole.significato: stealing, theft
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin clepto-, a combining form of Ancient Greek κλέπτης (kléptēs, “thief”), κλέπτω (kléptō, “to steal”), from Proto-Indo-European *klep- (“to steal”). Doublet of klepto-.

parole.significato: A neume denoting a descending set of three tones.
parole.testo: From Latin clīmax, from Ancient Greek κλῖμαξ (klîmax, “ladder, staircase”), from κλίνω (klínō, “to lean, slant”).

parole.significato: A rhetorical device in which a series is arranged in ascending order.
parole.testo: From Latin clīmax, from Ancient Greek κλῖμαξ (klîmax, “ladder, staircase, [rhetorical] climax”), from κλίνω (klínō, “to lean, slant”).

parole.significato: A particular region defined by its weather or climate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin clima, from Ancient Greek κλίμα (klíma, “(zone of) latitude”, literally “inclination”), from κλίνω (klínō, “to slope, incline”). See also climate.

parole.significato: A muscular spasm with regular contractions.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin clonus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek κλόνος (klónos), meaning a "violent, confused motion."

parole.significato: The final (bottom-most) fused vertebrae at the base of the spine, the tailbone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin coccyx, borrowed from Ancient Greek κόκκῡξ (kókkūx), referring to the curved shape of a cuckoo's beak when viewed from the side.

parole.significato: The complex, spirally coiled, tapered cavity of the inner ear of higher vertebrates, which contains the organ of Corti…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cochlea (“a snail”), from Ancient Greek κόχλιας (kókhlias, “a snail with a spiral shell”).

parole.significato: Any of various types of sea fish or the meat from said fish.
parole.testo: From Middle English cod, codde, of uncertain origin: * Oldest English form cotfich as a surname in the 13th century; for more see cot (“chamber, cottage”). * A bag or pouch, related to its bloated shape; see Etymology 2 below. * From Latin gadus, from Ancient Greek γάδος (gádos, “cod”) with a possib

parole.significato: A handbell used for summoning monks.
parole.testo: From Latin codon, from Ancient Greek κώδων (kṓdōn).

parole.significato: Someone who has coeliac disease.
parole.testo: From Latin coeliacus, from Ancient Greek κοιλιακός (koiliakós), from κοιλία (koilía, “belly”). By surface analysis, coel- + -i- + -ac. Cognate with coelom.

parole.significato: A lotion or liquid wash used as a cleanser for the eyes; an eye-salve.
parole.testo: From Latin collȳrium, from Ancient Greek κολλύριον (kollúrion, “poultice”). Doublet of koulouri.

parole.significato: A viny plant, of species Citrullus colocynthis, native to the Mediterranean Basin and Asia. It produces a lemon-sized,…
parole.testo: From Latin colocynthis, from Ancient Greek κολοκυνθίς (kolokunthís), ultimately Pre-Greek.

parole.significato: The punctuation mark ⟨:⟩.
parole.testo: From Latin cōlon (“a member of a verse of poem”), from Ancient Greek κῶλον (kôlon, “a member, limb, clause, part of a verse”).

parole.significato: Part of the large intestine; the final segment of the digestive system, after (distal to) the ileum and before (proxima…
parole.testo: From Latin cŏlon (“large intestine”), from Ancient Greek κόλον (kólon, “the large intestine, also food, meat, fodder”).

parole.significato: A statue of gigantic size. The name was especially applied to certain famous statues in antiquity, as the Colossus of N…
parole.testo: From Latin colossus, from Ancient Greek κολοσσός (kolossós, “large statue, especially the colossus of Rhodes”), from an unknown Pre-Greek etymon (and erroneously associated with κολοφών).

parole.significato: A person who makes a great discovery.
parole.testo: From Latin columbus (“a dove”). Doublet of Colombo. The common noun and verb are references to the Italian explorer.

parole.significato: Either of two great circles (meridians) that intersect at the poles and either the equinoxes or solstices.
parole.testo: From Latin colurus, ultimately from Ancient Greek κόλουρος (kólouros, “truncated, dock-tailed”).

parole.significato: A cloud of dust surrounding the nucleus of a comet.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin coma (“hair of the head”), borrowed from Ancient Greek κόμη (kómē, “hair of the head”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to comedy, as a literary genre.
parole.testo: From Latin comicus, from Ancient Greek κωμικός (kōmikós, “relating to comedy”), from κῶμος (kômos, “carousal”).

parole.significato: The punctuation mark ⟨,⟩ used to indicate a set of parts of a sentence or between elements of a list.
parole.testo: From Latin comma, from Ancient Greek κόμμα (kómma), from κόπτω (kóptō, “to cut”).

parole.significato: Ordinary; not having any remarkable characteristics.
parole.testo: A calque of Latin locus commūnis, referring to a generally applicable literary passage, itself a calque of Ancient Greek κοινὸς τόπος (koinòs tópos).

parole.significato: A marine gastropod of the family Strombidae which lives in its own spiral shell.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin concha, borrowed from Ancient Greek κόγχη (kónkhē, “a mussel or cockle; a shell-like cavity”). Doublet of concha.

parole.significato: Any of a family of curves defined as the locus of points p, such that each p is on a line that passes through a given f…
parole.testo: From Latin concha (“mussel”) (from Ancient Greek κόγχη (kónkhē)) + -oid or directly from Ancient Greek κογχοειδής (konkhoeidḗs), referring to the curved outline of a mussel shell or anything in this form. By surface analysis, conch + -oid.

parole.significato: A wartlike growth on the skin or a mucous membrane, caused by certain types of HPV viruses, usually occurring in the ge…
parole.testo: From Latin condylōma, from Ancient Greek κονδύλωμα (kondúlōma, “wart”), from κόνδυλος (kóndulos).

parole.significato: A Roman unit of liquid measure reckoned as the volume of 10 Roman pounds of wine and equivalent to about 3.3 L although…
parole.testo: From Latin congius, from Ancient Greek κογχίον (konkhíon), from κόγχη (kónkhē) and κόγχος (kónkhos, “mussel shell”) + -ίον (-íon, “-y: forming diminutives”).

parole.significato: Of the same substance or essence.
parole.testo: From Latin consubstāntiālis, from con- + substāntia (“substance”), translating Ancient Greek ὁμοούσιον (homooúsion).

parole.significato: A living organism that feeds on feces or fecal matter.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin coprophagus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek κοπροφάγος (koprophágos), from κόπρος (kópros, “dung”) + -φάγος (-phágos, “eater; glutton”). Equivalent to copro- + -phage.

parole.significato: A short, vertical, swollen, underground stem of a plant (usually one of the monocots) that serves as a storage organ to…
parole.testo: From scientific Latin cormus, from Ancient Greek κορμός (kormós, “trunk stripped of its boughs”).

parole.significato: Corm.
parole.testo: By surface analysis, corm + -o-, from Latin cormus, from Ancient Greek κορμός (kormós, “trunk stripped of boughs”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to corm or corms.
parole.testo: From corm + -oid, from Latin cornus, from Ancient Greek κορμός (kormós).

parole.significato: A large, round, pendent chandelier, with spikes around its upper rim to hold candles or lamps, usually hung from the ro…
parole.testo: The noun is borrowed from Latin corōna (“crown; garland, wreath”), from Ancient Greek κορώνη (korṓnē, “type of crown; curved object (door handle, tip of a bow, stern of a ship, etc.)”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to turn, bend”). The English word is a doublet of crown, korona, koruna, krona

parole.significato: A member of the family Coronaviridae, comprising viruses which infect animals and human beings, and the genome of which…
parole.testo: From corona (“crown-like circle of light appearing around the sun”) + virus. Corona is derived from Latin corōna (“garland, wreath; crown”), from Ancient Greek κορώνη (korṓnē, “something curved; curved stern of a ship; end, point, tip”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to bend, turn”). The name

parole.significato: A device, curved stroke, or flourish formed with a pen, coming at the end of a book or chapter; a colophon. For example…
parole.testo: From the Latin corōnis, from the Ancient Greek κορωνίς (korōnís, “crasis coronis”, “editorial coronis”); cognate with the French coronis.

parole.significato: The conductor or leader of the chorus of a drama.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin coryphaeus, from Ancient Greek κορυφαῖος (koruphaîos, “leader of the chorus in an Ancient Greek drama”), from κορυφή (koruphḗ, “top of the head, crown”) (possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂- (“head, top; horn”)) + -ῐος (-ĭos, suffix forming adjectives meaning ‘bel

parole.significato: The conductor or leader of the dramatic chorus in Ancient Greece.
parole.testo: From Latin coryphaeus, from Ancient Greek κορυφαῖος (koruphaîos, “leader”), from κορυφή (koruphḗ, “head”).

parole.significato: Inflammation of the mucous membranes lining the nasal cavity, usually causing a running nose, nasal congestion and loss…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin corȳza, from Ancient Greek κόρυζα (kóruza, “nasal mucus”).

parole.significato: An aromatic plant (Tanacetum balsamita), once used to flavour ale (prior to use of hops); also used as a bookmark in Bi…
parole.testo: From Latin costum, from Ancient Greek κόστος (kóstos, “an Oriental aromatic plant”), and Maria (“the Virgin Mary”); only indirectly related to English rosemary.

parole.significato: A perennial tropical herbaceous plant of the genus Costus (family Costaceae).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin costus, from Ancient Greek κόστος (kóstos), from Sanskrit कुष्ठ (kuṣṭha).

parole.significato: A buskin anciently worn by tragic actors on the stage.
parole.testo: From Latin cothurnus, from Ancient Greek κόθορνος (kóthornos). Compare cothurnus.

parole.significato: A buskin used in ancient tragedy.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cothurnus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek κόθορνος (kóthornos).

parole.significato: An ancient game played by throwing wine at metal disks or pans, trying to knock them down or make them sink in a basin…
parole.testo: From Latin cottabus, from Ancient Greek κότταβος (kóttabos).

parole.significato: Each of the patches of villi on the foetal chorion in the placenta of ruminants and some other mammals.
parole.testo: From Latin cotylēdōn, from Ancient Greek κοτυληδών (kotulēdṓn, “cup-shaped cavity”), from κοτύλη (kotúlē, “cup”).

parole.significato: Sickness or indisposition caused by excessive eating or drinking.
parole.testo: From Latin crāpula (“intoxication”), from Ancient Greek κραιπάλη (kraipálē, “intoxication, hangover”).

parole.significato: To form craters in a surface.
parole.testo: First coined 1613, from Latin crātēr (“basin”), from Ancient Greek κρᾱτήρ (krātḗr, “mixing-bowl, wassail-bowl”).

parole.significato: A type of footwear consisting of a sole attached to the foot with fairly elaborate straps, distinguished by the Ancient…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin crepida, from Ancient Greek κρηπίς (krēpís). Doublet of crepis.

parole.significato: A crucial or decisive point or situation; a turning point.
parole.testo: From Latin crisis, from Ancient Greek κρίσις (krísis, “a separating, power of distinguishing, decision, choice, election, judgment, dispute”), from κρίνω (krínō, “pick out, choose, decide, judge”).

parole.significato: A perennial flowering plant (of the genus Crocus in the Iridaceae family). Saffron is obtained from the stamens of Croc…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin crocus, from Ancient Greek κρόκος (krókos, “crocus”), from an ancient Semitic language.

parole.significato: A rich person.
parole.testo: From Latin Croesus, from Ancient Greek Κροῖσος (Kroîsos), from Lydian.

parole.significato: An underground chamber; a crypt, an undercroft.
parole.testo: From Middle English croft, crofte, croufte, crufte (“crypt; vault”), from Old English cruft, from Latin crupta, crypta (“crypt; vault”), from Ancient Greek κρυπτή (kruptḗ), feminine form of κρῠπτός (krŭptós, “concealed, hidden; secret”), from κρύπτω (krúptō, “to conceal, hide; to obscure”) (further

parole.significato: A kind of clapper or castanet used in religious dances by groups in Ancient Greece (including the Korybants) and elsewh…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin crotalum, from Ancient Greek κρόταλον (krótalon, “clapper, castanet, rattle”). Doublet of crotal.

parole.significato: A cave or cavern.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin crypta (“vault”), from Ancient Greek κρυπτός (kruptós, “hidden”). Doublet of grotto.

parole.significato: To make something form into crystals.
parole.testo: From crystal + -ize. The double l reflects the classical stem found in its etyma, Latin crystallus and Ancient Greek κρύσταλλος (krústallos), rather than the simplified spelling of the English base noun. Compare Hellenistic Greek κρυσταλλίζειν (krustallízein, “to shine like crystal”), post‐classical

parole.significato: A Roman unit of liquid measure reckoned as the volume of 1600 Roman pounds of wine and equivalent to about 520 L althou…
parole.testo: From Latin culeus (“large leather sack, punishment of drowning within a sack, unit of bulk liquid measure”), from Ancient Greek κολεός (koleós, “sheath”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to cover”). Doublet of cullion and cojones.

parole.significato: The blending of the culinary arts, food science, and food technology.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin culina (“kitchen”) + Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía, “branch of study, to speak”).

parole.significato: An ancient Roman unit of liquid measure reckoned as the volume of 1⅔ Roman ounce of wine and equivalent to about 45 mL…
parole.testo: From Latin cyathus, from Ancient Greek κύαθος (kúathos, “ladle”), of uncertain origin. Doublet of kyathos.

parole.significato: A one-eyed giant from Greek and Roman mythology.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cyclōps, from Ancient Greek Κύκλωψ (Kúklōps, “Cyclops ['round eyes']”). The sense for copepods is a semantic loan from translingual Cyclops.

parole.significato: curved like the neck of a swan
parole.testo: from Latin cycnēus, from Ancient Greek κύκνειος (kúkneios).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Mount Cyllene in Arcadia.
parole.testo: From Latin Cyllēnius, from Ancient Greek Κυλλήνιος (Kullḗnios), from Κυλλήνη (Kullḗnē).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to cymatics.
parole.testo: First attested in 1828, from Latin cȳmat(is) (“sprout, swelling, hollow sphere”) + -ic, stem of cȳma, from Ancient Greek κῡ́μᾰτος (kū́mătos, “wave, billow, swell, sprout, fetus”), genitive of κῦμα (kûma). Compare the latter cymatics (1966) and the earlier Latin cȳmaticus (1753).

parole.significato: The study of visible effects of sound and vibration.
parole.testo: Coined by Hans Jenny from Latin cȳmat(is) (“sprout, swelling, hollow sphere”) + -ics, stem of cȳma, from Ancient Greek κῡ́μᾰτος (kū́mătos, “wave, billow, swell, sprout, fetus”), genitive of κῦμα (kûma).

parole.significato: A molding on the cornice, above the corona, often having a wavelike form (cyma).
parole.testo: From Latin cȳmatium (“ogee”), from the Ancient Greek κῡμάτιον (kūmátion), the diminutive form of κῦμα (kûma, “wave”). Equivalent to Latin cȳmat(is) (“sprout, swelling, hollow sphere”) + -ium, stem of cȳma, from Ancient Greek κῡ́μᾰτος (kū́mătos, “wave, billow, swell, sprout, fetus”), genitive of κῦμα

parole.significato: An instrument for compounding the resultant of two parallel, simple, harmonic waves.
parole.testo: From Latin cȳmat(is) (“sprout, swelling, hollow sphere”) + -o- + -graph, stem of cȳma, from Ancient Greek κῡ́μᾰτος (kū́mătos, “wave, billow, swell, sprout, fetus”), genitive of κῦμα (kûma). Compare cymograph.

parole.significato: Synonym of cymoscope.
parole.testo: From Latin cȳmat(is) (“sprout, swelling, hollow sphere”) + -o- + -scope, stem of cȳma, from Ancient Greek κῡ́μᾰτος (kū́mătos, “wave, billow, swell, sprout, fetus”), genitive of κῦμα (kûma).

parole.significato: A detector of electromagnetic waves.
parole.testo: First attested as cymatoscope in 1903 and as cymoscope in 1905; formed as cȳm- (the short stem of the Latin cȳma, from the Ancient Greek κῦμα (kûma), kūma, “wave”) + -o- + -scope. Cymatoscope is philologically prescribed in place of cymoscope because it preserves the long stem (κῡμᾰτ- (kūmăt-), kūma

parole.significato: Any disease of the tonsils, throat, or windpipe, typicalling with inflammation, swelling, and difficulty breathing and…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cy̆nanchē, from Ancient Greek κῠνᾰ́γχη (kŭnắnkhē, “a dog's collar, a bad kind of sore throat”). Doublet of quinsy.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to dogs.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cyno-, from the combining form of Ancient Greek κύων (kúōn, “dog”) formed with -ο- (-o-). Cf. cynic. By surface analysis, cyn- + -o-. Piecewise doublet of cano-.

parole.significato: A thin, translucent, usually black fabric, a kind of crape.
parole.testo: From Latin Cyprus, from Ancient Greek Κύπρος (Kúpros).

parole.significato: Like or belonging to the swifts (Cypselidae, now known as the Apodidae.)
parole.testo: Latin cypselus (“a kind of swallow”), from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Of or related to Cyrenaicism, the philosophical school founded by Aristippus of Cyrene and codified by Aristippus the Y…
parole.testo: From Latin Cȳrēnaicus, from Ancient Greek Κῡρηνᾰῐ̈κός (Kūrēnăĭ̈kós), from Κυρήνη (Kurḗnē, “Cyrene”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic”, adjective-forming suffix). Equivalent to Cyrene + -ic or a backformation from Cyrenaica.

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to Cythera, an island now part of Greece, at which the goddess Aphrodite came ashore on a seashell…
parole.testo: From Latin Cytherēius [from Ancient Greek Κυθερήϊος (Kutherḗïos), from Κύθηρα (Kúthēra) + -ήϊος (-ḗïos)] + -an.

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to Cyzicus
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Cȳzicēnus, from Ancient Greek Κυζικηνός (Kuzikēnós). By surface analysis, Cyzicus + -ene.

parole.significato: Cavity of an abdomen.
parole.testo: From Latin coelia, from Ancient Greek κοιλία (koilía, “hollow place”).

parole.significato: A metrical foot of three syllables of the shape | – ⏖ |
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin dactylus, from Ancient Greek δάκτυλος (dáktulos, “finger”), from the three bones of the finger corresponding to three syllables. Doublet of dactylus, date, and (possibly) digit.

parole.significato: Synonym of dactyl (“type of metrical foot”).
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin dactylus. Doublet of dactyl and date.

parole.significato: Skilful, ingenious, cunning.
parole.testo: From Latin daedalus, from Ancient Greek δαίδαλος (daídalos, “skillful”).

parole.significato: In the way of a daimon; befitting a demon; fiendish.
parole.testo: From daimon + -ic; from Latin demon (“spirit”), originally from Ancient Greek δαίμων (daímōn, “a god, goddess, divine power, genius, guardian spirit”). Doublet of demonic.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Damascus.
parole.testo: From Latin Damascēnus, from Ancient Greek Δαμασκηνός (Damaskēnós). By surface analysis, Damascus + -ene. The sense “pertaining to a sudden and complete change in one's beliefs” refers to the conversion of St Paul to Christianity on the road to Damascus.

parole.significato: Any one of the fifty daughters of Danaus.
parole.testo: From the stem of Latin Danais, from Ancient Greek Δαναΐς (Danaḯs), from Δαναός (Danaós, “Danaus”) + -ις (-is), literally “sprung of Danaus”. By surface analysis, Danaus + -id.

parole.significato: A thin layer of vascular contractile tissue that contains smooth muscle fibers but no fat and is situated directly bene…
parole.testo: From Latin dartos, from Ancient Greek δαρτός (dartós, “flayed”), from δέρω (dérō, “to skin, to flay”) + -τός (-tós, adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: Giving birth to a god or goddess.
parole.testo: From Latin deus (“god”) + -parous, calque from Ancient Greek Θεοτόκος (Theotókos, “birth-giver of God”), a traditional title of the Virgin Mary.

parole.significato: Relating to dolphins; delphine.
parole.testo: From Latin delphīnus (“dolphin”), from Ancient Greek δελφίς (delphís, “dolphin”) + -ic.

parole.significato: A temple dedicated to Apollo Delphinios.
parole.testo: From Latin delphīnus (“dolphin”) + -ion, from Ancient Greek δελφίς (delphís, “dolphin”).

parole.significato: The deltoid muscle, a triangular muscle on the human shoulder.
parole.testo: From Latin deltoideus, which was in turn from Ancient Greek adjective δελτοειδής (deltoeidḗs). See also: δέλτα (délta), the fourth letter of the Greek alphabet.

parole.significato: An evil supernatural being.
parole.testo: From Middle English demon, a borrowing from Medieval Latin dēmōn, daemōn (“lar, familiar spirit, guardian spirit”), from Ancient Greek δαίμων (daímōn, “dispenser, god, protective spirit”). Displaced native Old English sċucca (“evil spirit”) and Old English þyrs (“ogre or monster”). Doublet of daimon

parole.significato: Pertaining to demons or evil spirits; demoniac.
parole.testo: From Latin daemonicus, from Ancient Greek δαιμονικός (daimonikós, “possessed by a demon, sent by a demon”), from δαίμων (daímōn), equivalent to demon + -ic. Doublet of daimonic.

parole.significato: Pertaining to or characteristic of Demosthenes, a celebrated Athenian orator (384-322, B.C.), especially famous for his…
parole.testo: From Latin Demosthenicus, from Demosthenes, from Ancient Greek Δημοσθένης (Dēmosthénēs, “a celebrated orator”). The name means "strong with the people", from δῆμος (dêmos, “the people”) + σθένος (sthénos, “strength”).

parole.significato: An arborescent or dendritic agate.
parole.testo: From Latin dendrachates, from Ancient Greek δένδρον (déndron, “tree”) + ἀχάτης (akhátēs, “agate”). By surface analysis, dendr- + achate.

parole.significato: An instrument which, placed against the teeth, conveys sound to the auditory nerve; an audiphone.
parole.testo: From Latin dens, dentis (“tooth”) + Ancient Greek φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound”).

parole.significato: Any resolution to a story that does not pay due regard to the story's internal logic and that is so unlikely that it ch…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin deus ex māchinā (literally “god from a machine [i.e., a device, scaffolding, contrivance]”), a calque of Ancient Greek ἀπὸ μηχανῆς θεός (apò mēkhanês theós).

parole.significato: Two.
parole.testo: PIE word  *dwóh₁ Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *dwi- Proto-Hellenic *dwi- Ancient Greek δῐ- (dĭ-)bor. Latin di-bor. English di- Borrowed from Latin di-, from Ancient Greek δι- (di-, “two”).

parole.significato: Diabetes mellitus; any of a group of metabolic diseases whereby a person (or other animal) has high blood sugar due to…
parole.testo: From Latin diabētēs (“siphon”), from Ancient Greek διαβήτης (diabḗtēs), from Ancient Greek διαβαίνω (diabaínō, “to pass through”).

parole.significato: Synonym of tritone.
parole.testo: From Latin diabolus. Doublet of devil, diable, and diablo.

parole.significato: The process of, or an instance of, identification of the nature and cause of a medical condition or illness.
parole.testo: From Latin diagnōsis, from Ancient Greek διάγνωσις (diágnōsis), from διαγιγνώσκω (diagignṓskō, “to discern”), from διά (diá, “through”) + γιγνώσκω (gignṓskō, “to know”).

parole.significato: Dialectical (of or relating to dialectic)
parole.testo: From Latin dialecticus, from Ancient Greek δῐᾰλεκτῐκός (dĭălektĭkós).

parole.significato: A method of separating molecules or particles of different sizes by differential diffusion through a semipermeable memb…
parole.testo: From Latin dialysis, from Ancient Greek διάλυσις (diálusis). By surface analysis, dia- + -lysis. First use appears c. 1550.

parole.significato: powdered aromatic herbs, sometimes made into little balls and strung together
parole.testo: From Latin diapasma, Ancient Greek διάπασμα (diápasma), ultimately from πάσσω (pássō); compare French diapasme.

parole.significato: The musical octave.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin diapason, from Ancient Greek διαπασῶν (diapasôn), that is διά (diá, “through”) + πασῶν (pasôn, “all”) (χορδῶν (khordôn, “notes”)), “through all (notes)”.

parole.significato: The interval of the fifth or the harmonic ratio 3:2.
parole.testo: From Latin diapente, from Ancient Greek διά (diá, “through, across”) + πέντε (pénte, “five”).

parole.significato: Generating sweat or perspiration.
parole.testo: From Latin diaphorēticus, from Ancient Greek διαφορητικός (diaphorētikós); by surface analysis, diaphor(esis) + -etic.

parole.significato: The interval of a fourth or the harmonic ratio 4:3.
parole.testo: From Latin diatessarōn, from Ancient Greek διά (diá, “through, across”) + τεσσάρων (tessárōn) (genitive plural of τέσσαρες (téssares, “four”)).

parole.significato: Of or relating to education or teaching; didactic.
parole.testo: From Latin didascalicus (“didactic”), from Ancient Greek διδασκαλικός (didaskalikós, “didactic”). See also διδασκαλία (didaskalía, “teaching, instruction”).

parole.significato: Twin, twinned; growing or occurring in pairs.
parole.testo: Modern Latin, from Ancient Greek δίδυμος (dídumos, “twin”).

parole.significato: Relating to diet.
parole.testo: From Latin diaeteticus, from Ancient Greek διαιτητικός (diaitētikós).

parole.significato: A second marriage (as after the death or divorce of a spouse)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin digamia (“twice married”), from Ancient Greek διγαμία (digamía, “bigamy”), δίγαμος (dígamos), from δίς (dís, “twice”) + γάμος (gámos, “marriage”). By surface analysis, di- + -gamy.

parole.significato: Ambiguous or equivocal speech or discourse.
parole.testo: From Latin dilogia, from Ancient Greek διλογία (dilogía, “repetition”), from δίς (dís, “twice”) + -λογία (-logía, “-logy”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Roman emperor Diocletian.
parole.testo: From Latin Dioclētiānus, Latinate form of Ancient Greek Διοκλῆς (Dioklês). The Roman emperor was named so after his home town of Dioclea in Illyricum.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to Dionysus or to the Dionysia.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Dionȳsiacus, from Ancient Greek Διονυσιακός (Dionusiakós), from Δῐόνῡσος (Dĭónūsos, “Dionysus”) + -ακός (-akós).

parole.significato: A unit of measure of the power of a lens or mirror, equal to the reciprocal of its focal length in meters. Myopia is di…
parole.testo: From Latin dioptra, from Ancient Greek διόπτρα (dióptra).

parole.significato: A document issued by an educational institution testifying that the recipient has earned a degree or has successfully c…
parole.testo: PIE word  *dwóh₁ From Latin diplōma, from Ancient Greek δίπλωμα (díplōma, “folded paper, license”), from διπλόω (diplóō, “to double, fold over”), from διπλόος (diplóos, “double”).

parole.significato: A noun which has only two cases.
parole.testo: From Latin diptōtum, from Ancient Greek δίπτωτος (díptōtos), from δί- (dí-) + πτῶσις (ptôsis, “case”).

parole.significato: A round plate-like object that is thrown for sport.
parole.testo: 1656. From Latin discus, from Ancient Greek δίσκος (dískos, “disk, quoit, platter”). Doublet of dais, desk, disc, dish, disk, and diskos.

parole.significato: A double spondee; a metrical foot consisting of four long syllables.
parole.testo: Latin dispondeus, from Ancient Greek [Term?].

parole.significato: A couplet, a two-line stanza making complete sense.
parole.testo: From Latin distichon (“a poem of two verses, a distich consisting of a hexameter and a pentameter”), from Ancient Greek δίστιχον (dístikhon).

parole.significato: In mosquitoes, the distal segment of the gonopods.
parole.testo: From disti-, from Latin distare (“to stand apart”) + Ancient Greek στῦλος (stûlos, “pillar”). By surface analysis, disti- + -style + Latin -us.

parole.significato: A raucous and ardent choral hymn sung in ancient Athens in honor of the god Dionysus.
parole.testo: From Latin dithyrambus, from Ancient Greek δῑθύραμβος (dīthúrambos). According to the American Heritage Dictionary, it is of non-Indo-European origin (Pre-Greek substrate, Illyrian/Phrygian), related to θρίαμβος (thríambos) and ἴαμβος (íambos). Brandenstein also compares Sanskrit अङ्ग (aṅga, “member

parole.significato: A double trochee; a metrical foot made up of two trochees.
parole.testo: Latin ditrochaeus, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: A metrical foot of five syllables used in Greek tragedy for highly anguished scenes. The metrical pattern is typically:…
parole.testo: From Latin dochmius, from Ancient Greek δόχμιος (dókhmios, “oblique; dochmius”).

parole.significato: The days following the heliacal rising of Sirius, now in early August (Gregorian) at dates varying by latitude.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin diēs caniculārēs (“puppy days”), a calque of Ancient Greek κυνάδες ἡμέραι (kunádes hēmérai, “dog days”), from κυνάς (kunás, “of or related to dogs”), from Κῠ́ων (Kŭ́ōn, “the Dog”) in reference to the star Sirius, which appears in Homeric Greek as "Orion's dog". The return of Sirius t

parole.significato: An authoritative principle, belief or statement of opinion, especially one considered to be absolutely true and indispu…
parole.testo: From Latin dogma (“philosophical tenet”), from Ancient Greek δόγμα (dógma, “opinion, tenet”), from δοκέω (dokéō, “to seem good, think”). Treated in the 17th and 18th century as Greek, with plural dogmata. Compare decent.

parole.significato: A carnivorous cetacean, typically with a beak-like snout, famed for their intelligence and occasional willingness to ap…
parole.testo: From Middle English delphyn, from Latin delphīnus, from Ancient Greek δελφίς (delphís), from δελφύς (delphús, “womb”); the modern form in -ol- is probably influenced by the pronunciation of Middle French dauphin. Compare Swedish delfin. Doublet of dauphin. Displaced native Old English mereswīn (lite

parole.significato: Evil intent: malice or fraud.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dolus (“deceit, trickery”); akin to Ancient Greek δόλος (dólos, “bait, ruse”). Compare dolose, dolosity.

parole.significato: A chamber produced by a plant in which insects, mites, or fungi live.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin dōmatium, from Ancient Greek δωμάτιον (dōmátion, “chamber, bedroom”), diminutive of δῶμα (dôma, “house, dwelling place of animals”); akin to δόμος (dómos, “house”).

parole.significato: A canelike grass of southern Europe (Arundo donax), used for fishing rods, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin donax (“reed; also a marine fish”), from Ancient Greek δόναξ (dónax).

parole.significato: Gazella dorcas, a gazelle native to northern Africa and western Asia.
parole.testo: From Latin dorcas from Ancient Greek δορκάς (dorkás) + gazelle.

parole.significato: A spear-bearing soldier (nowadays, a statue of a man holding a spear, or appearing to do so).
parole.testo: From Latin doryphoros, from Ancient Greek [Term?], literally "spear-bearing".

parole.significato: Any of the genus Dracaena of liliaceous plants with woody stems and funnel-shaped flowers.
parole.testo: From the genus name Dracaena, from Latin dracaena, from Ancient Greek δράκαινᾰ (drákaină, “she-dragon”).

parole.significato: Very severe, cruel, or harsh.
parole.testo: From Latin Dracō (stem Dracōn-) + -ian, from Ancient Greek Δράκων (Drákōn), after the Athenian lawmaker Draco, known for making harsh laws. See δράκων (drákōn, “dragon”).

parole.significato: The roots and rhizomes of skunk cabbage, Symplocarpus foetidus
parole.testo: From the genus in which Symplocarpus foetidus was formerly classified, Dracontium, from Latin dracontium (“dragon-wort”), from Ancient Greek δρακόντιον (drakóntion).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the drama.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin drāmaticus. By surface analysis, drama + -tic.

parole.significato: A kind of fruit, with a fleshy exterior, formed from the exocarp and mesocarp, surrounding a hardened endocarp which pr…
parole.testo: Scientific Latin, from Latin drūpa (“wrinkled olive”), from Ancient Greek δρύππᾱ (drúppā).

parole.significato: The veneration of saints, distinguished from latria, the worship of God.
parole.testo: From Latin dulia, from Ancient Greek δουλεία (douleía, “slavery”), from δοῦλος (doûlos, “slave”).

parole.significato: A series comprising two parts, particularly in genre fiction.
parole.testo: Coined based on Latin duo (“two”) + Ancient Greek λόγος (lógos, “word”).

parole.significato: Difficult or laboured breathing.
parole.testo: Variant spelling of dyspnoea, a learned borrowing from Latin dyspnoea (“difficulty breathing”), from Ancient Greek δῠ́σπνοιᾰ (dŭ́spnoiă, “difficulty breathing, shortness of breath”), from δῠ́σπνοος (dŭ́spnoos, “short of breath, breathing with difficulty”, adjective) (also δῠ́σπνους (dŭ́spnous) by co

parole.significato: A hard, dense, deep black wood from various subtropical and tropical trees, especially of the genus Diospyros.
parole.testo: From earlier heben, hebeny, from Middle English ebenif, hebenyf (influenced by Late Latin hebeninus), from Ecclesiastical Latin ebenius (“of ebony”), from Latin hebenus (“ebon tree”), from Ancient Greek ἔβενος (ébenos), from Egyptian hbnj, U13:n-Z4:M3

parole.significato: A picture representing Jesus Christ wearing a crown of thorns, before his crucifixion.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin ecce homō̆ (“behold the man!”). See John 19:5 in the Bible.

parole.significato: The public legislative assembly of the Athenians.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ecclēsia, from Ancient Greek ἐκκλησία (ekklēsía). Doublet of Eccles.

parole.significato: An official of the Eastern Church, equivalent to a sacristan in the Western Church.
parole.testo: Latin ecclesiarcha, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: A member of the Athenian ecclesia (public legislative assembly).
parole.testo: From Middle English ecclesiaste, from Latin ecclēsiastēs, from Ancient Greek ἐκκλησιαστής (ekklēsiastḗs). By surface analysis, ecclesia + -ast.

parole.significato: church
parole.testo: From Latin ecclēsia, from Ancient Greek ἐκκλησία (ekklēsía), + -o-.

parole.significato: A sea urchin.
parole.testo: From Latin echīnus (“hedgehog; sea urchin”), from Ancient Greek ἐχῖνος (ekhînos).

parole.significato: Relating to an eclipse or the ecliptic.
parole.testo: From Middle English ecliptik, from Latin eclīpticus, from Ancient Greek ἐκλειπτικός (ekleiptikós).

parole.significato: A pastoral poem, often in the form of a shepherd's monologue or a dialogue between shepherds.
parole.testo: From Middle English eclog, from Latin ecloga, from Ancient Greek ἐκλογή (eklogḗ, “selection”).

parole.significato: Ecumenical.
parole.testo: From Latin oecūmenicus, from Ancient Greek οἰκουμενικός (oikoumenikós, “concerning ἡ οἰκουμένη (hē oikouménē, “the inhabited (earth)”)”, “the whole (known) world”). Cognate with French œcuménique. By surface analysis, ecumene + -ic.

parole.significato: A non-contagious acute or chronic inflammation of the skin, characterized by redness, itching, and the outbreak of oozi…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin eczema, from Ancient Greek ἔκζεμᾰ (ékzemă, “cutaneous eruption”), from ἐκζέω (ekzéō, “to boil out, break out”) + -μᾰ (-mă, nominal suffix).

parole.significato: Of or from Edessa.
parole.testo: From Latin Edessēnus, from Ancient Greek Ἐδεσσηνός (Edessēnós). By surface analysis, Edessa + -ene.

parole.significato: A Thracian people who dwelt mostly between the Nestus and the Strymon rivers in southern Thrace, but also once dwelt we…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Ēdōnī, from Ancient Greek Ἠδωνοί (Ēdōnoí). Doublet of hedon.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a certain school in Elea of Ancient Greek philosophers who taught that reality is stable and unchangi…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Eleāticus, from Ancient Greek ’Ελεατικός (’Eleatikós), from Ἐλέα (Eléa, “Elea, Velia”).

parole.significato: Amber.
parole.testo: From Latin ēlectrum, from Ancient Greek ἤλεκτρον (ḗlektron).

parole.significato: Any preparation of a medicine mixed with honey or other sweetener in order to make it more palatable to swallow.
parole.testo: From Middle English electuarie, eletuarie, electuary, from Latin electuarium, from Ancient Greek ἐκλείκτον (ekleíkton, “medicine which is licked away”), from ἐκλείχω (ekleíkhō, “to lick up”), from ἐκ (ek, “out, from”) + λείχω (leíkhō, “to lick”). Doublet of lekvar.

parole.significato: That part of an argument on which its conclusiveness depends; that which convinces or refutes an antagonist; a refutati…
parole.testo: Latin elenchus, from Ancient Greek ἔλεγχος (élenkhos, “refutation, scrutiny”); compare Old French elenche. Doublet of elenchus.

parole.significato: A technique of argument associated with Socrates wherein the arguer asks the interlocutor to agree with a series of pre…
parole.testo: From Latin elenchus, from Ancient Greek ἔλεγχος (élenkhos, “refutation, scrutiny, control”). Doublet of elench.

parole.significato: A complication of chronic filariasis, in which nematode worms block the lymphatic vessels, usually in the legs or scrot…
parole.testo: From Latin elephantiasis or directly from Ancient Greek ἐλεφᾰντῐ́ᾱσῐς (elephăntĭ́āsĭs).

parole.significato: A mark consisting of multiple full stops (with or without spaces), used to indicate omitted, missing, or illegible word…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin ellīpsis, from Ancient Greek ἔλλειψις (élleipsis, “omission”). Doublet of ellipse.

parole.significato: a eulogy
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ēlogium (“short saying, inscription”), from Ancient Greek ἐλεγεῖον (elegeîon, “elegy”), from ἔλεγος (élegos, “song, melody”). Doublet of elogy.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Elysian or Elysium, the location.
parole.testo: From Latin Elysium (from Ancient Greek Ἠλύσιον (Ēlúsion, “Elysium; one of the Elysian Fields”)) + -an (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A mineral consisting of silver chloride and silver bromide; a variety of bromian chlorargyrite.
parole.testo: From Latin embolus (“piston”), from Ancient Greek ἔμβολος (émbolos, “peg, wedge, stopper”).

parole.significato: An obstruction causing an embolism: a blood clot, air bubble or other matter carried by the bloodstream and causing a b…
parole.testo: The term was coined in 1848 by Rudolf Virchow From Latin embolus (“piston”), from Ancient Greek ἔμβολος (émbolos, “peg, stopper”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Emesa or its region.
parole.testo: From Latin Emesēnus, from Ancient Greek Ἐμεσηνός (Emesēnós).

parole.significato: Special weight or forcefulness given to something considered important.
parole.testo: From Latin emphasis, from Ancient Greek ἔμφασις (émphasis, “significance”), from ἐμφαίνω (emphaínō, “to present; to indicate”), from ἐν- (en-, “in”) + φαίνω (phaínō, “to show”).

parole.significato: To stress, give emphasis or extra weight to (something).
parole.testo: Latin, from Ancient Greek – see emphasis. By surface analysis, emphasis + -ize.

parole.significato: Having the quality of closing the pores of the skin.
parole.testo: From Latin emphracticus, from Ancient Greek ἐμφρακτικός (emphraktikós), from ἐμφράσσω (emphrássō), from ἐν- (en-) + φράσσω (phrássō).

parole.significato: A right to enjoyment of property with a given stipulation that the property will be improved or maintained in an agreed…
parole.testo: From Latin emphyteusis, from Ancient Greek ἐμφύτευσις (emphúteusis, “tenure of a type of leasehold”).

parole.significato: Empirical.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin empiricus, from Ancient Greek ἐμπειρῐκός (empeirĭkós, “experienced”), from ἐμπειρία (empeiría, “experience, mere experience or practice without knowledge, especially in medicine, empiricism”), from ἔμπειρος (émpeiros, “experienced or practised in”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + πεῖρα (pe

parole.significato: A city or region which is a major trading centre; also, a place within a city for commerce and trading; a marketplace.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin emporium (“trading station; business district in a city; market town”), from Ancient Greek ἐμπόριον (empórion, “factory, trading station; market”), from ἔμπορος (émporos, “merchant, trader; traveller”) + -ιον (-ion, suffix forming nouns). ἔμπορος is derived from ἐμ- (em-) (varian

parole.significato: A phantom; ghost; spectre.
parole.testo: Latin empusa, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the highest heaven or the empyrean.
parole.testo: From Latin empyreus, from Ancient Greek ἐμπύριος (empúrios, “fiery”), from ἐν (en, “en-”) + πῦρ (pûr, “fire”) (English pyre).

parole.significato: The highest heaven, supposed by the ancients to be a region of pure light and fire or else composed of ether, and somet…
parole.testo: From Latin empȳreus, from Ancient Greek ἐμπύριος (empúrios), from ἐν (en, “in”) + πῦρ (pûr, “fire”) (whence English pyre).

parole.significato: Containing the combustible principle of coal.
parole.testo: From Latin empyricus, from Ancient Greek ἐμπύριος (empúrios, “fiery”), from ἐν (en, “en-”) + πῦρ (pûr, “fire”).

parole.significato: Ambitious or competitive.
parole.testo: From Middle English emulous, from Latin aemulus (“striving to equal or excel, rivaling; in a bad sense, envious, jealous”) + -ous, from Ancient Greek ἁμιλλάομαι (hamilláomai, “strive, contend”), akin to Latin imitari (“to imitate”); see imitate.

parole.significato: Vivid, lively description.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin enargīa, from Ancient Greek ἐνάργεια (enárgeia, “sensory vividness”).

parole.significato: The eight days of celebration for the dedication of the church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem.
parole.testo: From Latin encaenia, from Ancient Greek ἐγκαίνια (enkaínia, “a festival of renewal or dedication”).

parole.significato: A festival held to mark the anniversary of the dedication of a church or temple; (especially), of the Temple at Jerusal…
parole.testo: From Latin encaenia, from Ancient Greek (τὰ) ἐγκαίνια ((tà) enkaínia, “dedication festival”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + καινός (kainós, “new”).

parole.significato: Warm praise, especially a formal expression of such praise; a tribute.
parole.testo: From Latin encōmium (“praise, eulogy”), from Ancient Greek ἐγκώμιον (enkṓmion, “laudatory ode, praise”), from ἐγκώμιος (enkṓmios, “of or pertaining to the victor”), from κῶμος (kômos, “festival, revel, ode”).

parole.significato: One of an ascetic 2nd-century sect of Christians who forbade marriage and counselled abstinence from meat.
parole.testo: Latin Encratitae (plural) from Ancient Greek ἐγκρατής (enkratḗs, “self-disciplined”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + κρᾰ́τος (krắtos, “strength”).

parole.significato: A person possessed by an evil ghost, spirit, or entity.
parole.testo: From Latin energumenus, from Ancient Greek ἐνεργούμενος (energoúmenos), from verb ἐνεργέω (energéō, “to influence”).

parole.significato: The commander of an enomoty.
parole.testo: From Latin enōmotarcha, from Ancient Greek ἐνωμοτάρχης (enōmotárkhēs).

parole.significato: A slight convex curvature introduced into the shaft of a column for aesthetic reasons, or to compensate for the illusio…
parole.testo: From Latin entasis, from Ancient Greek ἔντασις (éntasis, “tension, straining”), from ἐντείνω (enteínō, “to stretch or strain tight”).

parole.significato: Divinely inspired.
parole.testo: From Latin entheātus (“divinely inspired”), from Ancient Greek ἔνθεος (éntheos, “inspired, possessed by (a) god”) + -ātus.

parole.significato: Involuntary urination: urinary incontinence.
parole.testo: From Latin enuresis, from Ancient Greek ἐνούρησις (enoúrēsis); surface analysis parses uresis as a constituent.

parole.significato: Any effect of wind on land.
parole.testo: Likely from Eolus (“god of wind”), Aeolian (“relating to Eolus”), or aeolo- (“of woodwind instruments”), all via Latin Aeolus from Ancient Greek Αἴολος (Aíolos), plus -ation, a suffix denoting a process or the result of a process.

parole.significato: Of the wind; referring to the action or the power of wind.
parole.testo: From Latin Aeolicus, from Ancient Greek Αἴολος (Aíolos, “Aeolus, god of the winds”).

parole.significato: Eternity, the duration of the universe.
parole.testo: From Latin aeon, from Ancient Greek αἰών (aiṓn, “age, era”).

parole.significato: The adducing of particular examples so as to lead to a universal conclusion; the argument by induction.
parole.testo: From Latin epagōgē, from Ancient Greek ἐπᾰγωγή (epăgōgḗ, “a bringing in”). See epact.

parole.significato: A figure of speech by which the same word is used both at the beginning and at the end of a sentence.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin epanadiplōsis, from Ancient Greek ἐπαναδίπλωσις (epanadíplōsis, “doubling, folding”).

parole.significato: The repetition of the same word or clause after intervening matter.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin epanalepsis, from Ancient Greek ἐπανάληψις (epanálēpsis), from ἐπαναλαμβάνω (epanalambánō), from ἐπί (epí) + ἀνά (aná) + λαμβάνω (lambánō).

parole.significato: anaphora
parole.testo: Latin, from Ancient Greek ἐπαναφορά (epanaphorá, “reference”).

parole.significato: An 18- to 20-year-old man in ancient Greece undergoing military training.
parole.testo: Via Latin ephēbus, from Ancient Greek ἔφηβος (éphēbos, “adolescent”), from ἐπί (epí, “early”) + ἥβη (hḗbē, “manhood”), late 19th c.

parole.significato: Synonym of freckle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ephēlis, from Ancient Greek ἔφηλῐς (éphēlĭs, “a freckle”), from ἐπ- (ep-, “upon, over, epi-”) + ἥλῐος (hḗlĭos, “the sun”) + -ῐς (-ĭs, nominal suffix).

parole.significato: A depression in the sphenoid bone; the pituitary fossa.
parole.testo: From Latin ephippium (“saddlecloth”), from Ancient Greek ἐφίππιον (ephíppion), from ἐπῐ́ (epĭ́) + ἵππος (híppos, “horse”).

parole.significato: An allegiant of the Israelite tribal patriarch Ephraim, a member of the tribe purportedly descended from him, or an inh…
parole.testo: An adaptation of the Latin Ephraimītēs, Ephraimīta, from the Ancient Greek Ἐφραιμῑ́tης (Ephraimī́tēs), from Ἐφραίμ (Ephraím, “Ephraim”) + -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs, “one connected to, a member of”). Equivalent to Ephraim + -ite.

parole.significato: The layer of tissue between the pericardium and the heart.
parole.testo: New Latin, from Latin epi- (“over”) + Ancient Greek καρδία (kardía, “heart”). Attested in English from the 19th century.

parole.significato: An elegy; an ode to someone deceased.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin epicēdīon, from Ancient Greek ἐπικήδειον (epikḗdeion), neuter singular form of ἐπικήδειος (epikḗdeios), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + κῆδος (kêdos, “care”). Doublet of epicedium.

parole.significato: A syllogism in which the proof of the major or minor premise, or both, is introduced with the premises themselves, and…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐπιχείρημα (epikheírēma).

parole.significato: The pattern of cell wall thickening which forms the ornamentation on spores of certain types of mushroom (especially of…
parole.testo: From Latin cŏrĭum ("skin") with the Ancient Greek prefix ἐπί- ("on top of").

parole.significato: A small circle whose centre is on the circumference of a larger circle; in Ptolemaic astronomy it was seen as the basis…
parole.testo: From Latin epicyclus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίκυκλος (epíkuklos), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + κύκλος (kúklos, “circle”). The ad hoc complication sense is a generalization from the archetype supplied by the Ptolemaic astronomy sense.

parole.significato: The outer, protective layer of the skin of vertebrates.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin epidermis, from Ancient Greek ἐπιδερμίς (epidermís), ἐπί (epí, “on top of”) + δέρμα (dérma, “skin”). Equivalent to epi- + dermis.

parole.significato: An exclamation or reflection used to summarise or round off an argument or discourse.
parole.testo: From Latin epiphonema, from Ancient Greek ἐπιφώνημα (epiphṓnēma), from ἐπιφωνείν (epiphōneín, “call to”).

parole.significato: A rhetorical device where a sequence of rhetorical questions is used to criticise or blame, or more generally, to elici…
parole.testo: From Latin epiplexis (“rebuke”), from Ancient Greek ἐπίπληξις (epíplēxis, “rebuke”), from ἐπιπλήσσω (epiplḗssō, “to chastise”), from ἐπι- (epi-, “upon”) (see epi-) + πλήσσω (plḗssō, “to strike”).

parole.significato: A figure of speech by which one striking circumstance is added, in due gradation, to another; escalation to a climax.
parole.testo: From Latin epiplocē (“(rhetoric) connection”), from Ancient Greek ἐπιπλοκή (epiplokḗ, “plaiting together”), from ἐπιπλέκω (epiplékō, “to interweave”), from ἐπι- (epi-, “upon”) (see epi-) + πλέκω (plékō, “to plait”).

parole.significato: A literary composition in the form of a letter or series of letters, especially one in verse.
parole.testo: PIE word  *h₁epi The noun is derived from Middle English epistel, epistole, pistel (“letter; literary work in letter form; written legend or story; spoken communication; (Christianity) one of the letters by an apostle in the New Testament; extract from such a letter read as part of the Mass”) [and o

parole.significato: Of or relating to letters, or the writing of letters.
parole.testo: 1627, from Latin epistolārius, from epistola (“letter”) (English epistle) + -ārius, from Ancient Greek ἐπιστολή (epistolḗ) from ἐπιστέλλω (epistéllō, “to send a message”) from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + στέλλω (stéllō, “to prepare, send”). For the noun, compare Middle English pistelarie and Old English pis

parole.significato: Relating to letters or epistles, or in the form or style of them
parole.testo: From Latin epistolicus, from Ancient Greek ἐπιστολικός (epistolikós, “suited to or in the style of a letter”).

parole.significato: The study of letters and epistles.
parole.testo: From Latin epistola or its etymon Ancient Greek ἐπῐστολή (epĭstolḗ) + -ology.

parole.significato: The repetition of the same word or words at the end of successive phrases, clauses or sentences.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin epistrophē, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐπιστροφή (epistrophḗ).

parole.significato: A massive piece of stone or wood laid immediately on the abacus of the capital of a column or pillar; an architrave.
parole.testo: Latin epistylium, Ancient Greek: compare French épistyle.

parole.significato: A song or poem celebrating a marriage.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin epithalamium, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐπιθαλάμιον (epithalámion, “bridal song”), neuter form of ἐπιθαλάμιος (epithalámios), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + θάλαμος (thálamos, “inner chamber, wedding chamber”).

parole.significato: A figure by which permission is either seriously or ironically granted to someone to do what he or she proposes to do,…
parole.testo: From Latin epitrope, from Ancient Greek ἐπιτροπή (epitropḗ, “reference, arbitration”), from ἐπιτρέπω (epitrépō).

parole.significato: A person who gave or supposedly gave their name to a people, place, institution, etc.
parole.testo: From Latin eponymus, from Ancient Greek ἐπώνῠμος (epṓnŭmos), from ἐπί (epí, “upon, epi-”) + ὄνυμα (ónuma, “name”) + -ος (-os, suffix forming adjectives and nouns). Equivalent to epi- + -nym.

parole.significato: An epic.
parole.testo: From Latin epos, from Ancient Greek ἔπος (épos, “word, song, epic”).

parole.significato: Erotic literature, art, decoration, or other such work.
parole.testo: From neuter plural of Latin eroticus (“amatory”), from Ancient Greek ἐρωτικός (erōtikós). By surface analysis, erotic + -ica.

parole.significato: Causing an increase in mucus within the nose, and hence causing one to sneeze.
parole.testo: From Latin errhīnum, from Ancient Greek ἔρρινον (érrhinon), from ἐν (en, “in”) + ῥίς (rhís, “nostril”).

parole.significato: The root of sea holly, Eryngium maritimum, formerly candied and taken as confectionery and held to have aphrodisiac pro…
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin ēryngion, from Ancient Greek ἠρύγγιον (ērúngion), from ἤρυγγος (ḗrungos).

parole.significato: An acute, sometimes recurrent febrile disease caused by infection of a hemolytic streptococcus, associated with intense…
parole.testo: From Middle English erisipila, borrowed from Latin erysipelas, from Ancient Greek ἐρῠσῐ́πελᾰς (erŭsĭ́pelăs), probably related to ἐρῠθρός (erŭthrós, “red”) and πέλμᾰ (pélmă, “the sole of a foot”).

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to Erythrae
parole.testo: From Latin Erythraeus (from Ancient Greek Ἐρυθραῖος (Eruthraîos)) + -an.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Erythraean Sea
parole.testo: From Latin erythraeus (“reddish”) (as it was used in Erythraeum mare (“the Erythraean Sea”), from Ancient Greek ἐρυθρός (eruthrós, “red”)) + -an.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a dry north wind which blows in the eastern Mediterranean.
parole.testo: From Latin etesius (“annual”), from Ancient Greek ἐτήσιος (etḗsios, “annual”), from ἔτος (étos, “year”).

parole.significato: The substance formerly supposed to fill the upper regions of the atmosphere above the clouds, in particular as a medium…
parole.testo: From Middle English ēther (“the caelum aetherum of ancient cosmology in which the planets orbit; a shining, fluid substance described as a form of air or fire; air”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman ether and Middle French ether, ethere, aether, from Old French aether (“highest and purest part of the atm

parole.significato: Pertaining to the presupposition of an invisible air-like element permeating all of space, or to the higher regions bey…
parole.testo: From Latin aetherius (“of or pertaining to the ether, the sky, Heaven or the air or upper air”), from Ancient Greek αἰθέριος (aithérios, “of or pertaining to the upper air”). By surface analysis, ether + -ial.

parole.significato: Formed of ether; ethereal.
parole.testo: Latin aethereus, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of Ethiopia.
parole.testo: From Latin Aethiops from Ancient Greek Αἰθίοψ (Aithíops, “charred complexion”).

parole.significato: Ethiopian
parole.testo: From Latin aethiopicus, from Ancient Greek Αἰθιοπικός (Aithiopikós). By surface analysis, Ethiop + -ic.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a group of people having common racial, ancestral, national, religious or cultural origins.
parole.testo: From Middle English ethnik, from Latin ethnicus ("pagan", "heathen"), from Ancient Greek ἐθνικός (ethnikós, “of or for a nation, heathen”), from ἔθνος (éthnos, “a company", later "a people or nation, heathens”). By surface analysis, ethno- + -ic.

parole.significato: The scientific study of animalian behavior, especially that of nonhuman animals.
parole.testo: From the Latin ēthologia (“the art of depicting or imitating character”), from the Ancient Greek ἠθολογία (ēthología, “painting of character, especially by mimic gestures”), from ἠθολόγος (ēthológos, “painting character by mimic gestures”), from ἦθος (êthos, “character, especially moral character”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to Etna, a volcano in Sicily.
parole.testo: From Latin Aetnaeus, from Ancient Greek Αἰτναῖος (Aitnaîos), from Αἴτνη (Aítnē) + -αῖος (-aîos), equivalent to Etna + -ean.

parole.significato: Synonym of Euboean.
parole.testo: From Latin Euboicus, from Ancient Greek Εὐβοϊκός (Euboïkós). By surface analysis, Euboea + -ic.

parole.significato: applause
parole.testo: From Latin euge, from Ancient Greek εὖγε (eûge).

parole.significato: The belief that legends and mythology arise from exaggerated descriptions of historical people and events.
parole.testo: From Euhemerus + -ism, ultimately from Latin Euhēmerus, from Ancient Greek Εὐήμερος (Euḗmeros), an ancient Greek Sicilian Skeptic who proposed most or all mythology derived from historical figures and natural events which received supernatural characteristics only through retelling.

parole.significato: Someone who practices or upholds euhemerism, a person who believes all or most myths and legends arose from historical…
parole.testo: From euhemerism + -ist, from Latin Euhemerus, from Ancient Greek Εὐήμερος (Euḗmeros), an ancient Greek Sicilian Skeptic who proposed most or all mythology derived from historical figures and natural events which received supernatural characteristics only through retelling.

parole.significato: Of or relating to euhemerism.
parole.testo: From euhemerist + -ic, from euhemerism, from Latin Euhemerus, from Ancient Greek Εὐήμερος (Euḗmeros), an ancient Greek Sicilian Skeptic who proposed most or all mythology derived from historical figures and natural events which received supernatural characteristics only through retelling.

parole.significato: The fanciful invention of plausible historical figures and events as an attempt to rationalize mythology and legends
parole.testo: From euhemerize + -ation, ultimately from Latin Euhēmerus, from Ancient Greek Εὐήμερος (Euḗmeros), an ancient Greek Sicilian Skeptic who proposed most or all mythology derived from historical figures and natural events which received supernatural characteristics only through retelling.

parole.significato: To invent a plausible but fanciful historical origin for something in order to rationalize mythology and legends.
parole.testo: From euhemerism + -ize, ultimately from Latin Euhēmerus, from Ancient Greek Εὐήμερος (Euḗmeros), an ancient Greek Sicilian Skeptic who proposed most or all mythology derived from historical figures and natural events which received supernatural characteristics only through retelling.

parole.significato: The practice of sending the consecrated Eucharist to those not present, or the Eucharist itself so sent.
parole.testo: From Latin eulogia, from Ancient Greek εὐλογῐ́ᾱ (eulogĭ́ā).

parole.significato: An oration to honor a deceased person, usually at a funeral.
parole.testo: From Latin eulogium, apparently from a confusion between ēlogium (whence English elogium, elogy) and eulogia (from Ancient Greek εὐλογία (eulogía, “praise”), whence English eulogia); equivalent to eu- + logia ("good words"). Doublet of eulogium.

parole.significato: A castrated man.
parole.testo: From Middle English eunuk, from Middle French eunuque, from Latin eunūchus, from Ancient Greek εὐνοῦχος (eunoûkhos), from εὐνή (eunḗ, “bed”) + ἔχω (ékhō, “to have, keep”). Originally probably used to refer to a bed chamber attendant.

parole.significato: An acrid dull yellow or brown resin consisting of the concreted milky juice of several species of Euphorbia, formerly u…
parole.testo: From Latin euphorbium, from Ancient Greek εὐφόρβιον (euphórbion), from Εὔφορβος (Eúphorbos, “Euphorbus, physician to the Mauretanian king Juba II”) + -ιον (-ion, “related to”). The name is from εὔφορβος (eúphorbos, “well-fed”), from εὖ (eû, “well”) + φορβή (phorbḗ, “food, fodder”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Euripides (an ancient Greek tragedian).
parole.testo: Latin Eurīpidēus (from the Ancient Greek Εὐρῑπῐ́δειος, from Εὐρῑπῐ́δης, whence Euripides) + English -an

parole.significato: A strait; a narrow tract of water, where the tide or a current flows and reflows with violence, like the ancient firth…
parole.testo: From Latin eurīpus, from Ancient Greek εὔριπος (eúripos); from εὖ (eû, “well”) + ῥιπή (rhipḗ, “rushing motion”).

parole.significato: The east wind.
parole.testo: From Middle English Eurus, ewrus, from Latin eurus, from Ancient Greek εὖρος (eûros).

parole.significato: One who is comparable to Eusebius of Caesarea; an ecclesiastic historian.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Eusebius, borrowed from Ancient Greek Εὐσέβιος (Eusébios), from εὐσεβής (eusebḗs) + -ῐος (-ĭos).

parole.significato: A widespread rash usually occurring in children.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin exanthema, from Ancient Greek ἐξάνθημα (exánthēma), from ἐξανθέω (exanthéō), from ἐξ (ex) + ἄνθος (ánthos, “flower”).

parole.significato: departure; exodus, especially the exodus of the Israelites from Egypt
parole.testo: From Latin exodium, from Ancient Greek ἐξόδιον (exódion).

parole.significato: A sudden departure of a large number of people.
parole.testo: From Latin exodus, from Ancient Greek ἔξοδος (éxodos, “expedition, procession, departure”). Doublet of exodos. From late Old English only as a proper noun, Exodus, the biblical book; use as a common noun is from the early 17th century.

parole.significato: The act of bewitching, or enchanting
parole.testo: From Latin fascinare ("to bewitch"), possibly from Ancient Greek βασκαίνιεν (baskaínien, “to speak ill of; to curse”). Morphologically fascinate + -ion.

parole.significato: A transparent form of marble or alabaster, formerly sometimes used for windows.
parole.testo: Like phengite from Latin phengites, from Ancient Greek φέγγος (phéngos). Superficially contains -ite.

parole.significato: A kind of medieval reliquary or shrine containing the sacred effigies and relics of a saint.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin feretrum, from Ancient Greek φέρετρον (phéretron). Doublet of feretory.

parole.significato: Forms of pronouns or verbs used for the speaker or writer of the sentence in which they occur.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin prīma persōna, itself a calque of Ancient Greek πρῶτον πρόσωπον (prôton prósōpon). Displaced native Old English forma had, literally, "form hade".

parole.significato: Resembling the genus Fistularia (cornetfishes); having a long, tubular body.
parole.testo: From Fistulari(a) (“genus of cornetfishes”) + -oid (“resembling”), from Latin fistula (“pipe, tube”) and Ancient Greek εἶδος (eîdos, “form, likeness”). By surface analysis, fistule + -arioid.

parole.significato: An operation to create a surgical connection between a fistula and the intestine.
parole.testo: From fistulo- (“fistula”) + entero- (“intestine”) + -stomy (“mouth, surgical connection”), from Latin fistula (“pipe, tube”), Ancient Greek ἔντερον (énteron, “intestine”), and Ancient Greek στόμα (stóma, “mouth”).

parole.significato: A carotenoid pigment found in the chloroplasts of brown algae.
parole.testo: From Latin fūcus (from Ancient Greek φῦκος (phûkos, “seaweed”)) + ξανθός (xanthós, “yellow”) + -in.

parole.significato: An ancient Berber tribe inhabiting Gaetulia.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Gaetūlī, from Ancient Greek Γαίτουλοι (Gaítouloi).

parole.significato: A bitter, aromatic resin or gum, extracted from plants of the genus Ferula, that resembles assafoetida and has been use…
parole.testo: From Latin galbanum (“galbanum”), from Ancient Greek χαλβάνη (khalbánē, “galbanum”).

parole.significato: A physician.
parole.testo: From Middle English Galen, from Latin Galēnus, from Ancient Greek Γαληνός (Galēnós), from γαλήνη (galḗnē, “calm, tranquillity”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Galilee, or a native or inhabitant thereof.
parole.testo: Originated 1605–15 from Latin Galilaeus [from Ancient Greek Γαλιλαῖος (Galilaîos)] + -an.

parole.significato: A verse consisting of four Ionics a minore, with variations and substitutions.
parole.testo: From Latin Galli + iambus. Used by the Galli, priests of the Phrygian goddess Cybele. The first element, Ancient Greek γάλλος (gállos), was said by Ovid to be named after a Phrygian river.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the river Ganges.
parole.testo: From Latin Gangēticus, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek Γαγγητικός (Gangētikós), from Γάγγης (Gángēs, “(River) Ganges”).

parole.significato: a gargle; a liquid used to gargle with.
parole.testo: From Latin gargarisma, from Ancient Greek γαργάρισμα (gargárisma).

parole.significato: To gargle (rinse or wash mouth and throat).
parole.testo: From Latin gargarizo, from Ancient Greek γαργαρίζω (gargarízō).

parole.significato: A fermented fish sauce popular as a condiment in Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: From Latin garum, from Ancient Greek γάρον (gáron, “the fish whose intestines were originally used in the condiment's production”).

parole.significato: A tribe of Scythia settled near the river Borysthenes
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Gelōnī, from Ancient Greek Γελωνοί (Gelōnoí).

parole.significato: Someone who has the Gemini star sign.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin geminī, plural of geminus (“twin”), calque of Ancient Greek Δίδυμοι (Dídumoi), calque of Akkadian 𒀯𒈠𒀸 (māšu), calque of Sumerian 𒀯𒈦𒋰𒁀 (ᵐᵘˡMAŠ.TAB.BA, “the Divine Twins, in Mesopotamia identified as Lugal-irra and Meslamta-ea; name of constellation”). See Lugal-irra and Meslamta-e

parole.significato: The origin, start, or point at which something comes into being.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin genesis (“generation, nativity”), from Ancient Greek γένεσις (génesis, “origin, source, beginning”). Related to Ancient Greek γίγνομαι (gígnomai, “to be produced, become, be”). Doublet of kind, gens, and jati.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the casting of horoscopes at a person's birth
parole.testo: From Latin genethliacus, from Ancient Greek γενεθλιακός (genethliakós, “belonging to a birthday”).

parole.significato: A birthday ode.
parole.testo: Via Latin genethliacon from Ancient Greek γενεθλιακόν (genethliakón, “of or related to a birthday”, neuter sg.).

parole.significato: Any of various herbs of the family Gentianaceae found in temperate and mountainous regions with violet or blue flowers.
parole.testo: Via Middle English from Latin gentiāna, which, according to Pliny the Elder, was named after Gentius (Ancient Greek Γένθιος (Génthios)), the last king of Illyria, who supposedly discovered the plant's medicinal benefits. This has been dismissed as folk etymology but the word may still ultimately be

parole.significato: Of or relating to geometry.
parole.testo: From Latin geōmetricus, from Ancient Greek γεωμετρικός (geōmetrikós), from γεωμέτρης (geōmétrēs). By surface analysis, geometer + -ic or geo- + -metric.

parole.significato: radiotelephony clear-code word for the letter G.
parole.testo: Name of an early saint, from Middle English George, from Latin Geōrgius, from Ancient Greek Γεώργῐος (Geṓrgĭos), from γεωργός (geōrgós, “farmer, earth worker”), from γῆ (gê, “earth”) (combining form γεω- (geō-)) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”) Doublet of Jorge and Geevarghese.
