The aircraft autopilot sense i

parole.significato: Any flowering plant of the genus Geranium, of family Geraniaceae.
parole.testo: From Latin geranium, from Ancient Greek γερᾰ́νῐον (gerắnĭon), from γέρᾰνος (gérănos, “crane”) + -ῐον (-ĭon, diminutive suffix).

parole.significato: Do not tempt or torment me; I reject you, your statements, or your beliefs.
parole.testo: Originally uttered by Christ in the King James Bible, Matthew 16:23: “get thee behind me, Satan”; Latin vāde retrō, Satanā; Ancient Greek ὕπαγε ὀπίσω μου, Σατανᾶ (húpage opísō mou, Satanâ).

parole.significato: A Dacian tribe inhabiting the regions of the lower Danube.
parole.testo: From Latin Getae, from Ancient Greek Γέται (Gétai).

parole.significato: Of a pale grey or bluish-green, especially when covered with a powdery residue.
parole.testo: From Latin glaucus, from Ancient Greek γλαυκός (glaukós, “blue-green, blue-grey”), 1670s. See Irish glas.

parole.significato: A list of difficult words or specialized terms used in a particular book or document, or in a particular domain of know…
parole.testo: From Middle English glosarie, from Latin glossārium, from Ancient Greek γλῶσσα (glôssa, “tongue”). Doublet of glossarium.

parole.significato: Showing all great circles as straight lines, and thus preserving the shortest distances between any two locations.
parole.testo: From Latin gnōmonicus, Ancient Greek γνωμονικός (gnōmonikós, “judging by rule”). Compare French gnomonique. See gnomon.

parole.significato: Any of various small fish from the large family Gobiidae, in which the pelvic fins are fused to form a disc-shaped suck…
parole.testo: From Latin gobius (“gudgeon”), from Ancient Greek κωβιός (kōbiós), a type of small fish, of unknown ultimate origin. See also gudgeon.

parole.significato: witchcraft, demonic magic, necromancy.
parole.testo: From Latin goetia, from Ancient Greek γοητεία (goēteía, “witchcraft”), from γόης (góēs, “sorceror”).

parole.significato: A vicious female monster from Greek mythology with sharp fangs and hair of living, venomous snakes. One of the three si…
parole.testo: From Middle English gorgon, from Latin Gorgō, from Ancient Greek Γοργώ (Gorgṓ), from γοργός (gorgós, “terrible”). Possibly from the same root as the Sanskrit word "garğ" (गर्जन), which is defined as a guttural sound, similar to the growling of a beast, thus possibly originating as an onomatopoeia.

parole.significato: Drawn, pictorial.
parole.testo: From Latin graphicus (“belonging to painting or drawing”), from Ancient Greek γραφικός (graphikós, “belonging to painting or drawing, picturesque, of or for writing; of style, lively”), from γραφή (graphḗ, “drawing, painting, writing, a writing, description, etc.”), from γράφω (gráphō, “scratch, car

parole.significato: Shortened form of Gregory Peck, a neck
parole.testo: Via Latin Grēgorius, from post-classical Ancient Greek Γρηγόριος (Grēgórios, “watchful, vigilant”), from Ancient Greek ἐγείρω (egeírō, “awaken, arouse”).

parole.significato: A Roman surveying instrument having plumb lines hanging from four arms at right angles.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin grōma, from Ancient Greek γνῶμᾰ (gnômă)

parole.significato: An officer who had various powers and duties connected with the gymnasia, such as the payment of training, oil, or othe…
parole.testo: From Latin gymnasiarchus, from Ancient Greek γυμνασίαρχος (gumnasíarkhos).

parole.significato: A large room or building for indoor sports.
parole.testo: From Latin gymnasium, from Ancient Greek γυμνάσιον (gumnásion, “exercise, school”), from γυμνός (gumnós, “naked”), because Greek athletes trained naked.

parole.significato: A sport involving the performance of sequences of movements requiring physical strength, flexibility, and kinesthetic a…
parole.testo: From gymnastic: see -ics; from Latin gymnasticus, from Ancient Greek γυμναστικός (gumnastikós), from γυμναστής (gumnastḗs, “athlete, gymnast”), from γῠμνᾰ́ζω (gŭmnắzō, “to train, exercise”), from γυμνός (gumnós, “naked”), because Greek athletes trained naked. By surface analysis, gymnast + -ics.

parole.significato: Gymnastic; athletic.
parole.testo: From Latin gymnicus, from Ancient Greek γυμνικός (gumnikós), from γυμνός (gumnós, “naked”).

parole.significato: The women's quarters in a household; (hence, loosely) any building or area for women.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gynaecēum, gynaecīum, from Ancient Greek γυναικεῖον (gunaikeîon), from γυνή (gunḗ, “woman”) (stem: γῠναικ- (gŭnaik-)) + -εῖον (-eîon, noun-forming suffix meaning “place or building associated with a specific purpose or person”).

parole.significato: A gynaeceum.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gynaecōnītis, from Ancient Greek γυναικωνῖτις (gunaikōnîtis).

parole.significato: A mineral consisting of hydrated calcium sulphate. When calcinated, it forms plaster of Paris.
parole.testo: From Latin gypsum, from Ancient Greek γύψος (gúpsos). Doublet of gesso.

parole.significato: A swirling vortex.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gȳrus (“circle; circular motion”), from Ancient Greek γῦρος (gûros, “circle; ring”), from Proto-Indo-European *gew- (“to bend; to curve”). The English word is a doublet of gyro and gyrus.

parole.significato: A magical plant mentioned by John Milton, said to be good against enchantments.
parole.testo: Coined by John Milton for the play Comus around 1634 (see quotation below). Various scholars suggest that the word comes from a classical source such as Latin Haemonia (“Thessaly”, a place associated with magic), Ancient Greek αἷμα (haîma, “blood”), or Ancient Greek αἵμων (haímōn, “skillful”).

parole.significato: A kingfisher whose nesting by the sea was said, in classical mythology, to cause the Gods to restrain the wind and wave…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English Alceoun, from Latin halcyōn, alcyōn (“kingfisher”), from Ancient Greek ἀλκυών (alkuṓn).

parole.significato: A period of calm during the winter, when storms do not occur.
parole.testo: From halcyon, from Latin Alcyone, from Ancient Greek Ἀλκυόνη (Alkuónē), daughter of Aeolus and wife of Ceyx. When her husband died in a shipwreck, Alcyone threw herself into the sea whereupon the gods transformed them both into halcyon birds (kingfishers). When Alcyone made her nest on the beach, wa

parole.significato: A treatise upon fish or the art of fishing, especially in Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: From Latin halieuticus ("halieutic, of or about fishing"), from Ancient Greek ἁλιευτικός (halieutikós) (alieutikós, "of or about fishermen"), from ἁλιεύς (halieús, “fisherman”). The Christianity definition comes from the fish being a symbol of the Christian faith.

parole.significato: The condition of having stale or foul-smelling breath.
parole.testo: Coined by doctor Joseph William Howe in 1874 and described as being derived from the Latin hālitus (literally “whiff, breath”) and the Ancient Greek νόσος (nósos, literally “disease”). It can be also understood as combination of the Latin hālitus and the English suffix -osis.

parole.significato: A wood-nymph who was physically a part of her tree; she would die if her tree were felled.
parole.testo: From Latin Hamadryas, from Ancient Greek Ἁμαδρυάς (Hamadruás), from ἅμα (háma, “together”) + δρῦς (drûs, “tree”).

parole.significato: A certain stone with spangles of gold color in it, known to Pliny, perhaps golden mica or yellow mica schist.
parole.testo: From Latin hammochrȳsos, (h)ammochrȳsus, from Ancient Greek ἀμμόχρῡσος (ammókhrūsos), from ἄμμος (ámmos, “sand”) + χρῡσός (khrūsós, “gold”).

parole.significato: Any primate of the evolved clade (half of the order) which comprises all apes (including hominoids), monkeys and even (…
parole.testo: From Neo-Latin Haplorrhini, from Ancient Greek ἁπλόος (haplóos, “simple”) + ῥίς (rhís, “nose”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to harmony.
parole.testo: From Latin harmonicus, from Ancient Greek ἁρμονικός (harmonikós), from ἁρμονία (harmonía, “harmony”). By surface analysis, harmony + -ic. Doublet of armónico.

parole.significato: A grappling hook.
parole.testo: Adapted from Latin harpagō, gen. harpagōnis, from Ancient Greek ἁρπάγη (harpágē, “hook”), from ἁρπάζω (harpázō, “to snatch away, to carry off, to seize, to captivate”), of uncertain origin. Doublet of harpoon.

parole.significato: A student of law or medicine at Cambridge who, being of the same standing as the students in arts in his year, is allow…
parole.testo: According to a 17th century chronicler, from Latin sophister Henricianus after King Henry VIII, but remodeled to fit a fanciful Ancient Greek *ἐρίσοφος (*erísophos, “very wise indeed”), from ἐρι- (eri-) + σοφός (sophós).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the patriotic Jewish family to which the Maccabees belonged; Maccabean.
parole.testo: From Latin Asmonaeus (latinized name of the family's founder) + English -an, from (Hellenic) Ancient Greek Ἀσαμωναῖος (Asamōnaîos), from Hebrew חַשְׁמוֹנַאי (ḥašmōnay).

parole.significato: Ebony.
parole.testo: From Middle English ebenif, hebenyf (influenced by Late Latin hebeninus), from Ecclesiastical Latin ebenius (“of ebony”), from Latin hebenus (“ebon tree”), from Ancient Greek ἔβενος (ébenos), from Egyptian hbnj, U13:n-Z4:M3

parole.significato: A great public sacrifice to the gods, originally of a hundred oxen; also, a great number of animals reserved for such a…
parole.testo: The noun is a learned borrowing from Latin hecatombē (“great sacrifice of a hundred oxen, hecatomb”), from Ancient Greek ἑκατόμβη (hekatómbē, “great sacrifice of a hundred oxen, hecatomb; any animal sacrifice or large sacrifice”, from ἑκᾰτόν (hekătón, “hundred”) + βοῦς (boûs, “cattle, cow, ox”)). Th

parole.significato: Sometimes in the form Hector: a blustering, noisy, turbulent fellow; a braggart, bully.
parole.testo: From Hector (“in Greek and Roman mythology, a character in Homer’s Iliad who is the greatest warrior of Troy”), from Late Middle English Hector (“warrior with the qualities of Hector”), from Latin Hectōr or Ancient Greek Ἕκτωρ (Héktōr), from ἕκτωρ (héktōr, “holding fast”), from ἔχειν (ékhein), prese

parole.significato: snail farming
parole.testo: From helici- + culture, from the genus of snails Helix, from helix, from Latin helix, from Ancient Greek ἕλιξ (hélix, “something twisted”).

parole.significato: helix, spiral
parole.testo: From Latin helic- + -o-, from Ancient Greek ἕλιξ (hélix).

parole.significato: A curve on the surface of a cylinder or cone such that its angle to a plane perpendicular to the axis is constant; the…
parole.testo: From Latin helix, from Ancient Greek ἕλιξ (hélix, “something twisted or spiral”).

parole.significato: A variety of agate, sprinkled with spots of red jasper.
parole.testo: From Latin haemachātēs, from Ancient Greek *αἱμᾰχᾱ́της (*haimăkhā́tēs), from αἷμᾰ (haîmă, “blood”) + ᾰ̓χᾱ́της (ăkhā́tēs, “agate”).

parole.significato: A Roman unit of liquid measure reckoned as the volume of ⁵⁄₆ Roman pound of wine, equivalent to around 0.27 L.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hēmīna (“half-sextarius”), from Ancient Greek ἡμῑ́νᾱ (hēmī́nā).

parole.significato: Half of the celestial sphere, as divided by either the ecliptic or the celestial equator .
parole.testo: From Latin hemisphaerium, from Ancient Greek ἡμισφαίριον (hēmisphaírion), from ἡμι- (hēmi-, “half”) + σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “sphere”). Equivalent to hemi- + sphere. Displaced native Old English healftrendel (literally “half-sphere”).

parole.significato: A semitone.
parole.testo: Latin hemitonium, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: A heavy release of blood within or from the body.
parole.testo: From Latin haemorrhagia, from Ancient Greek αἱμορραγία (haimorrhagía, “a violent bleeding”), from αἱμορραγής (haimorrhagḗs, “bleeding violently”), from αἷμα (haîma, “blood”) + -ραγία (-ragía), from ῥηγνύναι (rhēgnúnai, “to break, burst”); see ῥήγνῡμῐ (rhḗgnūmĭ) for more.

parole.significato: Having eleven syllables.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hendecasyllabus, from Ancient Greek ἑνδεκασύλλαβος (hendekasúllabos), from ἕνδεκα (héndeka, “eleven”) + συλλαβή (sullabḗ, “syllable”).

parole.significato: A line, verse, or word that comprises eleven syllables.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hendecasyllabus, from Ancient Greek ἑνδεκασύλλαβος (hendekasúllabos); equivalent to hendeca- + syllable.

parole.significato: A variety of barite that emits a foetid odour when rubbed or heated.
parole.testo: From Latin hepatitis, an unknown precious stone, from Ancient Greek ἧπαρ (hêpar, “liver”); compare French hépatite.

parole.significato: A valuable metal alloy in antiquity, thought to have been an alloy of copper with gold and silver, mixed and treated to…
parole.testo: From the Latin hēpatizon, from the Ancient Greek ἡπᾰτῐ́ζον (hēpătĭ́zon), from ἡπᾰτῐ́ζων (hēpătĭ́zōn, “liver-coloured”).

parole.significato: Any of a people who comprised a nomadic confederation in Central Asia during the 5th–6th centuries CE.
parole.testo: Hypercorrect respelling of Ephthalite, with unetymological initial h-, from Latin Ephthalītēs, from Ancient Greek Ἐφθαλίτης (Ephthalítēs), from Bactrian Ηβοδαλο (Ēbodalo) + Ancient Greek -ίτης (-ítēs).

parole.significato: A government of seven people.
parole.testo: From New Latin heptarchia, from Ancient Greek ἑπτά (heptá, “hepta-: seven”) + -αρχία (-arkhía, “-archy: rule”). Equivalent to hepta- + -archy.

parole.significato: A rectangular pillar bearing a bust of Hermes, once used as a boundary marker and later as decoration.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Herma, a Latinization of Hermēs, from Ancient Greek Ἑρμῆς (Hermês).

parole.significato: A female hero.
parole.testo: From Latin hērōīna, from late Ancient Greek ἡρωΐνη (hērōḯnē) (2nd century), a feminine equivalent of ἥρως (hḗrōs, “hero, demigod”), equivalent to hero + -ine (suffix forming feminine nouns). * English from 1587. The sense of "female lead character" is from 1715.

parole.significato: A temple dedicated to a hero, often over his supposed tomb.
parole.testo: From Latin hērōon, from Ancient Greek ἡρῷον (hērōîon), from ἡρῷος (hērōîos, “of a hero”).

parole.significato: Seeking infamy.
parole.testo: From Herostratus + -ic (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives from nouns). Herostratus is a learned borrowing from Latin Hērostratus, from Ancient Greek Ἡρόστρατος (Hēróstratos), from Ἥρᾱ (Hḗrā, “Greek goddess of marriage, women, and family”) + στρᾰτός (strătós, “army, military for

parole.significato: Fame (or infamy) won through crime, destruction, or some other misdeed.
parole.testo: Herostratic is derived from Herostratus (learned borrowing from Latin Hērostratus, from Ancient Greek Ἡρόστρατος (Hēróstratos) + -ic (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives from nouns)). Herostratus (died c. 356 B.C.E.) was a Greek arsonist who sought fame by destroying the second T

parole.significato: A viral infection, caused by Human alphaherpesvirus 1 and Human alphaherpesvirus 2, marked by painful, watery blisters…
parole.testo: From Latin herpēs, from Ancient Greek ἕρπης (hérpēs, “herpes”, literally “a creeping”), from ἕρπειν (hérpein, “to creep”).

parole.significato: Synonym of Hesiodic (“relating to the ancient Greek poet Hesiod”).
parole.testo: Akin to Hesiod + -ean, from Latin Hēsiodēus, from Ancient Greek Ἡσιόδειος (Hēsiódeios).

parole.significato: Synonym of Hesiodic (“relating to the ancient Greek poet Hesiod”).
parole.testo: Akin to Hesiod + -ian, from Latin Hēsiodīus, from Ancient Greek Ἡσιόδειος (Hēsiódeios).

parole.significato: A group of nymphs who tend a blissful garden filled with trees that grew golden apples in a far western corner of the w…
parole.testo: From Latin Hesperides, from Ancient Greek Ἑσπερίδες (Hesperídes).

parole.significato: Six.
parole.testo: From Latin hexa-, from Ancient Greek ἑξα- (hexa-), from ἕξ (héx, “six”). By surface analysis, hex- + -a-. Piecewise doublet of sexa-.

parole.significato: A polygon with six sides and six angles.
parole.testo: From Latin hexagōnum, from Ancient Greek ἑξάγωνον (hexágōnon). By surface analysis, hexa- + -gon. Piecewise doublet of sexagon.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to priests or other religious authorities, especially pharaonic priests of Ancient Egypt.
parole.testo: From Latin hieraticus, from Ancient Greek ἱερατικός (hieratikós), from ἱερατεία (hierateía, “priesthood”), from ἱερατεύω (hierateúō, “be a priest”), from ἱερεύς (hiereús, “priest”), from ἱερός (hierós, “sacred”). Use pertaining to the Egyptian writing system originates with the Greek phrase γράμματα

parole.significato: Of or relating to sacred writing.
parole.testo: From Latin hierographicus, Ancient Greek ἱερός (hierós, “sacred”) + γραφικός (graphikós, “of or pertaining to writing”).

parole.significato: Very funny; causing great merriment and laughter.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin hilaris (“cheerful”) + -ious, from Ancient Greek ἱλαρός (hilarós, “cheerful, merry”).

parole.significato: A great amount of amusement, usually accompanied by much laughter.
parole.testo: From Latin hilaritās (“cheerfulness”), from hilaris (“cheerful”), from Ancient Greek ἱλαρός (hilarós, “cheerful”). By surface analysis, Latin hilar(ō) + -i- + -ty.

parole.significato: The second term of the legal year, running from January to March or April, during which the upper courts of England and…
parole.testo: Hilary + term. The name Hilary is from the Latin Hilarius (“Latin name of Saint Hilary of Poitiers”), hilarius (“more cheerful, more joyful”), from hilarē (“cheerful, joyful”), from hilaris (“cheerful, light-hearted, lively”), from Ancient Greek ἱλαρός (hilarós, “cheerful, glad, happy, joyful, merry

parole.significato: The hybrid offspring of a stallion (male horse) and a she-ass (female donkey).
parole.testo: From Latin hinnus, from Ancient Greek ἴννος (ínnos), γίννος (gínnos). Possibly cognate with hinnire (“to whinny”).

parole.significato: centaur
parole.testo: From Latin hippocentaurus, from Ancient Greek ῐ̔πποκένταυρος (hĭppokéntauros).

parole.significato: An ancient love philter obtained from a mare or foal in heat.
parole.testo: From Latin hippomanes, from Ancient Greek ἱππομᾰνής (hippomănḗs); see hippo- and the related suffix -mania.

parole.significato: A semi-aquatic, herbivorous, African hoofed mammal of the family Hippopotamidae.
parole.testo: From Latin and New Latin hippopotamus, from Ancient Greek ἱπποπόταμος (hippopótamos), from ἵππος (híppos, “horse”) (English hippo-) + ποταμός (potamós, “river”). First attested in the 1560s. Displaced displaced English nicker (from native Old English nicor) and river horse.

parole.significato: A creature that is half bull and half horse.
parole.testo: From Latin hippotaurus, from Ancient Greek ἱππόταυρος (hippótauros), from ἵππος (híppos, “horse”, English hippo-) + ταῦρος (taûros, “bull”).

parole.significato: Synonym of historiaster (“an inferior historian”).
parole.testo: From Latin historicus (“historical”) + -aster (suffix denoting incomplete or partial resemblance, and hence sometimes having a derogatory connotation). Historicus is derived from historia (“history”) + -icus (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives), and is modelled after Ancient Gre

parole.significato: A large merchantman ship in Ancient Greece.
parole.testo: From Latin holcas, from Ancient Greek ὁλκάς (holkás). Compare hulk.

parole.significato: Synonym of sea cucumber.
parole.testo: Latin holothuria, plural, a sort of water polyp, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: The plant Angelica archangelica.
parole.testo: From Middle English Holi Gost, from Old English Hāliġ Gāst, a calque of Latin Spīritus Sānctus, which in turn is a calque of Ancient Greek Πνεῦμα τὸ Ἅγιον (Pneûma tò Hágion), from πνεῦμα (pneûma, “breath, vital force, soul”) + ἅγιος (hágios, “holy”)), a calque of Hebrew רוּחַ הָקֹדֶשׁ (rûaḥ hā-qōḏeš

parole.significato: Resembling or relating to the epic poetry of Homer.
parole.testo: From Latin homēricus (“of or pertaining to Homer; Homeric”), from Ancient Greek Ὁμηρικός (Homērikós), from Ὅμηρος (Hómēros, “Homer”) (possibly from ὅμηρος (hómēros, “hostage”), a nickname) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós, suffix forming relational adjectives) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *-kos (suffix formin

parole.significato: Pertaining to the belief established in the fourth century as a middle ground between the homoousian and homoiousian po…
parole.testo: From Latin homoeus, from Ancient Greek ὅμοιος (hómoios, “like, similar”), + -an.

parole.significato: The relationship of being homologous; a homologous relationship.
parole.testo: From Latin homologia, from Ancient Greek ὁμολογία (homología, “agreement, assent”); compare French homologie. By surface analysis, homo- + -logy. In topology, first used by French polymath Henri Poincaré, in the sense (close to what is now called a bordism) of a relation between manifolds mapped int

parole.significato: A word that sounds or is spelled the same as another word (but not necessarily both).
parole.testo: From Latin homōnymum, from Ancient Greek ὁμώνυμον (homṓnumon), nominalized from the neuter of ὁμώνῠμος (homṓnŭmos, “homonymous”). By surface analysis, hom- + -onym.

parole.significato: Of the same tenor or tone
parole.testo: Latin homotonus, from Ancient Greek [Term?].

parole.significato: Synonym of chronometric, of or related to horologia or horology.
parole.testo: From Latin horologicus, from Ancient Greek. Equivalent to horo- + logic or horology + -ic.

parole.significato: Synonym of chronometer or clock, a timekeeping device.
parole.testo: From Latin horologium, from Ancient Greek ὡρολόγιον (hōrológion). In reference to Eastern Orthodoxy, via its Byzantine Greek development. See menologium. Doublet of horologe.

parole.significato: The study or measurement of time
parole.testo: From Latin horologia, from horo- + -logia, equivalent to Ancient Greek ὥρα (hṓra, “period of time, hour”) + -λογία (-logía, “-ology: study or proper knowledge of”). Equivalent to horo- + -ology.

parole.significato: A cry of praise or adoration to God in liturgical use among the Jews, and said to have been shouted in recognition of t…
parole.testo: From Latin osanna, hosanna, from Ancient Greek ὡσαννά (hōsanná), from Aramaic אושענא/ܐܘܫܥܢܐ ('ōsha‘nā), from Biblical Hebrew הוֹשַׁע נָא (hōsha‘ nā, “please save”).

parole.significato: Any member of the genus Cynoglossum of small-flowered herbs and shrubs of the Old World.
parole.testo: From Middle English houndestonge, from Old English hundes tunge (“hound’s tongue (cynoglossum officinale)”), a calque of Latin cynoglossos, itself from Ancient Greek κυνόγλωσσον (kunóglōsson, literally “hound’s tongue”). Compare Dutch hondstong, German Hundszunge.

parole.significato: Of the colour of a hyacinth (either the gem or the flower); reddish-gold (chiefly with reference to hair).
parole.testo: From Latin hyacinthinus, from Ancient Greek ὑακίνθινος (huakínthinos), from ὑάκινθος (huákinthos); corresponding to hyacinth + -ine.

parole.significato: Causing a discharge of water; expelling serum effused into any part of the body, as in dropsy.
parole.testo: From Latin hydragogus (“conveying off water”), from Ancient Greek ὑδραγωγός (hudragōgós, “to lead”). Compare French hydragogue.

parole.significato: Mead, especially one of low alcohol content.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hydromel, hydromeli, from hydro- (from Ancient Greek ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”)) + mel (“honey”).

parole.significato: a denomination, sect, church, or other group which professes to be Christian but uses water to administer the Eucharist…
parole.testo: From Latin hydroparastatae from Ancient Greek ὑδρο- (hudro-, “water”) + παραστάτης (parastátēs, “defender”), from παρίστημι (parístēmi, “to stand by, defend”).

parole.significato: An aversion to water, as a symptom of rabies; the disease of rabies itself.
parole.testo: From Middle English idroforbia (“hydrophobia”), from Latin hydrophobia, from Ancient Greek ὑδροφοβία (hudrophobía), from ὑδρο- (hudro-), combining form of ῠ̔́δωρ (hŭ́dōr, “water”), + φοβία (phobía, “phobia”). The word is analysable as hydro- + -phobia.

parole.significato: Synonym of physical or material.
parole.testo: From hyle + -ical, originally translating Latin hylicus in notes on Irenaeus's Against Heretics after the manner of earlier psychical and pneumatical, from Ancient Greek ὑλικός (hulikós, “wooden, material”), from ῡ̔́λη (hū́lē, “wood, matter”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic, forming adjectives”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to marriage.
parole.testo: From Latin hymenaeus (from Ancient Greek ὑμεναῖος (humenaîos, “matrimonial”)) + -al. Compare hymen.

parole.significato: Open-air, outdoor, exposed to the sky.
parole.testo: From Latin hypaethrus, from Ancient Greek ὕπαιθρος (húpaithros), from ὑπό (hupó) + αἰθήρ (aithḗr, “air, ether”).

parole.significato: The use of a grammatical modifier which syntactically modifies an item other than the one it belongs to semantically, g…
parole.testo: From Latin hypallagē, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ὑπαλλαγή (hupallagḗ), from ὑπό (hupó, “hypo-”) + ἀλλάσσειν (allássein, “to exchange”).

parole.significato: In ancient musical theory, the lowest-pitched fixed note in the nearer tetrachord on a lyre, always pitched a perfect f…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin hypatē, from Ancient Greek ὑπάτη (hupátē, literally “highest/nearest [string]”). The hypate was the "highest" in the sense of being the string on a lyre nearest the player and physically above the remaining strings (compare a modern guitar, where the low E string is ne

parole.significato: An inversion of the usual or logical order of words or phrases, for emphasis or poetic effect.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hyperbaton, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ὑπερβατόν (huperbatón, “overstepping”), from ὑπερβαίνω (huperbaínō), from ὑπέρ (hupér) + βαίνω (baínō, “walk”).

parole.significato: Deliberate overstatement, particularly extreme overstatement.
parole.testo: From Middle English iperbole, yperbole, from Latin hyperbolē, from Ancient Greek ὑπερβολή (huperbolḗ, “excess, exaggeration”), from ὑπέρ (hupér, “above”) + βάλλω (bállō, “to throw”, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷelH-). Doublet of hyperbola.

parole.significato: Of or relating to hyperbole.
parole.testo: From Latin hyperbolic(us), from Ancient Greek ὑπερβολικός (huperbolikós). First attested in the 15th century. By surface analysis, hyperbol(e) + -ic.

parole.significato: Which has an extra syllable added to the last dipody (foot of a verse).
parole.testo: Recorded from circa 1700; from Latin hypercatalēcticus, from Ancient Greek ὑπερκατάληκτος (huperkatálēktos).

parole.significato: The addition of one or two syllables to the last foot of a verse
parole.testo: Coined in the late 1880s as a back-formation from hypercatalectic, from Latin hypercatalēcticus, from Ancient Greek ὑπερκαταληκτικός (huperkatalēktikós), from ὑπερ- (huper-, “over”) + καταληκτικός (katalēktikós, “incomplete”)

parole.significato: That part of the architrave which is over a door or window.
parole.testo: From Latin hyperthyrion, from Ancient Greek ὑπερθύριον (huperthúrion).

parole.significato: An underfloor space or flue through which heat from a furnace passes to heat the floor of a room or a bath.
parole.testo: From Latin hypocaustum, from Ancient Greek ὑπόκαυστον (hupókauston), from Ancient Greek ὑπό (hupó, “underneath”) + καυστόν (kaustón, “burnt offering”).

parole.significato: A mark ⟨⸒⟩ in late Classical and Byzantine Greek used as a form of interpunct to show two words should be read separate…
parole.testo: From Latin hypodiastolē, from Ancient Greek ὑποδιαστολή (hupodiastolḗ), from ὑπό (hupó, “under, lower”) + διαστολή (diastolḗ, “separation, distinction”), from διαστέλλω (diastéllō, “separate”), from διά (diá, “through, during”) + στέλλω (stéllō, “order, arrange”).

parole.significato: Existing or growing underground.
parole.testo: From Latin hypogaeus, hypogēus (from Ancient Greek ὑπόγειος (hupógeios)) + -an.

parole.significato: An underground room or cavern (also used figuratively).
parole.testo: From Latin hypogaeum, from Ancient Greek ὑπόγειον (hupógeion), a noun use of the neuter singular of ὑπόγειος (hupógeios, “underground”).

parole.significato: A lesser proposition or subsumption within a larger syllogism.
parole.testo: From Latin hypolēmma, from Ancient Greek ὑπόλημμᾰ (hupólēmmă, “supposition”), from ὑπο- (hupo-, “lesser”) + λῆμμα (lêmma, “assumption”).

parole.significato: The side of a right triangle opposite the right angle.
parole.testo: From Latin hypotenusa, from Ancient Greek ὑποτείνουσα πλευρά (hupoteínousa pleurá, “side subtending [the right angle]”), from ὑποτείνουσα (hupoteínousa, “stretching, extending, subtending”), active participle of ὑποτείνω (hupoteínō, “subtend, stretch under”).

parole.significato: In Scotland, a landlord's right over the stocking (cattle, implements, etc.), and crops of his tenant, as security for…
parole.testo: From Latin hypothēca (“pledge, mortgage”), from Ancient Greek ὑποθήκη (hupothḗkē, “warning, pledge”).

parole.significato: To pledge (something) as surety for a loan; to pawn, mortgage.
parole.testo: From Latin hypothecatus, past participle of hypotheco, hypothecare. This was in turn derived from Ancient Greek ὑποθήκη (hupothḗkē, “pledge”), from the verb ὑποτίθημι (hupotíthēmi, “to pledge as surety”).

parole.significato: the portion of the capital of a column that is below the annulets, and above the end of the shaft
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hypotrachelium, from Ancient Greek ὑποτραχήλιον (hupotrakhḗlion), from ὑπό (hupó, “under”) + τράχηλος (trákhēlos, “neck”).

parole.significato: A vivid, picturesque description of scenes or events.
parole.testo: New Latin, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Synonym of Hyrcanian.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Hyrcānus, from Ancient Greek Ὑρκανός (Hurkanós).

parole.significato: Any of several aromatic bushy herbs, of the genus Hyssopus, native to Southern Europe and once used medicinally.
parole.testo: Via Latin hȳsōpum, from Ancient Greek ὕσσωπος (hússōpos), of Semitic origin.

parole.significato: Hysterical; relating to hysteria.
parole.testo: From Latin hystericus, from Ancient Greek ὑστερικός (husterikós, “suffering in the uterus, hysterical”), from ὑστέρα (hustéra, “womb”).

parole.significato: Of, or arising from hysteria.
parole.testo: From hysteric + -al, from Latin hystericus, from Ancient Greek ὑστερικός (husterikós, “suffering in the womb, hysterical”), from ῠ̔στέρᾱ (hŭstérā, “womb”).

parole.significato: Synonym of iamb.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ïambus (“a certain poetic meter”), from Ancient Greek ἴαμβος (íambos).

parole.significato: A member of an Olympian dynasty, the "house of Iamus", an extended family of seers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Iamidēs, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek Ἰαμίδης (Iamídēs), from Ἴαμος (Íamos, “Iamus”) + -ίδης (-ídēs, “son of”, patronymic suffix).

parole.significato: Any of various long-legged wading birds in the family Threskiornithidae, having long downcurved bills used to probe the…
parole.testo: Mentioned in the Wycliffe Bible (Lev. 11:17) as ybyn or ibin, as ibys from 16th century and ibis shortly after. From Latin ībis, from Ancient Greek ἶβις (îbis), from Egyptian h-b-G26 (hbj) (compare Coptic ϩⲓⲃⲱⲓ (hibōi) or ϩⲓⲡ (hip)).

parole.significato: An Egyptian mongoose (Herpestes ichneumon), found in Africa and southern Europe.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ichneumōn, from Ancient Greek ἰχνεύμων (ikhneúmōn, “tracker”), from ἴχνος (íkhnos, “track, footstep”).

parole.significato: Fish glue, isinglass; a glue prepared from the sounds (swimming bladders) of various fishes.
parole.testo: From Latin ichthyocolla, from Ancient Greek ἰχθυόκολλα (ikhthuókolla, “fish-glue”), from ἰχθύς (ikhthús, “fish”) + κόλλα (kólla, “glue”).

parole.significato: An image, symbol, picture, portrait, or other representation, usually as an object of religious devotion.
parole.testo: From Latin īcōn, from Ancient Greek εἰκών (eikṓn, “likeness, image, portrait”). Eastern Orthodox Church sense is attested from 1833. Computing sense first recorded in 1982.

parole.significato: A collection of icons.
parole.testo: From Latin īconothēca from Ancient Greek εἰκονοθήκη (eikonothḗkē) from εἰκών (eikṓn) + θήκη (thḗkē).

parole.significato: An excess of bile pigments in the blood; jaundice.
parole.testo: From the Latin icterus, from the Ancient Greek ἴκτερος (íkteros, “jaundice”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to Mount Ida, the name given to a mountain near ancient Troy, and to a mountain of Crete, sometimes held to…
parole.testo: From Latin Idaeus (from Ancient Greek Ἰδαῖος (Idaîos)) + -an.

parole.significato: An abstract archetype of a given thing, compared to which real-life examples are seen as imperfect approximations; pure…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin idea (“a (Platonic) idea; archetype”), from Ancient Greek ἰδέα (idéa, “notion, pattern”), from εἴδω (eídō, “to see”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“to know; see”). Cognate with French idée. Doublet of idée. Related to idol, idolum, and eidolon.

parole.significato: A disease or condition arising spontaneously or having no known cause.
parole.testo: From Latin idiopathia, from Ancient Greek ἰδιοπάθεια (idiopátheia). By surface analysis, idio- + -pathy. First appears c. 1634, in the publications of Philiatreus (fl. 1630).

parole.significato: An insubstantial image; a spectre or phantom.
parole.testo: From Latin īdōlum. Doublet of aidoru, eidolon, and idol and related to idea.

parole.significato: Any poem or short written piece composed in the style of Theocritus's short pastoral poems, the Idylls.
parole.testo: From Latin īdyllium, from Ancient Greek εἰδύλλιον (eidúllion), from diminutive of εἶδος (eîdos, “form, shape”).

parole.significato: Disruption of the normal propulsive ability of the gastrointestinal tract, due to failure of peristalsis.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin īleus, from Ancient Greek εἰλεός (eileós, “intestinal obstruction”).

parole.significato: A specific version, edition, translation, or copy of the above-mentioned Homeric text.
parole.testo: From Latin Iliadis, genitive of Ilias, from Ancient Greek Ἰλιάς (Iliás), the poem about Ἴλιον (Ílion, an alternative name for Troy). By surface analysis, Ili- + -ad.

parole.significato: Not susceptible to death; living forever; never dying.
parole.testo: From Latin immortālis, from prefix im- (“not”) (from in-) + mortālis (“mortal”) (from mors (“death”), combining form mort- + adjectival suffix -alis), equivalent to im- + mortal. Displaced native undeadly, from Old English undēadlīċ. The term referring to the Persian soldiers was a Calque of Ancient

parole.significato: Deriving from the linguistic expression used; for reason of ambiguity, division, etc.
parole.testo: From Latin in dictione, translation of Ancient Greek παρὰ τὴν λέξιν (parà tḕn léxin), which appears in chapter 4 of Aristotle’s Sophistical Refutations.

parole.significato: Asleep, sleeping.
parole.testo: In Ovid’s Metamorphoses, Morpheus is the god of dreams, and subsequently he was often referred to as the god of sleep. The name is borrowed from Latin Morpheus, from Ancient Greek Μορφεύς (Morpheús), from μορφή (morphḗ, “form, shape”) (alluding to the fact that Morpheus appeared in dreams in the for

parole.significato: Relating to or denoting the group of Indo-European languages comprising Sanskrit and the modern Indian languages which…
parole.testo: From Latin indicus from Ancient Greek ἰνδικός (indikós), from Ἰνδία (Indía). Doublet of indigo.

parole.significato: A constructed language devised by Lancelot Hogben (1895–1975).
parole.testo: From Latin inter- + Ancient Greek γλῶσσα (glôssa, “language”).

parole.significato: A dogmatic and unproved proposition or dictum that is accepted solely on the authority of someone who is known to have…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ipse dīxit (“he himself said it”), calque of Ancient Greek αὐτὸς ἔφα (autòs épha). Originally used by the followers of Pythagoreanism, who claimed this or that proposition to be uttered by Pythagoras himself. Extended during the Middle Ages to the statements of Aristotle, and mor

parole.significato: An officer in Ancient Greece having functions corresponding to those of a Justice of the Peace.
parole.testo: From Latin īrēnarcha, īrēnarchēs, from Ancient Greek εἰρηνάρχης (eirēnárkhēs), from εἰρήνη (eirḗnē, “peace”) + ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “rule”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to a rainbow.
parole.testo: Formed from (the stem of) Latin īris, Ancient Greek ἶρις (îris) + -al.

parole.significato: A plant of the genus Iris, common in the northern hemisphere, and generally having attractive blooms (See Iris (plant)…
parole.testo: From Middle English iris, from Latin īris, from Ancient Greek ἶρις (îris, “rainbow”). Presuming an earlier form *ϝῖρις (*wîris), possibly from a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *w(e)ih₁-ro- (“a twist, thread, cord, wire”), from *weh₁y- (“to turn, twist, weave, plait”). If so, it would be cognate t

parole.significato: An introduction, especially (particularly capitalized) Porphyry's introduction to the works of Aristotle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin īsagōgē, from Ancient Greek εἰσαγωγή (eisagōgḗ, “lead-in”), from εἰς (eis, “into”) + ἀγωγή (agōgḗ, “to lead”).

parole.significato: The lowest of the three bones that make up each side of the pelvis.
parole.testo: 17th century, from Latin ischium, from Ancient Greek ἰσχίον (iskhíon, “hip joint”).

parole.significato: The inability to empty the bladder
parole.testo: Latin ischuria, Ancient Greek ἰσχουρία (iskhouría, “retention of urine”), from ἴσχω (ískhō, “to keep back, restrain”) + οὖρον (oûron, “urine”).

parole.significato: A temple dedicated to the worship of the Egyptian goddess Isis.
parole.testo: From Latin Iseum, from Ancient Greek Ἴσειον (Íseion), from Ἶσις (Îsis, “Isis”). By surface analysis, Isis + Latin -eum.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the goddess Isis or her worship.
parole.testo: From Latin īsiacus, from Ancient Greek Ἰσιακός (Isiakós).

parole.significato: Having (at least) two sides of equal length, used especially of a triangle or trapezoid.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin īsoscelēs, from Ancient Greek ἰσοσκελής (isoskelḗs, “equal-legged”), from ἴσος (ísos, “equal”) + σκέλος (skélos, “leg”) + -ής (-ḗs, adjective suffix). See also iso-.

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of
parole.testo: From the Latin Isrāēlīta (“Israelite”), from the Ancient Greek Ἰσρᾱηλῑ́της (Isrāēlī́tēs, “Israelite”), from Ἰσρᾱήλ (Isrāḗl, “Israel”), from the Hebrew יִשְׂרָאֵל (Yiśrāʼēl, “Israel”); by surface analysis, Israel + -ite.

parole.significato: A narrow strip of land, bordered on both sides by water, and connecting two larger landmasses.
parole.testo: Borrowing from Latin isthmus (“a strip of land between two seas”), from Ancient Greek ῐ̓σθμός (ĭsthmós, “neck, narrow passage”), possibly from εἶμῐ (eîmĭ, “to go”). Cognate to Old Norse eið (“isthmus”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Italian peninsula.
parole.testo: Via Latin ītalicus from Ancient Greek Ἰταλικός (Italikós), from Ἰταλία (Italía, “Italy”).

parole.significato: A depiction of an erect penis.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ithyphallus, from Ancient Greek ἰθύφαλλος (ithúphallos, “Bacchic phallus," literally "straight penis”).

parole.significato: A person who is pessimistic about the present and foresees a calamitous future; a prophet of doom.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Jeremias, from Ancient Greek Ἰερεμίας (Ieremías), from Hebrew יִרְמְיָה (yirm'yá, “Jeremiah”, literally “Yahweh exalt”). Doublet of Jeremias.

parole.significato: A place of retirement or concealment.
parole.testo: From Middle English Iericho, from Old English Iericho, from Latin Ierīchō, from Ancient Greek Ἰερῑχώ (Ierīkhṓ), from Biblical Hebrew יְרִיחוֹ (yərīḥō), recorded early as Ugaritic 𐎊𐎗𐎃 (yrḫ). Regarding the "place of concealment" sense, see 2 Samuel 10:5.

parole.significato: The Christian savior.
parole.testo: From Middle English Jhesus, Iesus, from Latin Iēsūs, from Ancient Greek Ἰησοῦς (Iēsoûs), from Biblical Hebrew יֵשׁוּעַ (yēšū́aʿ), a contracted form of יְהוֹשֻׁעַ (yəhōšúaʿ, “Joshua”), meaning "the Lord saves". The form יֵשׁוּעַ (yēšū́aʿ) is attested in some of the later books of the Hebrew Bible (Ez

parole.parola: Joan's as good as my lady in the dark
parole.significato: Synonym of all cats are grey in the dark: Sex is enjoyable regardless of the status, physical attractiveness, or social…
parole.testo: From or alongside the use of Joan as a sexually available member of the lower classes found in related expressions such as He is our Ladies Chaplaine, but serves Ione and Joan's as good as this French lady. Ultimately a calque of Latin and Ancient Greek expressions such as πᾶσα γυνὲ τοῦ λύχνου ἀρθέν

parole.significato: A person who shows remarkable patience, especially in the face of great misfortune.
parole.testo: From Latin Iob, from Ancient Greek Ἰώβ (Iṓb), from Biblical Hebrew אִיּוֹב (ʾiyyōḇ), related to אָיַב (ʾāyaḇ, “to be an enemy”) and אוֹיֵב (ʾōyēḇ, “enemy”).

parole.significato: The smallest letter or stroke of any writing; an iota.
parole.testo: The noun is borrowed from Latin iōta (“the letter iota of the Ancient Greek alphabet”), from Ancient Greek ἰῶτα (iôta, “ninth letter of the Ancient Greek alphabet; (figurative) very small part of writing, jot”), from Phoenician 𐤉 (y‬, “tenth letter of the Phoenician abjad, yodh”). Doublet of iota an

parole.significato: Jesus! (an exclamation used to express shock or surprise at something negative)
parole.testo: From Middle English Iudas, from Latin Iudas, from Ancient Greek Ἰούδας (Ioúdas), from Hebrew יְהוּדָה (y'hudá). Doublet of Judah.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Judea.
parole.testo: From Latin iūdaeus [from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαῖος (Ioudaîos), from Ἰουδά (Ioudá, “Judah”) + -ιος (-ios)] + -an. By surface analysis, Judah + -ean.

parole.significato: Judean, Judaic, Jewish
parole.testo: From Latin iūdaeus (“Jewish”), from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαῖος (Ioudaîos), ultimately from Biblical Hebrew יְהוּדָה (Yehûdâ, “Judah”).

parole.significato: A bird, the wryneck, once thought a bird of ill omen (Jynx torquilla).
parole.testo: An adaptation of the Latin iynx (“wryneck”), itself an adaptation of the Ancient Greek ἴϋγξ (íünx, “Eurasian wryneck, Jynx torquilla; spell or charm; passionate yearning”).

parole.significato: Synonym of accusation.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin catēgoria, from Ancient Greek κᾰτηγορῐ́ᾱ (kătēgorĭ́ā). Doublet of category.

parole.significato: A sticky brown resin obtained from species of rockrose, used mainly in perfume.
parole.testo: From Latin lādanum, from Ancient Greek λήδανον (lḗdanon, “gum”), from λήδον (lḗdon, “rockrose”), from a Semitic language; compare Akkadian 𒆷𒁷𒉡 (ladinnu).

parole.significato: A maze-like structure built by Daedalus in Knossos, containing the Minotaur.
parole.testo: From Middle English laberynt, laberynthe, from Latin labyrinthus, from Ancient Greek λᾰβύρῐνθος (lăbúrĭnthos, “a maze”).

parole.significato: Of speech or writing, communicative through the use of as few words as possible.
parole.testo: From Latin Lacōnicus (“Spartan”), from Ancient Greek Λακωνικός (Lakōnikós, “Laconian”). Laconia was the region inhabited and ruled by the Spartans, who were known for their brevity in speech.

parole.significato: Extreme brevity in expression.
parole.testo: From Latin Laconia, from Ancient Greek Λακεδαίμων (Lakedaímōn, “the region surrounding the city of Sparta”).

parole.significato: Synonym of Laestrygonian
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Laestrȳgōn, from Ancient Greek Λαιστρῡ́γων (Laistrū́gōn).

parole.significato: A member of a mythical Greek tribe of man-eating giants.
parole.testo: From Laestrygon [from Latin Laestrȳgōn, from Ancient Greek Λαιστρῡ́γων (Laistrū́gōn)] + -ian.

parole.significato: The upper part of the cochlear duct.
parole.testo: From Latin lagēna (“flagon; large flask”), from Ancient Greek λάγηνος (lágēnos, “flask, pitcher”). alternative form of λᾰ́γῡνος (lắgūnos)

parole.significato: The ptarmigan.
parole.testo: From the Latin lagōpūs, from the Ancient Greek λαγώπους (lagṓpous), from λαγώς (lagṓs, “hare”) + πούς (poús, “foot”); compare lagopod, lagopode. The bird was given this name because its feet resemble those of a hare.

parole.significato: A monster preying upon human beings, who sucked the blood of children, often described as having the head and breasts o…
parole.testo: From Latin lamia, from Ancient Greek Λάμια (Lámia).

parole.significato: A slave who carried torches before consuls, emperors and other high officials both during the later Roman Republic and…
parole.testo: From Latin lampadārius, from lampada, from Ancient Greek λαμπάς (lampás, “candle”).

parole.significato: Synonym of Laodicean.
parole.testo: From Latin Laodicēnus, from Ancient Greek Λαοδικηνός (Laodikēnós).

parole.significato: Having leaves like those of the bay laurel.
parole.testo: An etymological hybrid of the Latin laurus (“bay laurel”) and the English -phyllous (from the Ancient Greek φύλλον, phúllon, “leaf”).

parole.significato: One of two oval bodies hanging from the interior walls of the body in the Acanthocephala.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin lēmniscus (“pendent ribbon”), from Ancient Greek λημνῐ́σκος (lēmnĭ́skos), from Λῆμνος (Lêmnos, “a Greek island Lemnos”) + -ίσκος (-ískos, “noun-forming diminutive suffix”).

parole.significato: Someone with a Leo star sign
parole.testo: From Latin leō (“lion”), calque of Ancient Greek λέων (léōn), calque of Akkadian 𒉈𒍑 (nēšu)/Akkadian 𒌨𒄞𒆷 (urgulû), from Sumerian 𒌨𒄞𒆷 (UR.GU.LA, “lion; name of constellation”). Doublet of Leon, leu, lev, lion, and Lyon.

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to Leontini
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Leontīnus, from Ancient Greek Λεοντῖνος (Leontînos).

parole.significato: To (cause to) take part in lesbian sex, or other lesbian activity.
parole.testo: From Latin Lesbiana, from Ancient Greek Λέσβος (Lésbos) + Latin adjective suffix -iana; by reference to Sappho of Lesbos (whence also sapphist, sapphic), known for her sentimental poems about women. This sense of the word may have been borrowed from, or influenced by, the German cognate lesbisch, wh

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or in accordance with levirate marriage.
parole.testo: From levirate + -ical. From Latin levir (“a husband's brother, brother-in-law”), akin to Ancient Greek δᾱήρ (dāḗr). Compare French lévirat (“leviration”).

parole.significato: A lexical item corresponding to the set of all words (or of all multi-word expressions) that are semantically related t…
parole.testo: From Latin lexis, from Ancient Greek λέξις (léxis, “word”) + -eme, a suffix indicating a fundamental unit in some aspect of linguistic structure, on the model of phoneme.

parole.significato: word; lexeme.
parole.testo: Derived from lexis, a borrowing from Latin lexis, itself from Ancient Greek λέξις (léxis).

parole.significato: Concerning the vocabulary, words, sentences or morphemes of a language.
parole.testo: From Latin lexis, from Ancient Greek λέξις (léxis, “word”) + -al.

parole.significato: Someone with a Libra star sign.
parole.testo: From Latin lībra (“scales, balance”), calque of Ancient Greek ζυγόν (zugón), calque of Akkadian 𒀯𒍣𒁀𒉌𒌈 (ᵐᵘˡzibānītum, “scales”), from Sumerian 𒀯𒍣𒁀𒀭𒈾 (ᵐᵘˡZI.BA.AN.NA, “scales”). Doublet of arratel, libbra, libra, lira, litra, litre, livre, and rottol.

parole.significato: In Ancient Greek musical theory, the higher-pitched of the two movable notes in the nearer tetrachord on a lyre, pitche…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin lichanos, from Ancient Greek λιχανός (likhanós, “the forefinger”).

parole.significato: Any of many symbiotic organisms, being associations of algae and fungi, often found as white or yellow-to-blue–green pa…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin līchēn, from Ancient Greek λειχήν (leikhḗn), from λείχω (leíkhō, “to lick”). Originally used of liverwort; the modern sense first recorded 1715.

parole.significato: Of or relating to, or of the nature of, lientery.
parole.testo: From Latin lientericus, ultimately from Ancient Greek λειεντερία (leientería), see lientery. Compare French lientérique.

parole.significato: A form of diarrhea in which food passes through the body with little or no digestion.
parole.testo: From Latin leinteria, ultimately from Ancient Greek λειεντερία (leientería), which is composed of λεῖος (leîos) and ἔντερον (énteron); compare French lientérie.

parole.significato: Any of several flowers in the genus Lilium of the family Liliaceae, which includes a great many ornamental species.
parole.testo: From Middle English lilie, from Old English lilie, from Latin līlia, plural of līlium, from Ancient Greek λείριον (leírion). See there for more.

parole.significato: A meadow nymph.
parole.testo: Latin limoniades, plural, Ancient Greek λειμωνιάδες (leimōniádes), from λειμών (leimṓn, “meadow”).

parole.significato: The process of forming stonelike deposits or calculi formed in an internal organ, such as a gallstone in the gall bladd…
parole.testo: From Latin lithiasis, from Ancient Greek λιθίασις (lithíasis, “lithiasis”), from λίθος (líthos, “stone”).

parole.significato: Coral.
parole.testo: From Modern Latin lithophyton, from Ancient Greek roots λίθος (líthos, “stone”) + φυτόν (phutón, “plant”).

parole.significato: Any of various moths once grouped in the former family Lithosiidae, now mostly classified in the subfamily Arctiinae of…
parole.testo: From Latin Lithosia, the typical genus, from Ancient Greek λίθος (líthos, “a stone, a rock”).

parole.significato: liturgical
parole.testo: From Latin lītūrgicus, from Ancient Greek λειτουργικός (leitourgikós). By surface analysis, liturgy + -ic.

parole.significato: A lobe.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin lobus, from Ancient Greek λοβός (lobós).

parole.significato: Normal post-partum vaginal discharge; blood, mucus, and placental tissue that are discharged from a female's vagina (si…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin lochia, from Ancient Greek λοχεία (lokheía), neuter plural of λοχείος (lokheíos, “of childbirth”), from λόχος (lókhos, “childbirth”).

parole.significato: A military unit headed by a lochagus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin lochus, from Ancient Greek λόχος (lókhos).

parole.significato: Of any metre rhythmically intermediate between ordinary speech (or prose) and song (or poetry), typically combining dac…
parole.testo: From Latin logaoedicus, from Ancient Greek λογᾰοιδῐκός (logăoidĭkós), from λόγος (lógos, “speech, prose”) + ἀοιδή (aoidḗ, “song”) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós, “-ic”).

parole.significato: Dispute over the meaning of words
parole.testo: From Latin logomachia, from Ancient Greek λογομαχία (logomakhía).

parole.significato: The lotus eaters; a people visited by Ulysses who subsisted on the lotus.
parole.testo: Latin, from Ancient Greek Λωτοφάγος (Lōtophágos).

parole.significato: A member of the Lotophagi; a lotus eater.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Lōtophagus, from Ancient Greek Λωτοφάγος (Lōtophágos, literally “lotus eater”).

parole.significato: Synonym of George Lucas.
parole.testo: From Latin Lucas, from Ancient Greek Λουκᾶς (Loukâs). See the Greek entry for more.

parole.significato: The love of play.
parole.testo: Latin lūdus (“play”) + English -philia (from the Ancient Greek φιλία (philía, “love”, “fondness”))

parole.significato: A werewolf.
parole.testo: From Latin lycanthrōpus, from Ancient Greek λυκάνθρωπος (lukánthrōpos) – a compound of λύκος (lúkos, “wolf”) + ἄνθρωπος (ánthrōpos, “man, human”). By surface analysis, lyc- + -anthrope.

parole.significato: Epithet of Apollo
parole.testo: From Latin Lycēus [from Ancient Greek Λύκειος (Lúkeios, of uncertain meaning; possibly “wolf-killing”, “Lycian” or “luminous”), epithet of Apollo] + -an.

parole.significato: A public hall designed for lectures, readings, or concerts.
parole.testo: From Latin Lyceum, from Ancient Greek Λύκειον (Lúkeion) (the name of a gymnasium, or athletic training facility, near Athens where Aristotle established his school), from Λύκειος, from Proto-Greek *λύκη), "light." The meaning of the epithet "Lyceus" later became associated with Apollo's mother Leto,

parole.significato: Inflammation of the lymphatic channels, the result of infection at a site distal to the channel.
parole.testo: From Latin lympha (“lymph”) + Ancient Greek ἄγγος (ángos, “vessel”) + -itis.

parole.significato: Any of several medium-sized wild cats of the genus Lynx.
parole.testo: From Middle English lynx, linx, lenx, lynce, from Latin lynx, from Ancient Greek λύγξ (lúnx), from Proto-Hellenic *lúnks, from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“white; light; bright”), because of the cat's seemingly glowing eyes and ability to see in the dark. Doublet of onza and ounce. Displaced English

parole.significato: A plinth or step above the cornice of the podium in an ancient temple.
parole.testo: From Latin lysis, from Ancient Greek λύσις (lúsis, “a loosening”). Compare -lysis.

parole.significato: A member of the Maccabees (a liberation movement in Israel who established Jewish independence in the Land of Israel in…
parole.testo: From the Latin Maccabaeus, from the Ancient Greek Μᾰκκᾰβαῖος (Măkkăbaîos), from the Biblical Hebrew מַכַּבִּי (makkabbī).

parole.significato: To devise a plot or secret plan; to conspire.
parole.testo: First attested in 1537; borrowed from Latin machinātus, perfect active participle of machinor (“to invent, devise; to scheme, plot”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from māchina (“machine, contrivance, device, scheme”), an early borrowing from Ancient Greek. See also machine.

parole.significato: A spicy red bark from India, imported to the Roman Empire in the first century CE, possibly the fragrant resin of Ailan…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin macir; doublet of mace.

parole.significato: A member of a Thracian or Illyrian tribe once occupying the area between Paionia and Thrace.
parole.testo: From Latin Maedi, from Ancient Greek Μαῖδοι (Maîdoi).

parole.significato: A female follower of Dionysus (“the god of wine”), associated with intense revelling.
parole.testo: From Latin Maenad- (“frenzied female follower of Bacchus”), root of Maenās, from Ancient Greek μαινάς (mainás, “raving, frantic”), from μαίνομαι (maínomai, “to be mad, to rage”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to mind; to think; spiritual activity”).

parole.significato: A magician, wizard, sorcerer, witch, warlock or mystic.
parole.testo: From Middle English mages (plurale tantum), from Latin magus, from Ancient Greek Μάγος (Mágos), from the hapax Old Persian 𐎶𐎦𐎢𐏁 (m-gu-u-š /⁠maguš⁠/). Doublet of magus.

parole.significato: Pertaining to magma or magmatism.
parole.testo: From (the stem of) Latin magma + -ic, from Ancient Greek μάγμα (mágma, “thick unguent”), from μαγίς (magís, “kneaded mass”).

parole.significato: A magician; (derogatory) a conjurer or sorcerer, especially one who is a charlatan or trickster.
parole.testo: From Latin magus, from Ancient Greek μάγος (mágos, “magician”), from Μάγος (Mágos, “Magian”), of an indeterminate Old Iranian origin (see Μάγος for details). Doublet of mage.

parole.significato: To cause a syllable that contains a short vowel to scan as metrically long (heavy) instead of metrically short (light)…
parole.testo: In reference to Latin syllaba positiōne longa (“long syllable by position”), itself a calque of Ancient Greek συλλαβὴ μακρὰ θέσει (sullabḕ makrà thései).

parole.significato: Abnormal softening of organs or tissues of the human body.
parole.testo: From Latin malacia, from Ancient Greek μαλακία (malakía, “softness, sickness”). By surface analysis, malac- (“soft”) + -ia (“disease”).

parole.significato: A thick mineral pitch.
parole.testo: From Latin maltha, from Ancient Greek μάλθα (máltha).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Mandaeans.
parole.testo: From Latin Mandaeus [from Ancient Greek Μανδαῖος (Mandaîos), from Mandaic ࡌࡀࡍࡃࡀࡉࡉࡀ (mandaiia), from ࡌࡀࡍࡃࡀ (manda, “knowledge”)] + -an.

parole.significato: Violent derangement of mind; madness; insanity.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mania, from Ancient Greek μανία (manía, “madness”).

parole.significato: Synonym of Manichaean
parole.testo: From Latin Manichaicus, from Ancient Greek Μανιχαϊκός (Manikhaïkós).

parole.significato: A clavichord.
parole.testo: From Latin monochordon, from Ancient Greek μονόχορδον (monókhordon), influenced by Latin manus (“hand”). So called because it originally had only one string. See monochord.

parole.significato: A beast with the body of a lion (usually red), the tail of a scorpion, and the head/face of a man with a mouth filled w…
parole.testo: From Latin mantichōras, from Ancient Greek μαρτιχόρας (martikhóras, “man-eater; tiger”), from Old Persian *martyahvārah (“man-eater”), from 𐎶𐎼𐎫𐎡𐎹 (m-r-t-i-y /⁠martyaʰ⁠/, “man”).

parole.significato: Any of various large insects of the order Mantodea that catch insects or other small animals with their powerful forele…
parole.testo: From New Latin mantis, from Ancient Greek μάντις (mántis, “soothsayer”). Distant doublet of mind via Proto-Indo-European *méntis. Noncognate with mantissa.

parole.significato: Resembling marble or a marble statue; cold, smooth, white, etc.; marblelike.
parole.testo: From Latin marmoreus (“of, pertaining to, consisting of or made of marble; resembling marble; adorned with statues”) + English -al (suffix forming adjectives). Marmoreus is derived from marmor (“block or piece of marble; marble building or statue”) (from Ancient Greek μάρμᾰρος (mármăros, “marble”))

parole.significato: A mammal of the infraclass Marsupialia, including those where the female has a pouch in which it rears the young throug…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin marsūpial, from marsūpiālis (“of a purse”) and marsūpium (“purse, pouch”), from Ancient Greek μαρσύπιον (marsúpion) or μαρσύππιον (marsúppion), variants of μαρσίππιον (marsíppion), diminutive of μάρσιππος (mársippos, “bag, pouch”).

parole.significato: The external pouch in which female marsupials rear and feed the young.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin marsūpium, from Ancient Greek μαρσίππιον (marsíppion), diminutive of μάρσιππος (mársippos, “pouch”), perhaps of Oriental origin.

parole.significato: A miniature greenhouse with a humidifier, used for growing mushrooms.
parole.testo: * From Latin Martha, from Ancient Greek Μάρθα (Mártha), from Aramaic מָרְתָא (mārtā, “mistress”), feminine of מרא (mārā). Doublet of Marfa. * (humidity chamber): From the use of Martha Stewart-branded storage closets in the construction of early units.

parole.significato: A shrine in honor of a (usually religious, notably Christian) martyr, possibly at his grave.
parole.testo: From Late Latin martyrium (also 'martyrdom'), from Ancient Greek (martyrion), from (martys) 'witness'.

parole.significato: A social system in which the mother is head of household, having authority over men and children, and lineage is traced…
parole.testo: Coined after patriarchy, from Latin māter (“mother”) and Ancient Greek ἄρχω (árkhō, “to rule”). By surface analysis, matri- + -archy.

parole.significato: Having mostly maternally inherited characteristics.
parole.testo: From Latin mātr- + -o- + Ancient Greek κλίνειν (klínein) + -ous.

parole.significato: A large stately tomb or a building housing such a tomb or several tombs.
parole.testo: From Middle English mausoleum, from Latin Mausōlēum, from Ancient Greek Μαυσωλεῖον (Mausōleîon, “Mausoleum, the grand tomb built around 353–351 BCE at Halicarnassus for Mausolus, a ruler of Caria and satrap of the Achaemenid Empire; one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World”), from Μαύσωλος (Maú

parole.significato: One of the turns of a winding, crooked, or involved course.
parole.testo: From Latin Maeander, from Ancient Greek Μαίανδρος (Maíandros) – a river in Asia Minor (present day Turkey) known for its winding course (modern Turkish Menderes).

parole.significato: The branch of physics that deals with the action of forces on material objects with mass.
parole.testo: From Latin mēchanicus, from Ancient Greek μηχανικός (mēkhanikós), from μηχανή (mēkhanḗ, “machine, tool”).

parole.significato: A dark green mass, the contents of the fetal intestines during the later stages of mammalian gestation, that forms the…
parole.testo: From Latin mēcōnium (“opium; excrement of a newborn child”), from Ancient Greek μηκώνιον (mēkṓnion, “poppy-juice, opium”), from μήκων (mḗkōn, “poppy”).

parole.significato: Any of a Western Iranian people who inhabited the ancient region of Media.
parole.testo: From Latin Medus, from Ancient Greek Μῆδος (Mêdos).

parole.significato: Any of various European and North African herbs, of the genus Medicago, several of which are grown for fodder etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English medike, from Latin mēdica, from Ancient Greek μηδίκη (mēdíkē), short for Μηδικὴ πόα (Mēdikḕ póa, “Median grass”); so called because medick was imported from Media to Greece during the Greco-Persian Wars.

parole.significato: The adoption of Persian interests by a Greek, regarded as treachery.
parole.testo: From Latin mēdismus, from Ancient Greek μηδισμός (mēdismós). By surface analysis, Mede + -ism.

parole.significato: A mostly enclosed sea that has limited exchange of deep water with outer oceans, and where the water circulation is dom…
parole.testo: PIE word  *médʰyos The word mediterranean is from Latin mediterrāneus (“inland, remote from the coast”) + English -an (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘of or pertaining to’). Mediterrāneus is derived from medius (“middle”) + terra (“dry land, ground”), modelled after Ancient Greek μεσόγαιος

parole.significato: Irish elk
parole.testo: New Latin, from Ancient Greek, meaning "great horn".

parole.significato: Pertaining to, or in honour of, Cybele.
parole.testo: Latin Megalesius, from Ancient Greek word for "the Great", a surname of Cybele, the Magna Mater.

parole.significato: Of, from, or pertaining to, Megara
parole.testo: Derived from Latin megaricus, from Ancient Greek Μεγαρικός (Megarikós). Also Megara + -ic.

parole.significato: A sporangium which produces only megaspores
parole.testo: From neo-Latin, from mega- (“major”) + sporangium. The prefix is from Ancient Greek μέγας (mégas, “great”), and the base from spora + Ancient Greek ἀγγεῖον (angeîon, “vessel”).

parole.significato: A Scythian tribe which dwelt in Pontus
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Melanchlaenī, from Ancient Greek Μελάγχλαινοι (Melánkhlainoi).

parole.significato: Filled with or affected by melancholy—great sadness or depression, especially of a thoughtful or introspective nature.
parole.testo: From Latin melancholicus, from Ancient Greek μελαγχολικός (melankholikós, “atrabilious, impulsive, of atrabilious or melancholic temperament”), from μελαγχολία (melankholía, “melancholy”). By surface analysis, melancholy + -ic.

parole.significato: A tan or dark skin discoloration, particularly common in pregnant women, thought to be caused by the stimulation of mel…
parole.testo: From Latin melasma, from Ancient Greek μέλασμα (mélasma), from μελαίνειν (melaínein, “to blacken”) + -σμα (-sma), from μέλας (mélas, “black”).

parole.significato: Consisting of or containing honeylike matter; said of certain encysted tumours.
parole.testo: From Latin meliceris (“a kind of tumor”), from Ancient Greek μελικηρίς (melikērís, “honeycomb”), from μέλι (méli, “honey”) + κηρός (kērós, “wax”).

parole.significato: A fragrant plant of the genus Melilotus, often having small yellow or white flowers.
parole.testo: From Latin melilōtos, from Ancient Greek μελίλωτος (melílōtos), from μέλι (méli, “honey”) + λωτός (lōtós, “lotus”); later reinforced by Old French mellilote.

parole.significato: Objects that are connected to or remind their owner of past events.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin memorābilia (“things to be remembered”); its use as noun is after Ancient Greek ἀπομνημονεύματα (apomnēmoneúmata) of the neuter plural of memorābilis (“memorable”). Its English use is perhaps after the Latin title Memorabilia of Xenophon’s collection of Socratic dialogues.

parole.significato: The three membranes that envelop the brain and spinal cord.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mēningēs, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek μῆνιγξ (mêninx, “membrane”).

parole.significato: sycosis
parole.testo: From Latin mentāgra, from mentum (“chin”) + Ancient Greek ἄγρα (ágra, “a catching”).

parole.significato: In Ancient Greek musical theory, the highest-pitched fixed note in the nearer tetrachord on a lyre, always pitched a pe…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin mesē, from Ancient Greek μέση (mésē, literally “middle [string]”).

parole.significato: An ancient instrument for finding two mean proportionals between two given lines, required in solving the problem of th…
parole.testo: From Latin mesolabium, from Ancient Greek μεσόλαβος (mesólabos).

parole.significato: The one who is ordained by God to lead the people of Israel, believed by Christians and Muslims to be Jesus Christ.
parole.testo: From Middle English Messyas, Messy, Messie, from Latin Messīās, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek Μεσσίας (Messías), from Aramaic ܡܫܺܝܚܳܐ (məšīḥā), from Biblical Hebrew מָשִׁיחַ (māšîaḥ, “anointed”). Doublet of Masih and Moshiach.

parole.significato: A rhetorical device whereby one word is metonymically substituted for another word which is itself a metonym; more broa…
parole.testo: From Latin metalēpsis, from Ancient Greek μετάληψις (metálēpsis, “succession”), from Ancient Greek μετά (metá, “after”) and λαμβάνω (lambánō, “to take”).

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or characteristic of metal.
parole.testo: From Latin metallicus, from metallum (“metal”), from Ancient Greek μέταλλον (métallon). Equivalent to metal + -ic.

parole.significato: A transformation, such as one performed by magic.
parole.testo: First attested in 1533, from Latin metamorphōsis, from Ancient Greek μεταμόρφωσις (metamórphōsis), from μετά (metá, “change”) + μορφή (morphḗ, “form”). Analyzable as meta- + -morph + -osis

parole.significato: Any change in a word made by altering its letters or sounds.
parole.testo: From Latin metaplasmus from Ancient Greek μεταπλασμός (metaplasmós).

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or situated at the forehead
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin metōpicus, from Ancient Greek μετωπικός (metōpikós).

parole.significato: Rhythm or measure.
parole.testo: From Old English, from Latin metrum, from Ancient Greek μέτρον (métron, “measure, rule, length, size, poetic metre”).

parole.significato: A metropolitan (bishop).
parole.testo: Latin metropolita, from Ancient Greek μητροπολίτης (mētropolítēs).

parole.significato: denizen, sojourner, stranger, outlander.
parole.testo: From Latin metoecus, from Ancient Greek μέτοικος (métoikos, “alien, outsider, foreigner”), combination of μετά (metá) and οἶκος (oîkos, “residency”). Cognate with French métèque.

parole.significato: Meum athamanticum, a European herb.
parole.testo: From Latin mēum (“umbelliferous plant, Meum athamanticum”), from Ancient Greek μῆον (mêon), probably from μεῖον (meîon, “lesser”) for its small size. The English form came perhaps via Middle French meu, a word with a single isolated attestation from the 14th century which only began to appear consis

parole.significato: spignel, Meum athamanticum
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mēum (“Meum athamanticum”), from Ancient Greek μῆον (mêon), probably from μεῖον (meîon, “lesser”) for its small size.

parole.significato: A very large champagne bottle (named after the King) with the capacity of about 30 liters, equivalent to 40 standard bo…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Midās, from Ancient Greek Μίδᾱς (Mídās), from Phrygian midas.

parole.significato: A form of acting without words; pantomime.
parole.testo: Possibly from Middle English mime, from Old English mīma (“a buffoon, jester, mime”), from Latin mimus, from Ancient Greek μῖμος (mîmos, “imitator, actor”), but more likely re-borrowed in modern times from French mime (“mimic actor”), from the same source.

parole.significato: Exhibiting mimesis.
parole.testo: From Latin mīmēticus or its etymon Ancient Greek μῑμητικός (mīmētikós, “imitative”). By surface analysis, mime + -etic.

parole.significato: To imitate, especially in order to ridicule.
parole.testo: From Latin mīmicus, from Ancient Greek μῑμικός (mīmikós, “belonging to mimes”), from μῖμος (mîmos, “imitator, actor”); see mime.

parole.significato: A monetary unit of ancient Greece and the Middle East, originally equivalent to the weight of a mina of silver.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mina, from Ancient Greek μνᾶ (mnâ, “mna”). Compare maneh, from Biblical Hebrew מָנֶה (māne), as well as maund.

parole.significato: A monastic church.
parole.testo: From Middle English mynster (see mynisterie), from Old English mynster, from Latin monastērium (“monastery”), from Ancient Greek μοναστήριον (monastḗrion, “monastery; solitary dwelling”). Doublet of monastery.

parole.significato: A member of a race said to be autochthonous to the Aegean area.
parole.testo: From Latin Minyes (from Ancient Greek Μινύες (Minúes)) + -an.

parole.significato: A kind of gladiator, known for wearing a Gallic helmet with the image of a fish.
parole.testo: From Latin mirmillō, from Ancient Greek μόρμυλος (mórmulos).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the dynasty begun by Mithridates I of Pontus or any of its kings named Mithridates, especially Mith…
parole.testo: From Latin Mithridāticus, from Ancient Greek Μιθριδατικός (Mithridatikós), from Μιθριδάτης (Mithridátēs) + -ικός (-ikós), from Old Median *Miθra-dāta (literally “Mithra-given”).

parole.significato: Something (especially a series of ideas, letters, words, etc.) used to help in remembering a thing; a memory aid.
parole.testo: Noun sense 1 (“something used to help in remembering a thing”) is borrowed from Latin mnēmonicum (“something used to help in remembering a thing”), from Ancient Greek μνημονικόν (mnēmonikón, “something used to help in remembering a thing”), a noun use of the neuter form of μνημονῐκός (mnēmonĭkós, ad

parole.significato: A metrical foot of three long syllables.
parole.testo: From Latin molossus, from Ancient Greek μολοσσός (molossós), properly "belonging to the Molossians", a people in the eastern part of Epirus.

parole.significato: A magic herb or plant used by Odysseus to overcome Circe.
parole.testo: From Latin mōly, from Ancient Greek μῶλυ (môlu) (probably a loanword).

parole.significato: One thing, one being, one item.
parole.testo: From Latin monas (“unit”) (from Ancient Greek μονάς (monás), from μόνος (mónos), from Proto-Indo-European *men-). By surface analysis, mono- + -ad.

parole.significato: A rare autosomal-dominant hair disease that results in short, fragile, broken hair with a beaded appearance.
parole.testo: From Latin mŏnīle (“necklace”) + Ancient Greek θρίξ (thríx, “hair”).

parole.significato: A musical instrument for experimenting with the mathematical relations of musical sounds, consisting of a single string…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin monochordon, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek μονόχορδον (monókhordon). By surface analysis, mono- + chord.

parole.significato: An ode, as in Greek drama, for a single voice, often specifically a mournful song or dirge.
parole.testo: From Latin monodia, from Ancient Greek μονῳδία (monōidía).

parole.significato: A duel; single combat.
parole.testo: From Latin monomachia, from Ancient Greek μονομαχία (monomakhía); μόνος (mónos, “single, alone”) + μάχομαι (mákhomai, “fight”).

parole.significato: A situation, by legal privilege or other agreement, in which solely one party (company, cartel etc.) exclusively provid…
parole.testo: From Latin monopōlium, from Ancient Greek μονοπώλιον (monopṓlion, “a right of exclusive sale”), from μόνος (mónos, “sole”) + πωλέω (pōléō, “to barter, sell”). By surface analysis, mono- + -poly.

parole.significato: A classical temple made up of one circle of columns supporting a roof.
parole.testo: From Latin monopteros, from Ancient Greek μονόπτερος (monópteros), from μονο- (mono-, “mono-”) + πτερόν (pterón, “wing; circle of columns”).

parole.significato: A noun which only occurs in one case.
parole.testo: From Latin monoptotum, from Ancient Greek μονόπτωτος (monóptōtos).

parole.significato: Having a single unvaried pitch.
parole.testo: From the post-Classical Latin monotonus (“unvarying in tone”) or its etymon the Ancient Greek μονότονος (monótonos, “steady”, “unwavering”); compare cognate adjectives, namely the French monotone, the German monoton, the Italian monotono, and the Spanish monótono, as well as the slightly earlier Eng

parole.significato: An acid derived from the mulberry.
parole.testo: Latin morus (“mulberry tree”) + Ancient Greek ξύλον (xúlon, “wood”) + -ic + acid. Named by Martin Heinrich Klaproth

parole.significato: Giving birth to multiple young at one time; synonym of multiparous and polytocous.
parole.testo: From Latin multi- + Ancient Greek τόκος (tókos).

parole.significato: One of the nine Ancient Greek deities of the arts.
parole.testo: From Middle English Muse, from Latin Musa, from Ancient Greek Μοῦσα (Moûsa).

parole.significato: A building or institution dedicated to the acquisition, conservation, study, exhibition, and educational interpretation…
parole.testo: From Latin mūsēum (“library, study”), from Ancient Greek Μουσεῖον (Mouseîon), shrine of the Muses (Μοῦσα (Moûsa)). Doublet of mosaic.

parole.significato: The fear of mice (and rats).
parole.testo: From Latin mūs (“mouse”) or Ancient Greek μῦς (mûs, “mouse”) + -phobia.

parole.significato: The condition of having abnormally large and dilated pupils due to illness or narcotics, particularly stimulants such a…
parole.testo: From Latin mydriasis, from Ancient Greek μυδρίᾱσις (mudríāsis, “undue enlargement of the pupil”), from μύδρος (múdros, “mass of red hot material in a forge”), possibly because the pupil is particularly bright or sparkling when dilated, or because of the red eye effect when exposed to a flash of ligh

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Myosotis, the forget-me-nots.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin myosōtis, from Koine Ancient Greek μυοσωτίς (muosōtís, literally “ears of a mouse”), from genitive of μῦς (mûs, “mouse”) and nominative plural of οὖς (oûs, “ear”).

parole.significato: A protein that acts as an inhibitor to the growth of muscle tissue.
parole.testo: Perhaps from myo- (“muscle”) + Latin statos, status, sto (“remain, stand, fix, set"”) or Ancient Greek στάσις (stásis, “inactivity, a freezing, state of motionlessness, arrest, a standing”). myo- + -statin?

parole.significato: One of a fierce tribe or troop who accompanied Achilles, their king, in the Trojan War.
parole.testo: From Latin Myrmidones, from Ancient Greek Μυρμιδόνες (Murmidónes), a tribe of warriors led by Achilles to the Trojan War. Folk etymology in Ovid's time derived the tribe's name from μυρμηδών (murmēdṓn, “ant-nest”), from μύρμηξ (múrmēx, “ant”)).

parole.significato: A soldier or a subordinate civil officer who executes orders of a superior without protest or pity (sometimes applied t…
parole.testo: From Myrmidon, from Latin Myrmidones, from Ancient Greek Μυρμιδόνες (Murmidónes).

parole.significato: A plum-like fruit from various trees of the genus Terminalia, formerly used in medicine and now in the dyeing industry;…
parole.testo: From Latin myrobalanum, myrobalanus (“ben nut”), from Ancient Greek μυροβάλανος (murobálanos), from μύρον (múron, “perfume”) + βάλανος (bálanos, “acorn”).

parole.significato: A red-brown resinous material, the dried sap of a tree of the genus Commiphora, especially Commiphora myrrha, used as p…
parole.testo: From Middle English mirre, from Old English myrre, from Latin myrrha, from Ancient Greek μύρρα (múrrha), from Semitic. Compare Arabic مُرّ (murr, “myrrh”, literally “bitterness”), Hebrew מור / מֹר (mōr, “myrrh”, literally “bitterness”). Compare מרור : maror.

parole.significato: A person who prepares an initiate for entry into a mystery cult, or who teaches mystical doctrines.
parole.testo: From Latin mystagōgus, Ancient Greek μυσταγωγός (mustagōgós). By surface analysis, mystic + -agogue.

parole.significato: Mythical; existing in myth.
parole.testo: 1660s; from Latin mȳthicus or Ancient Greek μυθικός (muthikós); equivalent to myth + -ic.

parole.significato: The ancient inhabitants of Nabataea, a region of Arabia inhabited by the Nabataeans that covers parts of northern Arabi…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Nabataeus (“Nabataean”), which was borrowed from Ancient Greek Ναβαταῖος (Nabataîos, “Nabataean”), which was borrowed from Nabataean Aramaic 𐢕𐢃𐢋𐢈 (nbṭw, “Nabataean”). Possibly cognate with Arabic نَبَطِيّ (nabaṭiyy, “Nabataean, Nabaṭ”), Arabic أَنْبَاط (ʔanbāṭ), and Hebrew נבטים

parole.significato: A Hebrew stringed instrument.
parole.testo: From Latin nabla, from Ancient Greek νάβλα (nábla, “Phoenician harp”), from ancient Hebrew נֵבֶל (nḗḇel) or a Phoenician cognate. Doublet of nebel, which comes via the modern Hebrew נֵ֤בֶל.

parole.significato: A female deity (nymph) associated with water, especially a spring, stream, or other fresh water.
parole.testo: From Latin Nāïas, from Ancient Greek Νᾱϊάς (Nāïás, “naiad”), from νάω (náō, “to flow”).

parole.significato: In the International System of Units and other metric systems of units, multiplying the unit to which it is attached by…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nānus (“dwarf”), borrowed from Ancient Greek νᾶνος (nânos, “dwarf”).

parole.significato: A form of dwarfism characterized by a very short trunk
parole.testo: From nano- (“dwarf”) + Latin cormus, Ancient Greek κορμός (kormós, “trunk”).

parole.significato: Naturally occurring liquid petroleum.
parole.testo: From Latin naphtha, from Ancient Greek νάφθα (náphtha, “naphtha”), from Old Persian *naftah, probably borrowed or assimilated from Akkadian 𒉌𒆳𒊏 (napṭu, “naphtha”) . The Greek mediation is reflected in the spelling – ‘ph’ and ‘th’ (from ‘φ’ and ‘θ’).

parole.significato: Narcissistic, loving oneself excessively.
parole.testo: From Latin narcissinus, from Ancient Greek ναρκίσσινος (narkíssinos), from νάρκισσος (nárkissos, “narcissus”).

parole.significato: The ointment nard.
parole.testo: From Latin nardus, from Ancient Greek νάρδος (nárdos).

parole.significato: A national standard variety of a language spoken in more than one region.
parole.testo: From natio(n) + -lect. The first component is from Latin nātiōn(em), with the second abbreviated from dialect, from Ancient Greek. Coined by Godelieve Laureys in 1997.

parole.significato: A shipmaster, a shipowner, a skipper
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nauclērus, from Ancient Greek ναύκληρος (naúklēros).

parole.significato: The recreation of a sea battle staged for entertainment.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin naumachia, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ναυμαχία (naumakhía). Compare naumachy.

parole.significato: A feeling of illness or discomfort in the digestive system, usually characterized by a strong urge to vomit.
parole.testo: From Middle English nausea, a borrowing from Latin nausea, from Ancient Greek ναυσία (nausía, “sea-sickness”), from ναῦς (naûs, “ship”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)neh₂-. Displaced native Old English wlǣtta.

parole.significato: To cause nausea in.
parole.testo: From earlier nauseat, from Latin nauseātus (“nauseated”), perfect past participle of nauseō (“to feel sea sick, nauseate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix, of participial origin)), from nausea, from Ancient Greek ναυσία (nausía), from ναῦς (naûs), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)neh₂-. By surface analys
