parole.significato: A marine mollusc, of the family Nautilidae native to the Pacific Ocean and Indian Ocean, which has tentacles and a spir…
parole.testo: From Latin nautilus, from Ancient Greek ναυτίλος (nautílos, “paper nautilus, sailor”).

parole.significato: The commander of a fleet.
parole.testo: From Latin navarchus, from Ancient Greek ναύαρχος (naúarkhos, “leader of the ships”), corresponding to navy + -arch.

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to the city of Naples, capital and largest city of Campania, Italy, or the surrounding metropolita…
parole.testo: From Latin neāpolītānus, from Neāpolis, from Ancient Greek Νεάπολις (Neápolis, literally “new city”), a Greek city in modern Naples. Doublet of naporitan.

parole.significato: The skin of a fawn, as worn by Dionysus, and as worn in his honor by his male followers and female followers (maenads)…
parole.testo: From Latin nebris, from Ancient Greek νεβρίς (nebrís), earlier νεβρός (nebrós, “fawn”).

parole.significato: The drink of the gods.
parole.testo: From Latin nectar, from Ancient Greek νέκταρ (néktar, “nourishment of the gods”), from Proto-Indo-European *neḱ- (“perish, disappear”) + *-tr̥h₂ (“overcoming”), from *terh₂- (“to overcome, pass through, cross over”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to nectar; nectarous.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin nectareus (“of nectar; sweet”), from Ancient Greek νεκτάρεος (nektáreos, “sweet as nectar, fragrant”), from νέκταρ (néktar, “nectar”).

parole.significato: The swede (rutabaga); turnip.
parole.testo: From Middle English neep, from Old English nǣp (“turnip, rape”), borrowed from Latin nāpus. Compare Icelandic næpa (“turnip”). Cognate with English turnip.

parole.significato: A beginner; a person who is new to a subject, skill, or belief.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin neophytus, from Ancient Greek νεόφυτος (neóphutos, “newly planted”), from νέος (néos, “new”) + φυτόν (phutón, “plant, child”). By surface analysis, neo- + -phyte.

parole.significato: A drug mentioned in Homer's Odyssey (c. 8th century B.C.E.) as bringing relief from anxiety or grief; hence, any drug o…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nēpenthes (“a drug bringing relief from grief”), from Ancient Greek νηπενθές (nēpenthés), neuter of νηπενθής (nēpenthḗs, “sorrow-banishing”), from νη- (nē-, “not”) + πένθος (pénthos, “grief”) (from πάσχειν (páskhein), present active infinitive of πάσχω (páskhō, “to be ill or inju

parole.significato: A semi-precious stone, one of the two types of stone commonly referred to as jade (the other being jadeite).
parole.testo: From Latin lapis nephriticus, via Ancient Greek λίθος (líthos) νεφριτικός (nephritikós), meaning kidney stone, because jade was believed to have cured kidney stones.

parole.significato: Any one of the fifty sea-nymphs who were daughters of the sea-god Nereus and attendants upon Poseidon (Neptune), and we…
parole.testo: From the stem of Latin Nērēis, from Ancient Greek Νηρηΐς (Nērēḯs), from Νηρεύς (Nēreús, “Nereus”) + -ις (-is), literally “sprung of Nereus”. By surface analysis, Nereus + -id.

parole.significato: In Ancient Greek musical theory, the highest-pitched fixed note in the farther tetrachord on a lyre, always pitched a p…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin nētē, from Ancient Greek νήτη (nḗtē, literally “lowest [string]”). It was "lowest" in the sense of being the farthest from the player and physically below the other strings, but was the highest in pitch. Compare the high E string in a modern guitar, which is farthest f

parole.significato: A nomad tribe of Scythia
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Neurī, from Ancient Greek Νευροί (Neuroí).

parole.significato: A puppet; a marionette
parole.testo: From Latin neurospaston, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: The study of nests.
parole.testo: From nido- (“nest”) + -logy (“study of”). From Latin nidus + French -logie (“from Latin -logia, from Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía)”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Nile or the people who live on its banks.
parole.testo: From Latin Nīlōticus, from Ancient Greek Νειλώτης (Neilṓtēs, “on the Nile”). Analyzable as Nile + -otic.

parole.significato: A treatise or written classification of diseases.
parole.testo: From post-classical Latin nosologia, formed as from Ancient Greek νόσος (nósos, “disease”) + Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía, “discourse, branch of knowledge”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to coins or money.
parole.testo: From Latin nummarius (“pertaining to money”), from nummus (“a coin, a piece of money”), akin to Ancient Greek νόμος (nómos, “a custom, law”).

parole.significato: A nymph.
parole.testo: From Latin nympha, from Ancient Greek νύμφη (númphē, “bride, nymph”). Doublet of nymph.

parole.significato: the European white water lily.
parole.testo: From Latin nymphaea, from Ancient Greek νυμφαῖα (numphaîa), feminine singular form of νυμφαῖος (numphaîos, “sacred to the nymphs”), from νύμφη (númphē, “nymph”). Sense 2 is a semantic loan from translingual Nymphaea, from the same Latin and Greek.

parole.significato: A shrine consecrated to water nymphs, often with a fountain.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin nymphaeum, from Ancient Greek νυμφαῖον (numphaîon), a substantivisation of νυμφαῖος (numphaîos, “sacred to the nymphs”), from νύμφη (númphē, “nymph”).

parole.significato: A silver coin minted in Ancient Greece, valued at a sixth of a drachma.
parole.testo: From Latin obolus, from Ancient Greek ὀβολός (obolós), from ὀβελός (obelós). Doublet of obole and pul.

parole.significato: Any of the daughters of Oceanus and Tethys; a sea-nymph.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Oceanis, from Ancient Greek Ὠκεανίς (Ōkeanís), from Ὠκεανός (Ōkeanós) + -ις (-is), literally “sprung of Oceanus”. By surface analysis, Oceanus + -id.

parole.significato: A polygon with eight sides and eight angles.
parole.testo: From Latin octagōnon, octōgōnon (“octagon”), and from its etymon Ancient Greek ὀκτάγωνον (oktágōnon, “octagon”), probably from Koine Greek ὀκτάγωνος (oktágōnos, “having eight corners”) + -ον (-on, suffix forming nouns). ὀκτάγωνος is derived from ὀκτᾰ- (oktă-, prefix meaning ‘eight’) (from ὀκτώ (oktṓ

parole.significato: Any of several marine molluscs of the order Octopoda, having no internal or external protective shell or bone (unlike t…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin octōpūs, from Ancient Greek ὀκτώπους (oktṓpous), from ὀκτώ (oktṓ, “eight”) + πούς (poús, “foot”). Piecewise doublet of octopod and octopede.

parole.significato: The household common to the individuals of a compound organism.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?], from Ancient Greek οἶκος (oîkos, “house”).

parole.significato: A married priest (chiefly Orthodox Christian and Uniate usage), as opposed to a hieromonk.
parole.testo: From Latin oeconomus, from Ancient Greek οἰκονόμος (oikonómos), from οἶκος (oîkos, “house”) + νόμος (nómos, “law, rule”).

parole.significato: An apartment, room, or hall in an ancient Roman dwelling house.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin oecus, from Ancient Greek οἶκος (oîkos, “house”).

parole.significato: A biting fly of the genus Oestrus; a botfly.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin oestrus (“gadfly, sting, frenzy”), from Ancient Greek οἶστρος (oîstros), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eys-, used to form words denoting passion; see also Latin īra (“anger”), Lithuanian aistra (“violent passion”), Avestan 𐬀𐬈𐬯𐬨𐬀 (aesma, “anger”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Mount Olympus, the highest mountain in Greece; or (Greek mythology) the Greek gods and goddesses who…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English Olympyan, from Latin Olympius (“of or relating to Mount Olympus”) and its etymon Ancient Greek Ὀλῠ́μπῐος (Olŭ́mpĭos, “of or relating to Mount Olympus; living on Mount Olympus; Olympian”) + English -an (suffix forming adjectives meaning ‘of or pertaining to’, or forming agent

parole.significato: The central part of the hilum of a seed, through which the nutrient vessels pass into the raphe or chalaza.
parole.testo: From the post-classical Latin omphalodium from Ancient Greek ὀμφαλοειδής (omphaloeidḗs, “navel-like”) itself from Ancient Greek ὀμφαλός (omphalós, “navel”).

parole.significato: The study of dreams and their interpretation.
parole.testo: From oneiro- + -logy, historically from Latin oneirologia from Ancient Greek ὄνειρος (óneiros, “dream”).

parole.significato: Being the only child of one’s parent (especially one’s father)
parole.testo: From Middle English oonlybigeten, equivalent to only + begotten. Compare also Middle English only geten, oonly geten (“only-begotten”, literally “only-gotten”) and Middle English onbygoten, oon be-gotyn, one bygeten, oon bigetun, oon bigeten (“only-begotten”, literally “one-begotten”). Calque of Lat

parole.significato: A centaur with the body of an ass, instead of a prototypical horse.
parole.testo: Late Latin onocentaurus, from Ancient Greek ὀνοκένταυρος (onokéntauros, from ὄνος (ónos, “ass”) + κένταυρος (kéntauros, “centaur”)).

parole.significato: Worship of the ass or donkey.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin onolatrīa, from the Ancient Greek ὀνολᾰτρείᾱ (onolătreíā), from ὄνος (ónos, “ass”) + λᾰτρείᾱ (lătreíā, “worship”).

parole.significato: The property of a word that sounds like what it represents.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin onomatopoeïa, from Ancient Greek ὀνοματοποιία (onomatopoiía, “the coining of a word in imitation of a sound”), from ὀνοματοποιέω (onomatopoiéō, “to coin names”), from ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”) + ποιέω (poiéō, “to make, to do, to produce”). By surface analysis, onomato- + -poeia.

parole.significato: onyx
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin onychinus, from Ancient Greek ὀνῠ́χῐνος (onŭ́khĭnos).

parole.significato: Any species of the suborder Serpentes; a snake or serpent.
parole.testo: From Latin ophidia (from Ancient Greek ὄφις (óphis, “snake”)) + -ian.

parole.significato: Any of various rocks having snake-like markings, such as a mottled greenish porphyry.
parole.testo: From Latin ophites, from Ancient Greek ὀφίτης (ophítēs) (Etymology 2, below). Compare Ophite.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the eyes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ophthalmicus, from Ancient Greek ὀφθᾰλμῐκός (ophthălmĭkós, “of or for the eyes”), from ὀφθᾰλμός (ophthălmós, “eye”) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós, “-ic”, adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: Sustained tetanic spasm in which the body is bent backwards and stiffened, as produced by various diseases.
parole.testo: From Latin opisthotonus, and its source, Ancient Greek ὀπισθότονος (opisthótonos), corresponding to opistho- + tonus (“muscle tension”).

parole.significato: A gum resin obtained from the root of Opopanax chironium, formerly used in medicine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin opopanax, from Hellenistic Greek ὀποπάναξ (opopánax), from Ancient Greek ὀπός (opós, “vegetable juice”) + πάναξ (pánax, “any of several plants believed to have medicinal benefits”).

parole.significato: A large group of musicians who play together on various instruments, usually including some from strings, woodwind, bra…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin orchēstra, borrowed from Ancient Greek ὀρχήστρα (orkhḗstra), from ὀρχέομαι (orkhéomai, “to dance”) + -τρᾰ (-tră, “a suffix used to form instrument nouns (pl.)”).

parole.significato: Synonym of orchiectomy.
parole.testo: From Latin orchis (wrongly interpreting orchid- as the stem), from Ancient Greek ὄρχις (órkhis, “orchid, testicle”) + -ectomy.

parole.significato: A procedure for fixation of a testis, often to move an undescended testicle into the scrotum and keep it there.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin orchis + -pexy, from Ancient Greek ὄρχις (órkhis, “testicle”) + πῆξις (pêxis, “fixing”).

parole.significato: An orchid; now specifically, a plant of the genus Orchis.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin orchis, from Ancient Greek ὄρχις (órkhis, “testicle”).

parole.significato: A mountain nymph; an anthropomorphic appearance of the spirit of a mountain.
parole.testo: From Latin Orēas, Orēadis, from Ancient Greek Ὀρειάς (Oreiás), from ὄρος (óros, “mountain”).

parole.significato: The affective and conative character of mental activity as contrasted with its cognitive aspect; the appetitive aspect…
parole.testo: From Latin orexis (“longing; appetite”), from Ancient Greek ὄρεξις (órexis, “desire”), from ὀρέγω (orégō, “to reach, stretch”).

parole.significato: A type of medieval polyphony which builds upon an existing plainsong.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin organum, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ὄργανον (órganon, “organ, instrument, tool”). Doublet of organ, organon, and orgue.

parole.significato: A valuable yellow metal known to the Ancient Greeks and Romans; now sometimes interpreted as referring to a natural all…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin orichalcum, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ὀρείχαλκος (oreíkhalkos), from dative singular of ὄρος (óros, “mountain”) + χαλκός (khalkós, “copper”).

parole.significato: A kind of orphanage in ancient times.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin orphanō̆trophīum, from Ancient Greek ὀρφανοτροφεῖον (orphanotropheîon).

parole.significato: A hospital for orphans.
parole.testo: From Latin orphanō̆trophīa (cf. orphanō̆trophīum, from Ancient Greek ὀρφανοτροφεῖον (orphanotropheîon)), from Ancient Greek ὀρφᾰνός (orphănós, “orphan”) + τροφή (trophḗ, “nourishment, food; nurture, rearing, upbringing”). By surface analysis, orphan + -o- + -trophy.

parole.significato: Of a projection used in maps, architecture etc., in which the rays are parallel.
parole.testo: From ortho- + -graph + -ic. Compare French orthographique, Latin orthographus, Ancient Greek ὀρθογράφος (orthográphos).

parole.significato: Any of several antelopes, of the genus Oryx, native to Africa, which have long, straight horns
parole.testo: From Latin ory̆x, from Ancient Greek ὄρῠξ (órŭx, “a pickax; an oryx (the antelope)”).

parole.significato: One of a pair of scent organs in the larvae of certain swallowtail butterflies.
parole.testo: New Latin, from Ancient Greek ὀσμή (osmḗ, “smell”), ὀσμητός (osmētós, “smelled”) + -τήριον (-tḗrion).

parole.significato: earache
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ōtalgia, from Ancient Greek ὠταλγία (ōtalgía).

parole.significato: The basal part of the ovipositor of some species of insects, typically the non-retractile sheath that remains exposed w…
parole.testo: From Latin ovum (“egg”) plus scāpus (“stem or shaft”), from Ancient Greek (Doric) σκᾶπος (skâpos).

parole.significato: Sour milk.
parole.testo: From Latin oxygala, from Ancient Greek ὀξύγαλα (oxúgala).

parole.significato: A figure of speech in which two words or phrases with opposing meanings are used together intentionally for effect.
parole.testo: First attested in the 17th century, noun use of 5th century Latin oxymōrum (adjective), neut. nom. form of oxymōrus (adjective), from Ancient Greek ὀξύμωρος (oxúmōros), compound of ὀξύς (oxús, “sharp, keen, pointed”) (English oxy-, as in oxygen) + μωρός (mōrós, “dull, stupid, foolish”) (English moro

parole.significato: A public area in ancient Greece and Rome dedicated to the teaching and practice of wrestling and other sports; a wrestl…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin palaestra, from Ancient Greek παλαίστρα (palaístra, “wrestling school”).

parole.significato: A Philistine.
parole.testo: From Latin Palaestinus, from Ancient Greek Παλαιστινὸς (Palaistinòs). Cognate with Middle French palestin, Palestin.

parole.significato: A manuscript or document that has been erased or scraped clean, for reuse of the paper, parchment, vellum, or other med…
parole.testo: From Latin palimpsēstus, from Ancient Greek παλίμψηστος (palímpsēstos, “scraped again”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Pallas, an epithet of Athena, the goddess of wisdom, and potentially to other female Greek figures su…
parole.testo: From Latin Palladius (“of or relating to Pallas”) + -an (suffix forming adjectives from nouns). Palladius is derived from Pallas (from Ancient Greek Παλλάς (Pallás), genitive Παλλάδος (Palládos), an epithet of Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom) + -ius (suffix forming adjectives from nouns).

parole.significato: A safeguard.
parole.testo: The sense of "safeguard" comes from Latin Palladium (the image of Pallas that protected Troy), from Ancient Greek Παλλάδιον (Palládion), from Παλλάς (Pallás), an epithet used before Athena.

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to ancient Palmyra or Palmyrena.
parole.testo: From Latin Palmȳrēnus, from Ancient Greek Παλμυρηνός (Palmurēnós). By surface analysis, Palmyra + -ene.

parole.significato: A remedy believed to cure all disease and prolong life that was originally sought by alchemists; a cure-all.
parole.testo: From Latin panacēa, from Ancient Greek πανάκεια (panákeia), from πανακής (panakḗs, “all-healing”), from πᾶν (pân, “all”) (equivalent to English pan-) + ἄκος (ákos, “cure”).

parole.significato: Synonym of pankration.
parole.testo: From Latin pancratium, from Ancient Greek παγκράτιον (pankrátion, “a complete contest”). Doublet of pankration.

parole.significato: A gland near the stomach which secretes a fluid into the duodenum to assist with food digestion.
parole.testo: Existing in English since the sixteenth century: from Latin pancreas, from Ancient Greek πάγκρεας (pánkreas), from πᾶν (pân, “all”) (equivalent to English pan-) + κρέας (kréas, “flesh”).

parole.significato: A person who furthers the illicit love affairs of others; a pimp or procurer, especially when male.
parole.testo: From Chaucer’s character Pandare (in Troilus and Criseyde), from Italian Pandaro (found in Boccaccio), from Latin Pandarus, from Ancient Greek Πάνδαρος (Pándaros). (See also Shakespeare’s Troilus and Cressida.)

parole.significato: Usually in the plural form Pandects: a compendium or digest of writings on Roman law divided in 50 books, compiled in t…
parole.testo: Sense 3 (“comprehensive treatise”) is from Latin pandectēs (“book that contains everything, encyclopedia”), from Ancient Greek πανδέκτης (pandéktēs, “encyclopedia”, literally “all-receiver”), from παν- (pan-, prefix meaning ‘all’) (from πᾶς (pâs, “all”)) + δέκτης (déktēs, “receiver, recipient”) (fro

parole.significato: A compound raceme.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pānicula, diminutive of pānus (“ear of millet, literally 'thread wound on a bobbin'”), from Ancient Greek πῆνος (pênos, “web”), πηνίον (pēníon, “bobbin”). Doublet of panocha.

parole.significato: Uttering ominous or prophetic voices; divining.
parole.testo: From Latin panomphaeus, borrowed from Ancient Greek πανομφαῖος (panomphaîos).

parole.significato: A Classical comic actor, especially one who works mainly through gesture and mime.
parole.testo: First appears c. 1606, from Latin pantomīmus, from Ancient Greek παντόμιμος (pantómimos), from πᾶς (pâs, “each, all”) + μιμέομαι (miméomai, “to mimic”). The verbal form first appears c. 1768.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the pope or the papacy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pāpa, from Ancient Greek πάππας (páppas).

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to Paphos, the mythical birthplace of the goddess of love on the island of Cyprus.
parole.testo: From Latin Paphius [from Ancient Greek Πάφιος (Páphios), from Πάφος (Páphos, “Paphos”) + -ιος (-ios)] + English -an.

parole.significato: The markedly reduced sepals of an Asteraceae floret that take the form of trichomes or scale attached to the ovary or s…
parole.testo: Via Latin pappus from Ancient Greek πάππος (páppos), an affectionate term for elderly men (referencing beards).

parole.significato: A plant (Cyperus papyrus) in the sedge family, native to the Nile river valley, paper reed.
parole.testo: From Middle English papirus, borrowed from Latin papȳrus, from Ancient Greek πάπυρος (pápuros), of unknown origin. Doublet of papyros.

parole.significato: coastal; native to the coast
parole.testo: From Latin paralius, from Ancient Greek παράλιος (parálios, “coastal, maritime”).

parole.significato: A solid figure, having six faces, all parallelograms, all opposite faces being similar and parallel.
parole.testo: From Latin parallēlepipedum, from Ancient Greek παραλληλεπίπεδος (parallēlepípedos, “with parallel surfaces”), from παράλληλος (parállēlos, “parallel”) + ἐπίπεδος (epípedos, “plane”).

parole.significato: A convex quadrilateral in which each pair of opposite edges are parallel and of equal length.
parole.testo: From Latin parallelogrammum, from Ancient Greek παράλληλος (parállēlos, “parallel”) + γραμμή (grammḗ, “line”).

parole.significato: The complete loss of voluntary control of part of a living body, such as one or more limbs.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin paralysis, from Ancient Greek παράλυσις (parálusis, “palsy”), from παραλύω (paralúō, “to disable on one side”). By surface analysis, para- + -lysis. Doublet of palsy.

parole.significato: An engraved tablet, usually of brass, set up in a public place.
parole.testo: Latin parapegma, Ancient Greek παράπηγμα (parápēgma) to fix beside: compare French parapegme.

parole.significato: A device for keeping track of cyclical events, particularly of stars, weather, seasons, and so on.
parole.testo: From Latin parapegma, from Ancient Greek παράπηγμα (parápēgma, “something fixed on or hung up”) .

parole.significato: The practice of paraphrasing: use of different words.
parole.testo: From Latin paraphrasis, from Ancient Greek παράφρασις (paráphrasis). Compare periphrasis.

parole.significato: One of two apartments adjoining the ancient stage, probably used as dressing rooms.
parole.testo: New Latin, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: The day of preparation before the (Jewish) Sabbath; Friday.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin parascevē, from Ancient Greek παρασκευή (paraskeuḗ, literally “preparation”).

parole.significato: A long ceremonial dagger from Roman times.
parole.testo: From Latin parazonium, from Ancient Greek παραζόνιον (parazónion).

parole.significato: A pard; a panther or leopard.
parole.testo: From Latin pardalis, from Ancient Greek πάρδαλις (párdalis), from an unattested Old Iranian word; compare Persian پلنگ (palang), Pashto پړانګ (pṙâng).

parole.significato: The study of proverbs.
parole.testo: From paremia (“proverb”) + -ology, from Latin paroemia, from Ancient Greek παροιμία (paroimía).

parole.significato: Something unimportant, incidental, or superfluous; a trifle
parole.testo: Latin parergon, Ancient Greek πάρεργον (párergon); παρά (pará, “beside”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”).

parole.significato: Synonym of sun dog (“a bright spot in the sky, usually one of two on the parhelic circle on both sides of the sun (or o…
parole.testo: From Latin parelion, from Ancient Greek παρήλιον (parḗlion), from παρά (pará) + ἥλιος (hḗlios, “sun”).

parole.significato: In Ancient Greek musical theory, the lower-pitched of the two movable notes in the nearer tetrachord on a lyre, pitched…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin parhypatē, from Ancient Greek παρυπάτη (parupátē, literally “next to the hypate, next-highest”). parole.significato: Of or relating to Parnassus, as the source of literary (especially poetic) inspiration; (hence) of or belonging to poet…
parole.testo: From Parnassus, from Latin Parnassus, from Ancient Greek Παρνασσός (Parnassós).

parole.significato: A work or performance that imitates another work or performance with ridicule or irony.
parole.testo: From Latin parōdia, from Ancient Greek παρῳδία (parōidía, “parody”), from παρά (pará, “besides”) + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”).

parole.significato: A proverb.
parole.testo: From Latin paroemia (“proverb”), from Ancient Greek παροιμία (paroimía, “proverb”).

parole.significato: A pun or play on words.
parole.testo: From Latin paronomasia, from Ancient Greek παρονομασία (paronomasía, “play upon words which sound alike”), from παρα- (para-) + ὀνομασία (onomasía, “naming”).

parole.significato: The people of Paropamisus in ancient Pakistan.
parole.testo: From Latin Paropamisadae, from Ancient Greek Παροπαμισάδαι (Paropamisádai), from Old Persian *Para-uparisaina (“beyond higher than the eagle”).

parole.significato: A Parthian.
parole.testo: From Latin Parthus, from Ancient Greek Πάρθος (Párthos).

parole.significato: Passover (biblical, Israelite, Jewish, or Christian Passover; this term also includes Quartodeciman Passover, observed…
parole.testo: From Latin pascha (“Passover”), from Ancient Greek πάσχα (páskha, “Passover”), from Aramaic פַּסְחָא (paskha), from Hebrew פֶּסַח (pésakh). Doublet of Pasch, paska, paskha, and Pesach.

parole.significato: A type of lesser priest in ancient Egypt, originally serving as a doorkeeper to a temple.
parole.testo: From Latin pastophorus, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek παστοφόρος (pastophóros), from παστός (pastós, “ceremonial curtain”) + -φόρος (-phóros, “bearer”), a loose calque of Demotic Egyptian jrj-ꜥꜣ, from Egyptian jrj-ꜥꜣ (“doorkeeper”), from jrj (“keeper”) + ꜥꜣ (“door”). parole.significato: The thin membrane that extends between the limbs and body of a bat or of gliding mammals.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin patagīum (“gilded edging of a woman's tunic”), from an unattested Ancient Greek παταγεῖον (patageîon), perhaps from πάταγος (pátagos, “clatter”).

parole.significato: Synonym of bottom: a passive usually-male partner in homosexual anal intercourse.
parole.testo: From Latin pathicus, from Ancient Greek παθικός (pathikós), from πάθος (páthos, “suffering, feeling”), from πάσχω (páskhō, “to feel, to suffer”).

parole.significato: Related to how emotions are manifested, especially in the face.
parole.testo: From Latin pathognomicus, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek παθογνωμικός (pathognōmikós), shortened form of παθογνωμονικός (pathognōmonikós, “pathognomonic”).

parole.significato: Having traits mostly inherited from the male parent
parole.testo: From Latin pātr- + -o- + Ancient Greek κλίνειν (klínein) + -ous.

parole.significato: The hiatus between prosodic units, e.g. at the end of a sentence.
parole.testo: From Latin pausa (“break”), from Ancient Greek παῦσις (paûsis). Doublet of pause.

parole.significato: Any of certain plants of the family Fabaceae: Pisum sativum and others.
parole.testo: Back-formation from pease, an original singular reinterpreted as a plural. Further from Middle English pese (“a pea”), from Old English pise, from Latin pisa, pisum, from Ancient Greek πίσον (píson).

parole.significato: Pathology of the foot.
parole.testo: Formed as pedo- (“foot”) + -pathy (“disease”); an etymological hybrid equivalent to the Latin pēs (“foot”) + the Ancient Greek πάθος (páthos, “suffering”).

parole.significato: Any winged horse; a pterippus.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English Pegase, Pegasus, from Latin Pēgasus, from Ancient Greek Πήγασος (Pḗgasos), traditionally associated with πηγή (pēgḗ, “spring, fountain, fountain fed by a spring”), especially used to denote springs of Ocean, where Perseus killed Medusa, from whose blood Pegasus sprang. parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the open sea.
parole.testo: From Latin pelagius [from Ancient Greek πελάγιος (pelágios), from πέλαγος (pélagos) + -ιος (-ios)] + -an.

parole.significato: Living in the open sea rather than in coastal or inland waters.
parole.testo: From Latin pelagicus (and possibly pelagus); from Ancient Greek πελαγικός (pelagikós), from πέλαγος (pélagos, “sea”). By surface analysis, -pelag + -ic.

parole.significato: Any of the extinct crocodile-like animals of genus †Pelagosaurus which lived during the Jurassic period.
parole.testo: From Latin pelagus from Ancient Greek πελαγικός (pelagikós), from πέλαγος (pélagos, “sea”) + -saur.

parole.significato: Any of various seabirds of the family Pelecanidae, having a long bill with a distendable pouch.
parole.testo: From Middle English pellican, pellicane, from Old English pellican (“pelican”), from Latin pelecānus, from Ancient Greek πελεκάν (pelekán), πέλεκυς (pélekus, “hatchet”).

parole.significato: A circumscribed, elevated, livid patch on the skin.
parole.testo: From Latin pelidnoma, from Ancient Greek πελίδνωμα (pelídnōma, “dark spot”).

parole.significato: A small shield, especially one of an approximately elliptical form, or crescent-shaped.
parole.testo: From Latin pelta, from Ancient Greek πέλτη (péltē, “shield”).

parole.significato: A noun having five cases.
parole.testo: From Latin pentaptōtum, from Ancient Greek πεντάπτωτος (pentáptōtos).

parole.significato: The commander of a platoon of fifty men.
parole.testo: From Latin pentēcontarchus, from Ancient Greek πεντηκόνταρχος (pentēkóntarkhos, literally “commander of fifty”).

parole.significato: A military unit commanded by a pentecontarch.
parole.testo: From Latin pentēcontarchia, from Ancient Greek πεντηκονταρχία (pentēkontarkhía). By surface analysis, pentecontarch + -y.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Mount Pentelicus (Penteliko Mountain), near Athens, famous for its fine white marble quarries.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Pentelicus, from Ancient Greek Πεντελικός (Pentelikós).

parole.significato: A prosal group of two and a half feet.
parole.testo: From Latin penthēmimeris, from Ancient Greek πενθημιμερής (penthēmimerḗs, “having five half-feet”): πέντε (pénte, “five”) + ἡμι- (hēmi-) + μέρος (méros, “part, metrical foot”).

parole.significato: A peplos, an Ancient Greek garment formed of a tubular piece of cloth folded back upon itself halfway down so that the…
parole.testo: From Latin peplum, from Ancient Greek πέπλον (péplon), accusative singular of πέπλος (péplos).

parole.significato: An upper garment worn by women in Ancient Greece and Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: A fruit of plants of the gourd family Cucurbitaceae, possessing a hard rind and producing many seeds in a single, centr…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pepō, from Ancient Greek πέπων (pépōn, “large melon”), from πέπων (pépōn, “ripe”), from πέπτω (péptō, “ripen”). Doublet of pumpion; compare pumpkin.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, capable of, or aiding digestion.
parole.testo: From Latin pepticus, from Ancient Greek πέψις (pépsis, “digestion”), a form of πέσσω (péssō).

parole.significato: A number that is the sum of all of its divisors except itself.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin numerus perfectus, with this use of perfectus itself a semantic loan from Ancient Greek τέλειος (téleios).

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to Pergamum.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Pergamēnus or its etymon Ancient Greek Περγαμηνός (Pergamēnós). By surface analysis, Pergam(um) + ene.

parole.significato: The membrane (or periosteum) which covers the outer surface of the skull.
parole.testo: From late Latin pericranium, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek περικράνιον (perikránion), noun use of the neuter form of περικράνιος (perikránios, “around the skull”), from περί (perí, “around”) + κρανίον (kraníon, “skull”).

parole.significato: The sum of the distance of all the lengths of the sides of an object.
parole.testo: From Latin perimetros, Ancient Greek περίμετρος (perímetros). Equivalent to peri- + meter.

parole.significato: The use of more words than are necessary to express the idea; a roundabout, or indirect, way of speaking; circumlocutio…
parole.testo: From Latin periphrasis from Ancient Greek περίφρασις (períphrasis), from περιφράζομαι (periphrázomai, “to consider all sides of an issue”), from περί (perí, “around”) + φράζω (phrázō, “to show, point out”). See phrase.

parole.significato: An account of a voyage, particularly those of Hanno and Arrian, recording ports and coastal landmarks.
parole.testo: From Latin periplūs (“account of a voyage”) and Ancient Greek περίπλους (períplous, “voyage, naval manouver, account of a voyage”), from περί (perí, “peri-: around”) + πλοῦς (ploûs, “voyage”), from πλεῖν (pleîn, “to sail”). Cf. French périple, Spanish periplo, & Italian periplo.

parole.significato: pneumonic (of or pertaining to pneumonia (an inflammation of the lungs))

parole.significato: Superfluity of words; verbosity; long-windedness.
parole.testo: From Latin perissologia, from Ancient Greek περισσός (perissós, “odd, uneven”) + Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía). By surface analysis, perisso- + logy or periss- + -ology.

parole.significato: In mammals, the serous membrane lining the cavity of the abdomen and that is folded over the viscera.

parole.significato: A loincloth worn by men and women in ancient Greece.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin perizoma. from Ancient Greek περίζωμα (perízōma).

parole.significato: A descendant of Perseus.

parole.significato: Any of the meteors in a meteor shower that appears to come from the constellation Perseus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Persēis f, from Ancient Greek Περσηΐς f (Persēḯs), from Περσεύς (Perseús) + -ις (-is). By surface analysis, Perseus + -id.

parole.significato: Synonym of Persian.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Persicus, from Ancient Greek Περσικός (Persikós), from Πέρσης (Pérsēs, “Persian”, noun) + -ικός (-ikós, adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: One of the scales of a leaf bud.
parole.testo: From Latin pērula, diminutive of pera (“wallet”), from Ancient Greek πήρα (pḗra). Compare French pérule.

parole.significato: A large broad-rimmed bell used for summoning monks.
parole.testo: From Latin petasius, from Ancient Greek πέτασος (pétasos, “petasus: a broad-brimmed hat”).

parole.significato: Any flying marsupial of the order Phalangeriformes, such as those in genera Petaurista, Phalanger, Acrobates.
parole.testo: From Latin petaurista (“a ropedancer, acrobat”), from Ancient Greek πετευριστής (peteuristḗs), from πετευρίζομαι (peteurízomai, “dance on a rope”), from πέτευρον (péteuron, “a pole, a stage for ropedancers”).

parole.significato: radiotelephony clear-code word for the letter P.

parole.significato: The logical fallacy of begging the question (i.e., "assuming the conclusion").

parole.significato: Petrifying; converting into stone.

parole.significato: In Ancient Greece, a metal medallion worn by men or used to ornament the harness of a horse.
parole.testo: From Latin phalerae, from Ancient Greek φάλαρα (phálara) (plural of φάλαρον (phálaron)).

parole.significato: Phallic priest thought to have been a precursor of the Christian stylite.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin phallobatēs, from Ancient Greek φαλλοβάτης (phallobátēs, literally “phallus-climber”). Doublet of phallobate (derived via the Latin adapted form phallobata; compare English stylobate).

parole.significato: The person who carries the phallus in a phallophoria
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin phallophorus, from Ancient Greek φαλλοφόρος (phallophóros). By surface analysis, phallo- + -phorus.

parole.significato: A penis, especially when erect.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin phallus (“membrum virile, phallus, or a figure thereof”), from Ancient Greek φαλλός (phallós).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Pharisees.
parole.testo: From Latin Pharisaicus, from Ancient Greek Φαρισαϊκός (Pharisaïkós). By surface analysis, Pharisee + -ic.

parole.significato: pharmaceutical
parole.testo: From Latin pharmaceuticus (“of drugs”), from Ancient Greek φαρμακευτικός (pharmakeutikós, “drug maker”).

parole.significato: Synonym of quack: a peddler of fraudulent medicines and cures.
parole.testo: From Latin pharmacopola, from Ancient Greek φαρμακοπώλης (pharmakopṓlēs), from φάρμακον (phármakon, “drug, charm, enchantment”) + -πώλης (-pṓlēs, “-seller, -monger”). Doublet of pharmacopolist.

parole.significato: Synonym of pharmacist: a person who sells medicine, an apothecary.
parole.testo: From Latin pharmacopola + -ist, from Ancient Greek φαρμακοπώλης (pharmakopṓlēs), from φάρμακον (phármakon, “drug, charm, enchantment”) + -πώλης (-pṓlēs, “-seller, -monger”). Cf. papyropolist. Doublet of pharmacopole.

parole.significato: The study of lighthouses or other forms of light-signalling.
parole.testo: From Latin Pharos or its source Ancient Greek Φάρος (Pháros) + -logy.

parole.significato: The French bean, or kidney bean.
parole.testo: From Latin phaselus, phaseolus, from Ancient Greek φάσηλος (phásēlos, “a kind of bean”). Compare French phaséole, faséole, English fesels.

parole.significato: any of several domesticated beans, of the genus Phaseolus, native to the Americas
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin phaseolus.

parole.significato: An apparition; a phantom.
parole.testo: From Latin phasma or Ancient Greek φάσμα (phásma). See phase.

parole.significato: Any of a series of dioctahedral micas of composition K(AlMg)₂(OH)₂(SiAl)₄O₁₀, similar to muscovite but with addition of…

parole.significato: Consisting of three prosodic feet, normally a spondee, dactyl, and spondee (or trochee), but admitting of some variatio…
parole.testo: From Latin Pherecratēus, by-form of Pherecratīus, from Ancient Greek Φερεκρᾰ́τειος (Pherekrắteios), from Φερεκρᾰ́της (Pherekrắtēs, “Pherecrates”), the name of the metre’s inventor.

parole.significato: Any of the discourses of Demosthenes against Philip II of Macedon, defending the liberty of Athens.
parole.testo: From Latin philippicus, from Ancient Greek φιλιππικός (philippikós), from Φίλιππος (Phílippos, “lover of horses”), from φίλος (phílos, “loving”) + ἵππος (híppos, “horse”).

parole.significato: The humanistic study of texts and their languages, especially ancient or classical languages.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English Philologie, from Latin philologia, from Ancient Greek φιλολογίᾱ (philologíā, “love of argument or reasoning, love of learning and literature”).

parole.significato: The shallow vertical groove running from the nasal septum to the center of the upper lip.
parole.testo: Borrowed from the Latin philtrum (“a love potion”), from Ancient Greek φῐ́λτρον (phĭ́ltron, “a love charm; the dimple in the upper lip”). Doublet of philter.

parole.significato: A solid mass formed by inflamed connective tissue, such as forms around an appendix in appendicitis.
parole.testo: From Latin phlegmōn, phlegmonē (“inflammation beneath the skin”), from Ancient Greek φλεγμονή (phlegmonḗ, “inflammation, fiery heat”), from φλέγω (phlégō, “burn”).

parole.significato: A seal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin phōca, from Ancient Greek φώκη (phṓkē).

parole.significato: Pertaining to the ancient Greek region of Phocis.
parole.testo: From Latin Phōcis (itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek Φωκίς (Phōkís)) + -an.

parole.significato: Pertaining to true seals (also known as earless seals, as opposed to eared seals such as sea lions); seallike.
parole.testo: From Latin phōca (“seal”) (from Ancient Greek φώκη (phṓkē)) + -ine.

parole.significato: Relating to the sounds of spoken language.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin phōnēticus, from Ancient Greek φωνητῐκός (phōnētĭkós). By surface analysis, phone + -etic.

parole.significato: A chemical element (symbol P) with an atomic number of 15, that exists in several allotropic forms.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin phōsphorus, from Ancient Greek φωσφόρος (phōsphóros, “the bearer of light”), from φῶς (phôs, “light”) + φέρω (phérō, “to bear, carry”).

parole.significato: divination using light
parole.testo: From photo- (“light”) + -mancy (“divination of”), from Latin -mantia, ultimately from Ancient Greek μᾰντείᾱ (mănteíā, “divination”).

parole.significato: Any of several perennial reeds, of the genus Phragmites, found in wetlands.
parole.testo: From Latin phragmītēs, from Ancient Greek φραγμίτης (phragmítēs).

parole.significato: A clan or kinship group consisting of a number of families claiming descent from a common ancestor and having certain c…
parole.testo: PIE word  *bʰréh₂tēr From Latin phrātria, from Ancient Greek φρατρία (phratría, “tribe, clan”), from φράτηρ (phrátēr) + -ία (-ía).

parole.significato: phrenitis
parole.testo: From Latin phrenesis, from Ancient Greek *φρένησις (*phrénēsis), a later equivalent of φρενῖτις (phrenîtis, “inflammation of the brain”). Doublet of frenzy.

parole.significato: Madness, especially as caused by inflammation of the brain; encephalitis, encephalomeningitis, or meningitis.
parole.testo: From Latin phrenītis, from Ancient Greek φρενῖτις (phrenîtis), from φρήν (phrḗn, “mind”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Phrygia, its people, or their culture.
parole.testo: From Latin Phrygiānus + English -an (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives). Phrygianus is derived from Phrygia + -ānus (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’); and Phrygia is from Ancient Greek Φρῠγῐ́ᾱ (Phrŭgĭ́ā, “region in Anatolia”), from Φρῠ́ξ (Phrŭ́x, “person from Phrygia”) (fu

parole.significato: An infestation by pubic lice (Pthirus pubis).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin phthīriāsis, from Ancient Greek φθειρίασις (phtheiríasis).

parole.significato: phthisic
parole.testo: From Latin phthisicus, from Ancient Greek: compare French phthisique. See phthisis.

parole.significato: An atrophy of the body or part of the body, especially pulmonary tuberculosis.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin phthisis, from Ancient Greek φθίσις (phthísis, “consumption, decline, wasting away”), from φθίω (phthíō, “to waste away”).

parole.significato: The ruler of a phyle in Ancient Greece.
parole.testo: From Latin phylarchus, from Ancient Greek φύλαρχος (phúlarkhos), from φῡλή (phūlḗ, “large clan or tribe of ancient Greece”).

parole.significato: A flattened petiole or leaf rachis that resembles and functions as a leaf, and may or may not be combined with an actua…
parole.testo: From Latin phyllodium, from Ancient Greek φυλλώδης (phullṓdēs, “resembling a leaf”).

parole.significato: A leaf, or something (flat) resembling a leaf.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin phyllon, from Ancient Greek φύλλον (phúllon, “leaf”). Doublet of phyllo, distantly also with foil, folio, and folium.

parole.significato: A rank in the classification of organisms, below kingdom and above class; also called a divisio or a division, especial…
parole.testo: From Latin phylum, from Ancient Greek φῦλον (phûlon, “tribe, race”).

parole.significato: Relating to or concerning existent materials; physical.
parole.testo: From Middle English phisik, from Latin physicus, from Ancient Greek φῠσῐκός (phŭsĭkós, “natural; physical”), from φύσις (phúsis, “origin, birth; nature, quality; form, shape; type, kind”), from φῠ́ω (phŭ́ō, “grow”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to appear, become, rise up”).

parole.significato: An art gallery, especially one exhibiting pictures.
parole.testo: From Latin pinacotheca, from Ancient Greek πινακοθήκη (pinakothḗkē).

parole.significato: A tablet or register.
parole.testo: From Latin pinax, from Ancient Greek πίναξ (pínax, “tablet”).

parole.significato: A small crab of the genus Pinnotheres, which live symbiotically in the shells of certain molluscs.
parole.testo: From Latin pīnotērēs, from Ancient Greek πινοτήρης (pinotḗrēs), from Ancient Greek πίνη (pínē, “pen shell”) + Ancient Greek τηρέω (tēréō, “to guard”).

parole.significato: Babesia, a genus of hematozoa that invades the red blood cells of humans and domesticated animals such as dogs and sheep
parole.testo: From Latin pirum (“pear”) + Ancient Greek πλάσμα (plásma, “image, formation”).

parole.significato: Someone with a Pisces astrological sign.
parole.testo: From Latin piscēs, the nominative plural of piscis (“fish”), calque of Ancient Greek ἰχθύες (ikhthúes, “fish (pl); name of constellation”). Compare Akkadian 𒁺𒉺𒉺 (DU.NU.NU, “fish-cord”); the constellation is often depicted as two fish tied by a ribbon.

parole.significato: A soft, black, tarry bitumen, intermediate between petroleum and asphalt.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pissasphaltus, from Ancient Greek πισσάσφαλτος (pissásphaltos), from πίσσα (píssa, “pitch”) + ἄσφαλτος (ásphaltos, “asphalt”).

parole.significato: Having faith; trusting
parole.testo: From Latin pisticus (“pure; genuine”), from Ancient Greek πιστικός (pistikós).

parole.significato: Membership of a particular planet or moon, by origin, birth, naturalization, ownership, allegiance or otherwise.
parole.testo: From planet + -ality from Latin planeta, planetes, from Ancient Greek πλανήτης (planḗtēs, “wanderer”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to planets; planetary.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin planeticus, from Ancient Greek πλανητικός (planētikós), from πλανητός (planētós, “wandering; planetary”), from πλανήτης (planḗtēs, “wanderer, planet”), from πλανάω (planáō, “to wander”) + -της (-tēs, masculine agent noun suffix).

parole.significato: A synthetic, solid, hydrocarbon-based polymer, whether thermoplastic or thermosetting.
parole.testo: From Latin plasticus (“of molding”), from Ancient Greek πλαστικός (plastikós), from πλάσσω (plássō, “to mold, form”). Doublet of plastique.

parole.significato: A small piece of plastic, metal, ivory, etc., for plucking the strings of a guitar, lyre, mandolin, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin plēctrum, from Ancient Greek πλῆκτρον (plêktron, “anything to strike with, an instrument for striking the lyre, a spear point”), from πλήσσειν (plḗssein, “to strike, to smite, to sting”). Displaced native Old English sleġel.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the pleura; pleural.
parole.testo: From Latin pleura. By surface analysis, pleur- + -o-.

parole.significato: A figure of speech in which a word is repeated so as not only to signify the individual thing denoted by it, but also i…
parole.testo: From Latin plŏcē, from Ancient Greek πλοκή (plokḗ, “complication”).

parole.significato: Any specific edition of a work by Plutarch, often specifically Plutarch's Lives
parole.testo: Via Latin Plūtarchus from Ancient Greek Πλούτᾰρχος (Ploútărkhos).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Pluto, the Greek and Roman god of the underworld; demonic, infernal.
parole.testo: The adjective is derived from Latin Plūtōnius (“of or relating to Pluto, Greek and Roman god of the underworld”) + -an (suffix forming adjectives). Plūtōnius is from Ancient Greek Πλουτώνιος (Ploutṓnios, “of or relating to Pluto”), from Πλούτων (Ploútōn, “Pluto”) (from πλοῦτος (ploûtos, “riches, wea

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or resembling air or other gases
parole.testo: From Latin pneumaticus, from Ancient Greek πνευματικός (pneumatikós, “relating to wind or air”), from πνεῦμα (pneûma, “wind, air, breath, spirit”), from πνέω (pnéō, “to blow, breath”).

parole.significato: Of, or relating to the lungs; pulmonary.
parole.testo: From the post-Classical Latin pneumonicus and its etymon, the Ancient Greek πνευμονικός (pneumonikós).

parole.significato: Any grass of the genus Poa, especially Poa annua.
parole.testo: From scientific Latin Poa (genus name), from Ancient Greek πόα (póa, “fodder”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to gout.
parole.testo: From Latin podagricus, from Ancient Greek ποδαγρικός (podagrikós, “gouty”).

parole.significato: A platform on which to stand, as when conducting an orchestra or preaching at a pulpit; any low platform or dais.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin podium, from Ancient Greek πόδιον (pódion, “base”), a diminutive of πούς (poús, “foot”). Doublet of pew.

parole.significato: The study of poesy or poetry.
parole.testo: From Latin poēsis [itself from Ancient Greek ποίησις (poíēsis)] + -logy.

parole.significato: The military commander-in-chief in Athens, one of the nine archonts.
parole.testo: From Latin polemarchus, from Ancient Greek πολέμαρχος (polémarkhos). By surface analysis, polem- + -arch.

parole.significato: Government that is in some manner chosen by the governed citizens.
parole.testo: From Latin politicus, from Ancient Greek πολιτικός (politikós), from πολίτης (polítēs, “citizen”) + -cracy.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the role of citizens in the organization and choice of government.
parole.testo: From Latin politicus, from Ancient Greek πολιτικός (politikós), from πολίτης (polítēs, “citizen”) + -cratic.

parole.significato: A state of many rulers, many leaders.
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek πολύς (polús, “many”) + ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “beginning”).

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Polygonum, especially knotgrass.
parole.testo: From Latin polygonium, from Ancient Greek πολύγονον (polúgonon). More at polygonum.

parole.significato: Someone gifted or learned to a great extent or in multiple disciplines; a great scholar.
parole.testo: From Latin polyhistor (“very learned”), from Hellenistic Ancient Greek πολυΐστωρ (poluḯstōr, “greatly learned”).

parole.significato: A cylindrical coelenterate, such as the hydra, having a mouth surrounded with tentacles.
parole.testo: From Latin polypus (“a polyp, a polypus in the nose”), from Ancient Greek πολύπους (polúpous, from πολύς (polús, “many”) + πούς (poús, “foot”)). Doublet of polypus.

parole.significato: A stylistic scheme in which words from the same root are used together, or a word is repeated in a different inflection…
parole.testo: Via Latin, from Ancient Greek πολύπτωτον (polúptōton), neuter of πολύπτωτος (polúptōtos, “having many cases”), from πολύς (polús, “many”) + πίπτω (píptō, “to fall”).

parole.significato: A medical phenomenon.
parole.testo: From Latin polypus, from Ancient Greek πολύπους (polúpous). Doublet of polyp.

parole.significato: A machine consisting of many pulleys
parole.testo: From Latin polyspaston (“hoisting-tackle with many pulleys”), from Ancient Greek πολύσπαστον (polúspaston, “compound pulley”).

parole.significato: dyshidrosis eczema
parole.testo: From Latin pompholyx, from Ancient Greek πομφόλυξ (pomphólux, “a bubble; the slag on the surface of smelted ore”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to kingdom of Pontus.
parole.testo: From Latin ponticus, from Ancient Greek Ποντῐκός (Pontĭkós), from Πόντος (Póntos, “Black Sea, Pontus”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic: forming adjectives”). Equivalent to Pontus + -ic. Doublet of bonduc and bundook.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a type of Ancient Greek wine.
parole.testo: Latin Pramnium, from Ancient Greek Πράμνιος (Prámnios).

parole.significato: A variety of cryptocrystalline of a green colour.
parole.testo: From Latin prasius, from Ancient Greek πράσιος (prásios, “of a green colour”), from πράσον (práson, “leek”).

parole.significato: Of a clear, light green color.
parole.testo: From Latin prasinus, from Ancient Greek πρᾰ́σῐνος (prắsĭnos, “leek-green, light green”).

parole.significato: The practical application of any branch of learning.
parole.testo: Partly from Latin prāxis and partly from its etymon Ancient Greek πρᾶξις (prâxis, “action, activity, practice”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or of the nature of a preposition.
parole.testo: From Latin praepositiō (“a setting before, a preposition”), a calque of Ancient Greek πρόθεσις (próthesis, “a setting before, preposition (grammar)”) + -al.

parole.significato: A potentially painful or harmful medical condition in which the erect penis does not return to its flaccid state (despi…
parole.testo: From Latin priapismus, from Priapus (“the god of procreation, the penis”) + -ism, from Ancient Greek πριαπισμός (priapismós).

parole.significato: An elongated tube from the head or connected to the mouth, of an animal.
parole.testo: From Latin proboscis, from Ancient Greek προβοσκίς (proboskís, “elephant's trunk”) literally "means for taking food," from προ- (pro-, “before”) + βόσκω (bóskō, “to nourish, feed”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *gʷeh₃- from which also comes βοτάνη (botánē, “grass, fodder”).

parole.significato: A rhetorical exercise in which the speaker raises an objection to his own argument and then immediately answers it, in…
parole.testo: From Latin procatalepsis (“anticipating and answering an objection”), from Ancient Greek προκατάληψις (prokatálēpsis, “seizing in advance”).

parole.significato: A metrical foot consisting of four short syllables.
parole.testo: From Latin proceleusmaticus, from Ancient Greek προκελευσματικός (prokeleusmatikós), to rouse to action beforehand, to incite.

parole.significato: Synonym of proem.
parole.testo: From Latin prooemium, from Ancient Greek προοίμιον (prooímion).

parole.significato: The assignment of something to a period of time that precedes it.
parole.testo: From Latin prolepsis, from Ancient Greek πρόληψις (prólēpsis, “preconception, anticipation”), from προλαμβάνω (prolambánō, “take beforehand, anticipate”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Prometheus, a demigod in Greek mythology who created mortals from clay and stole fire from Zeus to…
parole.testo: The adjective is derived from Prometheus (“demigod in Greek mythology”) + -an (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives; and forming agent nouns). Prometheus is a learned borrowing from Latin Promētheus, and from its etymon Ancient Greek Προμηθεύς (Promētheús), from προμηθής (promēthḗ

parole.significato: A medicine which preserves or defends against disease; a preventive.
parole.testo: From Latin prophylacticus, from Ancient Greek προφυλακτικός (prophulaktikós, “prophylactic”).

parole.significato: The prevention of, or the protective treatment for, disease.
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek πρό (pró, “before”) + φύλαξις (phúlaxis, “a watching, guarding”).

parole.significato: To pledge; to offer as a toast in the manner of drinking, that is, by drinking first and passing the cup.
parole.testo: From Latin propinō, from Ancient Greek προπῑ́νω (propī́nō, “to drink to someone's health”).

parole.significato: An aromatic glue-like substance produced by honeybees from tree resin, waxes, and their own secretions, used in the con…
parole.testo: From Latin propolis, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek πρόπολις (própolis, “suburb; propolis”) (apparently because the material was used by bees to extend their hives), from Ancient Greek προ- (pro-, “pro-”) + πόλις (pólis, “city”).

parole.significato: A vestibule or entrance, (especially) to a temple.
parole.testo: From Latin propylaeum, from Ancient Greek προπύλαιον (propúlaion), from προ- (pro-, “before”, “in front of”) + πύλη (púlē, “gate”).

parole.significato: The stage area between the curtain and the orchestra.
parole.testo: From Latin proscaenium (“in front of the scenery”), from Ancient Greek προσκήνιον (proskḗnion), from πρό (pró, “before”) + σκηνή (skēnḗ, “scene building”).

parole.significato: A study of the individuals in a group of people within a specific context and their relationships.
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting New Latin combining forms: prosopo- + -graphy; from the Latin prosōpographia (“description of a person’s appearance; description of an individual’s life”), from the Ancient Greek πρόσωπον (prósōpon, “face, person”) + -γρᾰφῐ́ᾱ (-grăphĭ́ā, “writing,

parole.significato: An artificial replacement for a body part, either internal or external.
parole.testo: Via Latin, from Ancient Greek πρόσθεσις (prósthesis, “addition”), from προστίθημι (prostíthēmi, “to add”), from πρός (prós, “towards”) + τίθημι (títhēmi, “to place”), from Proto-Indo-European *próti, *préti + *dʰédʰeh₁ti (“to be putting, to be placing”). By surface analysis, prosth- + -esis.

parole.significato: A plant, usually a pteridophyte, in gametophyte stage in the metagenesis cycle.
parole.testo: From Latin pro (“forwards”) + Ancient Greek θᾰλλός (thăllós, “young branch, twig”).

parole.significato: A negotiator; a factor, especially one who negotiates marriages.
parole.testo: Latin proxeneta, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: The town hall in an Ancient Greek city.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin prytanēum, from Ancient Greek πρυτανεῖον (prutaneîon), from πρύτανις (prútanis, “prytanis”) + -εῖον (-eîon, noun-forming suffix meaning “place or building associated with a specific purpose or person”). By surface analysis, prytanis + -eum.

parole.significato: An official in ancient Athens
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin prytanis, from Ancient Greek πρύτανις (prútanis).

parole.significato: An omasum.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin psalterium, from Ancient Greek ψαλτήριον (psaltḗrion). Doublet of psalter, psalterion, and psaltery.

parole.significato: A psephism.
parole.testo: From Latin psēphisma, and its source, Ancient Greek ψήφισμα (psḗphisma).

parole.significato: A false pregnancy: the appearance of signs and symptoms associated with pregnancy when the person or animal is not preg…
parole.testo: From pseudo- + cyesis, from Latin pseudo- + Ancient Greek κύησις (kúēsis).

parole.significato: A pathological liar
parole.testo: From Latin pseudologus (“liar”), from Ancient Greek ψευδολόγος (pseudológos, “speaking falsely, lying”). Equivalent to pseudo- + -logue.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a pseudonym.
parole.testo: From Latin pseudōnymus, from Ancient Greek ψευδώνῠμος (pseudṓnŭmos). By surface analysis, pseudonym + -ous.

parole.significato: The twenty-third letter of Classical and Modern Greek and the twenty-fifth letter of Old and Ancient Greek.
parole.testo: From Middle English psi, from Latin psī, from Ancient Greek ψεῖ (pseî), the name for the twenty-third letter of the alphabet (Ψ, ψ).

parole.significato: Parrot.
parole.testo: From Latin psittacus (“parrot”), from Ancient Greek ψιττακός (psittakós).

parole.significato: A cutaneous disease, especially psoriasis, scabies, or mange.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin psōra, from Ancient Greek ψώρα (psṓra).

parole.significato: The human soul, mind, or spirit.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin psychē, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, “soul”).

parole.significato: A spirit, deity, person, etc., who guides the souls of the dead to the afterlife.
parole.testo: From Latin psȳchopompus, from Ancient Greek ψῡχοπομπός (psūkhopompós), from ψῡχή (psūkhḗ, “soul”) + πομπός (pompós, “conductor”).

parole.significato: Any of several plants of Plantago subg. Psyllium.
parole.testo: From Latin psyllium, from Ancient Greek ψύλλιον (psúllion, “fleawort”), from ψύλλα (psúlla, “flea”) + -ιον (-ion, forming neuter diminutives).

parole.significato: Of or relating to ancient Carthage, its inhabitants, or their language.
parole.testo: From Latin Pūnicus, variant of Poenicus, from Poenus + -icus, from Ancient Greek Φοῖνιξ (Phoînix), from Mycenaean Greek 𐀡𐀛𐀑𐀍 (po-ni-ki-jo) under influence from φοινός (phoinós, “crimson red”) owing to its relation to Tyrian purple, apparently from or cognate with Egyptian fnḫw (“Asiatics, Semites”),

parole.significato: Of a purple hue.
parole.testo: From Middle English purple, purpel, from Old English purpul (“purple”, adjective), taken from Old English purpure (“purple colour”, noun), from Latin purpura (“purple dye, shellfish”), from Ancient Greek πορφύρα (porphúra, “purple-fish”), perhaps of Semitic origin. Doublet of purpura and purpure. Th

parole.significato: Pertaining to or affected with purpura (skin discoloration from blood inside it).
parole.testo: From Latin purpura (“purple”), from Ancient Greek πορφύρα (porphúra). The medical sense is from the English purpura (“the appearance of purple discolorations on the skin”). By surface analysis, purpura + -ic.

parole.significato: An unidentified large animal with horns, possibly the addax, mentioned in the Bible (Deuteronomy 14:5) as one of the an…
parole.testo: From Latin pygargus from Ancient Greek πύγαργος (púgargos), a compound of Ancient Greek πῡγή (pūgḗ, “rump”) + ἀργός (argós, “white”).

parole.significato: A member of various legendary races of dwarfs, or supernatural peoples of diminutive stature.
parole.testo: From Latin Pygmaeī, from Ancient Greek πυγμαῖος (pugmaîos, “a member of a legendary race of dwarves”), from πυγμή (pugmḗ, “fist (as small as a fist)”). In Ancient Greek, first mentioned by Homer; only applied to actual human races in the 19th century.

parole.significato: pylorus
parole.testo: From Latin pylōrus, from Ancient Greek πυλωρός (pulōrós, “gatekeeper”), from πύλη (púlē, “door, gate”) + οὖρος (oûros, “guard”) + -o-.

parole.significato: In vertebrates, including humans, a zone at the lower end of the stomach that leads to and opens into the duodenum.
parole.testo: From Latin pylōrus, from Ancient Greek πυλωρός (pulōrós, “gatekeeper”).

parole.significato: A pyramid.
parole.testo: From Middle English piramis, from Latin pȳramis, from Ancient Greek πυραμίς (puramís).

parole.significato: A funeral pile; a combustible heap on which corpses are burned.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin pyra (“pyre, funeral pile”), from Ancient Greek πυρά (purá), from πῦρ (pûr, “fire”). Doublet of fire.

parole.significato: Any of several daisy-like perennial African plants of the genus Tanacetum, especially Tanacetum cinerariifolium.
parole.testo: From Old English pyretre, from (and later reformed after) Latin pyrethrum (in Pliny), from Hellenistic Ancient Greek πύρεθρον (púrethron).

parole.significato: Fever.
parole.testo: From post-classical Latin pyrexia, from Ancient Greek πυρεξία (purexía, “feverishness”), from πυρετός (puretós, “fever”).

parole.significato: Fire, heat.
parole.testo: From Latin pyr, from Ancient Greek πῦρ (pûr, “fire”).

parole.significato: A variety of garnet, of a poppy or blood-red color, frequently with a tinge of orange. It is used as a gemstone.
parole.testo: From Latin pyrōpus, from Ancient Greek πυρωπός (purōpós, “fiery-eyed, fire-colored”), from Ancient Greek πῦρ (pûr, “fire”) + ὤψ (ṓps, “eye”); compare French pyrope.

parole.significato: Of or relating to fireworks.
parole.testo: From Latin pyrotechnica, from Ancient Greek πῦρ (pûr, “fire”) + τεχνικός (tekhnikós, “skillful, workmanlike”). Analyzable as pyro- + technic.

parole.significato: Pythagorean.
parole.testo: From Latin Pȳthagoricus, from Ancient Greek Πυθαγορικός (Puthagorikós), from Πυθαγόρας (Puthagóras, “Pythagoras”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Delphi or to its priestess, Pythia.
parole.testo: From Latin Pythius, from Ancient Greek πύθιος (púthios, “belonging to Pytho, the older name of Delphi and its environs”): compare French pythien.

parole.significato: Any of the family Pythonidae of nonvenomous constrictor snakes.
parole.testo: From Latin pȳthon, from Ancient Greek Πύθων (Púthōn), the name of the mythological enormous serpent at Delphi slain by Apollo, probably from Πυθώ (Puthṓ), older name of Delphi.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to, or resembling, a python (“large constricting snake of the family Pythonidae”); pythonlike.
parole.testo: From python (“snake of the family Pythonidae”) + -ic (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives from nouns). Python is derived from Latin Pȳthōn, from Ancient Greek Πῡ́θων (Pū́thōn, “Python, mythical serpent which lived at Delphi”), from Πῡθώ (Pūthṓ, “Pytho, ancient name of Delphi; Pyt

parole.significato: “quod erat faciendum”, “what was to have been done” – used to end a mathematical passage other than a proof.
parole.testo: From Latin quod erat faciendum (“what was to have been done”), from Ancient Greek ὅπερ ἔδει ποιῆσαι (hóper édei poiêsai).

parole.significato: Of, related to, or suffering from quadriplegia.
parole.testo: From quadri- (of Latin origins) and -plegic, from Ancient Greek πλήσσειν (plḗssein, “to strike”); probably patterned after paraplegic from the Ancient Greek παραπληγή (paraplēgḗ, “the paralysis of half of the body”).

parole.significato: which was to be proved; which was to be demonstrated.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin quod erat dēmōnstrandum (“that which was to be proved”), calqued from Ancient Greek ὅπερ ἔδει δεῖξαι (hóper édei deîxai, “precisely what was required to be proved”).

parole.significato: radish (especially the root of the plant)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin raphanus, from Ancient Greek ῥάφανος (rháphanos).

parole.significato: “Right reason”, which regards virtue as desirable in itself.
parole.testo: First attested in an English text in 1677; borrowed from Latin rēcta ratiō (“right reason”), a calque of Ancient Greek ὀρθὸς λόγος (orthòs lógos). Cf. Cicero, De leg. I, 7, I, 2: “Recta ratio - quae cum sit lex, lege quoque consociati homines cum diis putandi sumus.” Term used in a letter to "Tom" b

parole.significato: A great quantity of blood.
parole.testo: From Middle English Red See, Reede See, Rede See, reade sea, from Old English Rēad Sǣ, a calque of Latin Mare Rubrum, itself a calque of Ancient Greek Ἐρυθρᾱ̀ θάλασσα (Eruthrā̀ thálassa); equivalent to red + sea.

parole.significato: A fear or hatred of religion, religious faith, religious people or religious organizations.
parole.testo: From Latin religiō (“moral obligation, worship”) and Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos, “fear”).

parole.significato: Divination with wands or rods, especially to use a divining rod to find things below the ground.
parole.testo: From rhabdo- + -mancy, first attested in 1646. From Latin rhabdomantīa, from Ancient Greek ῥαβδομαντεία (rhabdomanteía), from ῥάβδος (rhábdos, “rod”) + μαντεία (manteía, “divination”).

parole.significato: A strict and just judge.
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek Ῥαδάμανθυς (Rhadámanthus).

parole.significato: The false rhubarb (Rheum rhaponticum)
parole.testo: From Latin rhaponticum, literally rha (“rhubarb”) ponticum (“Pontic; of the Black Sea”), from Ancient Greek ῥῆον (rhêon, “rhubarb”) and Ancient Greek Πόντος (Póntos, “Black Sea”).

parole.significato: Part of or similar to rhetoric, the use of language as a means to persuade.
parole.testo: From Middle English rethorycal, rethoricalle, rethorycall, from rethorik, rhetoric (noun) or Latin rēthoricus, rhētoricus, from Ancient Greek ῥητορικός (rhētorikós, “concerning public speaking”). By surface analysis, rhetoric + -al.

parole.significato: A type of discourse that has a characteristic configuration of topics, themes, and arguments.
parole.testo: From Latin rhētorica from Ancient Greek ῥήτωρ (rhḗtōr, “public speaker”) + from Latin lectus, form of Latin legō (“to read”).

parole.significato: Any disorder of the muscles, tendons, joints, bones, nerves, characterized by pain, discomfort and disability.
parole.testo: First attested 1601, from Latin rheumatismus (“rheum”), from Ancient Greek ῥευματισμός (rheumatismós, “humour, discharge, rheum”) from ῥευματίζομαι (rheumatízomai, “to suffer from a rheum”) from ῥεῦμα (rheûma, “stream, flow”) from ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow”)

parole.significato: Any large herbivorous ungulate mammal native to Africa and Asia of the family Rhinocerotidae, with thick, gray skin and…
parole.testo: From Latin rhīnocerōs, from Ancient Greek ῥῑνόκερως (rhīnókerōs, “nose-horned”), composed of ῥῑ́ς, ῥῑνός (rhī́s, rhīnós, “nose, of (the) nose”) + κέρας (kéras, “horn”).

parole.significato: Oleander (Nerium oleander).
parole.testo: The obsolete sense derives from Latin rhododendron (“oleander”), from Ancient Greek ῥοδόδενδρον (rhodódendron, “oleander”), from ῥόδον (rhódon, “rose”) + δένδρον (déndron, “tree”). The modern sense comes through the intermediary of the genus name Rhododendron, not closely related taxonomically, but

parole.significato: A parallelogram having all sides of equal length.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin rhombus, from Ancient Greek ῥόμβος (rhómbos, “rhombus, spinning top”). Doublet of rhomb and rhumb.

parole.significato: A dry rattling sound heard during breathing, due to deposits in the bronchial tubes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin rhonchus (“snoring”), from Ancient Greek ῥόγχος (rhónkhos) (Caelius Aurelianus), of imitative origin.

parole.significato: Having each successive word longer by a letter or syllable.
parole.testo: From Latin rhopalicus, from Ancient Greek ῥόπαλον (rhópalon, “club, bat”).

parole.significato: The variation of strong and weak elements (such as duration, accent) of sounds, notably in speech or music, over time;…
parole.testo: First coined in 1557, from Latin rhythmus, from Ancient Greek ῥυθμός (rhuthmós, “any measured flow or movement, symmetry, rhythm”), from ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow, run, stream, gush”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Eastern Roman Empire, that is, to the Byzantine Empire.
parole.testo: From post-Classical Latin Rōmaeus [calque of Ancient Greek Ῥωμαῖος (Rhōmaîos)] + -an. By surface analysis, Rome + -ean.

parole.significato: Aspiration on a vowel or semivowel in Ancient Greek.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin spīritus asper, from Ancient Greek δασὺ πνεῦμα (dasù pneûma).

parole.significato: One of the red dye products extracted from madder root, probably identical with ruberythrinic acid.
parole.testo: From Latin rubeus (“red”) + Ancient Greek ῥητίνη (rhētínē, “resin”).

parole.significato: An epithet of God in His role as protector of the Israelite army, usually translated (alongside YHWH or Elohim) as "Lor…
parole.testo: From Latin Sabaoth, from Ancient Greek Σαβαώθ (Sabaṓth), from Biblical Hebrew צְבָאוֹת (ts'vaót), plural of צָבָא (tsaváʾ, “army”).

parole.significato: Strict observance of the Sabbath.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sabbatismus, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: sugar
parole.testo: From Latin saccharum, ultimately from the same source as sugar.

parole.significato: Someone with a Sagittarius star sign.
parole.testo: From Latin sagittārius (“archer”), calque of Ancient Greek τοξότης (toxótēs); possibly adapted from Akkadian 𒀯𒉺𒉋𒊕 (pabilsaĝ, “the bow-armed god Pabilsaĝ”) (see Pabilsaĝ), from Sumerian 𒀯𒉺𒉋𒊕 (ᴹᵁᴸPA.BIL₂.SAG).

parole.significato: A rare mineral composed of ammonium chloride found around volcanic fumaroles and guano deposits.
parole.testo: From Middle English sal armenak, sal armoniac, salarmoniac, sal armoniacum, sal armoniak, sal armonyak, salarmonyak, salle armonyacke, salt armoniake, salt armonyac, from Latin sal ammōniacus, sal armōniacus (“salt of Amun, ammonium chloride”), named so because it was found near the temple of (Jupit

parole.significato: A native, or inhabitant of Samaria; especially one practising certain ethnoreligious traditions indigenous to that regi…
parole.testo: From Latin Samarītānus, from Ancient Greek Σαμαρείτης (Samareítēs), from Σαμαρεία (Samareía, “Samaria”), derived from Biblical Hebrew שֹׁמְרוֹנִים (Šōmərôním) and שֹׁמְרוֹן (Šōmərôn) respectively. Attested in Old English.

parole.significato: An ancient form of triangular harp having a very sharp, shrill tone.
parole.testo: From Latin sambūca, from Ancient Greek σαμβύκη (sambúkē), ultimately from Aramaic סַבְּכָא (sabbəḵā).

parole.significato: Realgar; red sulphide of arsenic.
parole.testo: From Latin sandaraca, from Ancient Greek σανδαράκη (sandarákē, “realgar”).

parole.significato: A kind of minium, or red lead, made by calcining lead carbonate, but inferior to true minium.
parole.testo: From Latin sandix, sandyx (“vermilion, or a colour like vermilion”), from Ancient Greek σάνδυξ (sándux).

parole.significato: A shrub of species Astragalus sarcocolla, native to Iran.
parole.testo: From Latin sarcocolla, from Ancient Greek σαρκοκόλλα (sarkokólla), from σάρξ (sárx, “flesh”) + κόλλα (kólla, “glue, adhesive”).

parole.significato: A stonen coffin, often with its exterior inscribed, or decorated with sculpture.
parole.testo: The noun is borrowed from Latin sarcophagus (“grave; sarcophagus; flesh-eating, carnivorous”), from Ancient Greek σᾰρκοφᾰ́γος (sărkophắgos, “sarcophagus; flesh-eating, carnivorous”) (so named from λῐ́θος σᾰρκοφᾰ́γος (lĭ́thos sărkophắgos, literally “flesh-eating stone”) a type of limestone found at A

parole.significato: Sardonic.
parole.testo: From Latin sardonius, from Ancient Greek Σαρδόνιος (Sardónios, “Sardinian”), earlier σαρδάνιος (sardánios).

parole.significato: A gemstone having bands of red sard; a variety of onyx or chalcedony.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English sardonix, sardonyx (c. 1382), from Latin sardonyx, from Ancient Greek σᾰρδόνῠξ (sărdónŭx). Doublet of sardoin.

parole.significato: A demon follower of Satan (principal evil spirit); a fallen angel.
parole.testo: From Middle English Sathan, Satan, from Old English Satan, from Latin Satan, from Ancient Greek Σατάν (Satán), from Hebrew שָׂטָן (satán, “adversary, accuser”). Compare Arabic شَيْطَان (šayṭān, “satan, devil”). Doublet of shaitan and shetani.

parole.significato: A governor of a Persian province.
parole.testo: From Middle English satrape, from Latin satrapēs (“governor”), from Ancient Greek σατράπης (satrápēs), from Old Median *xšaθrapāvan (literally “kingdom-protector”), which is cognate with Old Persian 𐎧𐏁𐏂𐎱𐎠𐎺𐎠 (xšaçapāvā); see there for more.

parole.significato: Any of various kinds of orchids.
parole.testo: Latin, from Ancient Greek σατύριον (satúrion, “a kind of orchid”) from Σάτυρος (Sáturos, “a Satyr”).

parole.significato: To cause great offense to (someone); to shock with something scandalous.
parole.testo: From Latin scandalizō, from Ancient Greek σκανδαλίζω (skandalízō). By surface analysis, scandal + -ize.

parole.significato: The carina or keel of papilionaceous flowers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scaphium, from Ancient Greek σκάφιον (skáphion).

parole.significato: Shaped like a boat.
parole.testo: From Latin scaphoides, from Ancient Greek σκᾰφοειδής (skăphoeidḗs, “like a bowl, hollow”), from σκᾰ́φη (skắphē, “boat, trough, bowl”).

parole.significato: A marine food fish, the scarus or parrotfish (family Scaridae).
parole.testo: From Latin scarus (“a kind of fish”), from Ancient Greek σκάρος (skáros, “parrot wrasse, Sparisoma cretense, syn. Scarus cretensis”).

parole.significato: A limping satiric meter in classical verse.
parole.testo: From Latin scāzon, from Ancient Greek σκάζων (skázōn), from σκάζω (skázō, “to limp”).

parole.significato: An outline or image universally applicable to a general conception, under which it is likely to be presented to the min…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin schēma, from Ancient Greek σχῆμα (skhêma, “form, shape”). Doublet of scheme.

parole.significato: An Egyptian or Persian measure of length, varying from thirty-two to sixty stadia.
parole.testo: From Latin schoenus, from Ancient Greek σχοῖνος (skhoînos, “a rush, a reed, a land measure”).

parole.significato: A very small interval equal to half a comma.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin schisma, from Ancient Greek σχίσμα (skhísma, “cleft, division”), whence the orthographic borrowing skhisma. Doublet of schism.

parole.significato: Any of several nocturnal fish, of the genus Sciaena, from the Eastern Atlantic, Mediterranean Sea and Black Sea; a croa…
parole.testo: From Latin sciaena, from Ancient Greek σκίαινα (skíaina, “a sea-fish”, perhaps “a kind of grayling” or “ombre”), from σκιά (skiá, “shadow, shade”) and -ινα (-ina, suffix forming related feminine nouns).

parole.significato: A plant of the genus Scilla; a squill.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scilla, from Ancient Greek σκίλλα (skílla). Doublet of squill.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the family Scincidae, or skinks.
parole.testo: Latin scincus a kind of lizard, from Ancient Greek σκίγγος (skíngos), σκίγκος (skínkos), + -oid. Compare skink.

parole.significato: A kind of stinging or biting insect; a flea, gnat, sandfly, or the like.
parole.testo: From Latin scinifes, cinifes or ciniphes, plural, from Ancient Greek σκνίψ (skníps, “gnat, small fly(, flea?)”), plural σκνῖφες (sknîphes) or σκνῖπες (sknîpes).

parole.significato: Pertaining to or characteristic of squirrels.
parole.testo: From Latin sciūrus (“squirrel”), from Ancient Greek σκίουρος (skíouros, “squirrel”), from σκιά (skiá, “shadow”) + οὐρά (ourá, “tail”), + -ine.

parole.significato: The abnormal lateral curvature of the spine.
parole.testo: From Latin scoliosis, from Ancient Greek σκολίωσις (skolíōsis, “twisting; torsion”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Scolopacidae, or sandpipers.
parole.testo: From Latin scolopax (“a snipe”), from Ancient Greek σκολόπαξ (skolópax).

parole.significato: A mythical sea-creature, reputed to be able to disgorge its bowels to dislodge any fishing-hook.
parole.testo: From Latin scolopendra, from Ancient Greek σκολόπενδρα (skolópendra).

parole.significato: An idiot: a buffoon.
parole.testo: Latin scomma (“a taunt, jeer, scoff”), from Ancient Greek σκῶμμα (skômma, “jest, gibe”).

parole.significato: A small European migratory owl, Otus scops, that winters in sub-Saharran Africa.
parole.testo: From Latin scops, from Ancient Greek σκώψ (skṓps, “a type of small owl”), from σκοπός (skopós, “watcher”), from σκέπτομαι (sképtomai, “to look at”).

parole.significato: Full of rocks; rocky.
parole.testo: From Latin scopulosus, from scopulus (“a rock”), from Ancient Greek σκόπελος (skópelos).

parole.significato: The slag or dross that remains after the smelting of metal from an ore.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English, from Latin scōria, from Ancient Greek σκωρία (skōría), from σκῶρ (skôr, “dung”).

parole.significato: Someone with a Scorpio star sign
parole.testo: From Latin scorpiō (“scorpion”), from Ancient Greek σκορπίος (skorpíos), calque of Akkadian 𒀯𒄈𒋰 (zuqaqīpu, “scorpion; constellation name”), calque of Sumerian 𒀯𒄈𒋰 (ᴹᵁᴸGIR₂.TAB). Doublet of scorpion.

parole.significato: Any of the order Scorpiones of arachnids related to spiders, characterised by two large front pincers and a curved tail…
parole.testo: From Middle English scorpioun, skorpioun, schorpion, schorpiun, partly from Old English sċorpio and partly from Anglo-Norman scorpïun, Old French scorpïon, escorpïon; all from Latin scorpiō, ultimately from Ancient Greek σκορπίος (skorpíos). The cheerleading move is so called because of the resembla

parole.significato: A concave molding with a lower edge projecting beyond the top.
parole.testo: From Latin scotia, from Ancient Greek σκοτία (skotía, “dark, shadowy”).

parole.significato: A small fish of the family Cottidae, usually lacking scales. Often found on river bottoms and in tidal pools.
parole.testo: From earlier scorpene, from Latin scorpaena, from Ancient Greek σκόρπαινα (skórpaina, “kind of fish”), diminutive of σκορπίος (skorpíos). Compare scorpionfish.

parole.significato: A kind of large drinking cup used in Ancient Greece and Ancient Rome, especially by poor people.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scyphus (“cup”), from Ancient Greek σκῠ́φος (skŭ́phos).

parole.significato: A cylinder with a strip of parchment wound around it on which a message is written, used for cryptography by the ancien…
parole.testo: From Latin scytale (“cylinder used for encoding and decoding”), from Ancient Greek σκυτάλη (skutálē, “club, baton, cylinder used for encoding and decoding”).

parole.significato: Any member of the family Scytalinidae of very slender burrowing fish called graveldivers.
parole.testo: From Latin Scytalinidae, from Ancient Greek σκυτάλη (skutálē, “club”) + -ινος (-inos, “-ine”) + -ίδης (-ídēs, “-id”). Equivalent to scytale + -ine + -id.

parole.significato: A tetralone derivative involved in certain redox reactions.
parole.testo: From scytale + -one, from Latin scytale, from Ancient Greek σκυτάλη (skutálē, “club”).

parole.significato: A Scythian.
parole.testo: From Latin Scytha, from Ancient Greek Σκύθης (Skúthēs). Doublet of Saca, Saka, and Shaka.

parole.significato: Pertaining to (what is now classified as) the superorder Selachimorpha or division Selachii, comprising the sharks; or,…
parole.testo: From the (disused) genus name Selache, from Latin selachē, from the plural of Ancient Greek σέλαχος (sélakhos, “shark”).

parole.significato: Relating to the Greek-Macedonian dynasty which ruled (312–63 BCE) an empire created by Seleucus out of the eastern conq…
parole.testo: From Latin Seleucides, from Ancient Greek Σελευκίδης (Seleukídēs), named after Seleucus I Nicator. Equivalent to Seleucus + -id.

parole.significato: A Gaulish tribe in the Roman period.
parole.testo: Via Latin from Ancient Greek Σήνωνες (Sḗnōnes), originally the capital of the Gaulish people of the same name.

parole.significato: A dark brown pigment made from the secretions of the cuttlefish.
