parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sēpia (“cuttlefish”), from Ancient Greek σηπία (sēpía). Cognate with Italian seppia, Portuguese siba, and Spanish sepia.

parole.significato: A temple or other religious institution dedicated to the syncretic Greco-Egyptian deity Serapis.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?], from Ancient Greek Σεραπεῖον (Serapeîon).

parole.significato: Synonym of Chinese or Northern Chinese, chiefly in the context of ancient Greco-Roman knowledge of China and its role a…
parole.testo: From Seres + -ian, from Latin Seres (“the ancient northern Chinese”), from Ancient Greek, possibly from the Old Chinese word for silk.

parole.significato: Synonym of Chinese or Northern Chinese, in the context of ancient Greco-Roman knowledge of China.
parole.testo: From Latin Sēricus, from Ancient Greek Σηρικός (Sērikós), from Σῆρες (Sêres, “Seres”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic”), from σήρ (sḗr, “silkworm”), possibly from Old Chinese 絲 (*sə, “silk”). Equivalent to Seres + -ic. Doublet of Serican.

parole.significato: Synonym of silken, made of silk.
parole.testo: From Latin sēricus, from Ancient Greek σηρῐκός (sērĭkós), from σήρ (sḗr, “silkworm”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic”), possibly ultimately from the Old Chinese word for silk. Doublet of silk and serge.

parole.significato: Synonym of Chinese or Northern Chinese, chiefly in the context of ancient Greco-Roman knowledge of China.
parole.testo: From Latin Sēricānus, from Sērica (“Serica, China, ancient northern China”) + -ānus (“-an”), from Ancient Greek Σηρικά (Sēriká), from σήρ (sḗr, “silkworm”), and possibly ultimately from Old Chinese 絲 (*sə, “silk”). Equivalent to Serica + -an. Doublet of Seric.

parole.significato: Of or relating to silk; consisting of, or resembling silk; silky.
parole.testo: From Latin sēricus (“silken”), sēricum (“Seric material; silk”), from Sēricus (“belonging to the Seres”): Sērēs, Ancient Greek Σῆρες (Sêres, “a people of Eastern Asia, the modern Chinese, celebrated for their silken fabrics”). Compare silk, serge.

parole.significato: A nonessential amino acid, CH₂OH.CH(NH₂)COOH, found in most animal proteins, notably silk.
parole.testo: From Latin sericus (“silken”). The compound was first obtained from silk protein, a particularly rich source, in 1865. See also serge.

parole.significato: A tropical Asian plant (Sesamum indicum) bearing small flat seeds used as food and as a source of oil.
parole.testo: From late Middle English sisamie, from Latin sīsamum, sēsamum, from Ancient Greek σήσαμον (sḗsamon), from Aramaic שושמא (šūššmā), shortening of שומשומא (šumššumā), from Akkadian 𒊭𒈦𒌑𒈬 (šamaššammū, “oil plant”), compound of 𒉌𒄑 (šaman, “oil”) and 𒌑 (šammum, “plant”). The modern pronunciation is perhaps

parole.significato: Herpes zoster, caused by Human herpes virus 3, in genus Varicellovirus.
parole.testo: From Latin cingulus, variant of cingulum (“girdle”), translating Ancient Greek ζώνη (zṓnē), ζωστήρ (zōstḗr).

parole.significato: A pagan female oracle or prophetess, especially the Cumaean sibyl.
parole.testo: From Latin Sibylla, from Ancient Greek Σίβυλλα (Síbulla).

parole.significato: A member of an Italic tribe who inhabited eastern Sicily during the Iron Age.
parole.testo: From Latin Siculi, from Ancient Greek Σικελός (Sikelós). See also Sicily. Greek historians including Thucydides suggested Siculus, a legendary king and son of Italus, as the progenitor of the Sicels.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Silenus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Sīlēnicus, from Ancient Greek Σῑληνῐκός (Sīlēnĭkós). By surface analysis, Silenus + -ic.

parole.significato: A plant, thought to be extinct, used in Ancient Greece and Ancient Rome in cooking and as a contraceptive.
parole.testo: From Latin silphium, from Ancient Greek σίλφιον (sílphion).

parole.significato: A fish of the genus Silurus, such as the sheatfish.
parole.testo: From Latin silurus (“a sort of river fish”), from Ancient Greek σίλουρος (sílouros, “a very large sort of river fish”).

parole.significato: The scientific study of forests.
parole.testo: From silva + -o- + -logy. From Latin silva (“forest”) + Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía, “study of”). Coined by Roeloff Oldeman in 1990 in his book Forests: elements of silvology.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to apes and monkeys.
parole.testo: From Latin sīmia (“ape, monkey”), from Ancient Greek σιμός (simós, “snub-nosed”).

parole.significato: snub or snub-nosed
parole.testo: From Latin simus, from Ancient Greek σιμός (simós, “flat-nosed, snub-nosed”).

parole.significato: Synonym of Chinese.
parole.testo: From Sinae + -an, from Latin Sinae, from Ancient Greek Σῖναι (Sînai), q.v.

parole.significato: An alkaloidal amine found in seeds of black mustard (Brassica nigra, syns. Rhamphospermum nigrum, Sinapis erysimoides,…
parole.testo: Latin sinapi, sinapis (“mustard”), Ancient Greek: compare French sinapine.

parole.significato: An essential or indispensable element, condition, or ingredient.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin [condiciō] sine quā nōn (“[condition] without which not”), an expression which originated in the works of Boethius as a translation of some Aristotelian expression (perhaps Ancient Greek οὗ οὐκ ἄνευ (hoû ouk áneu); compare also Modern Greek εκ των ων ουκ άνευ (ek ton on ouk ánef)

parole.significato: Synonym of Sinitic, of or related to the family of Chinese languages.
parole.testo: From Latin Sinensis (“Chinese”) + -ian, from Sinae (“Southern Chinese; Southern China”) + -ensis (“-ese”), from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: A tube that connects adjacent chambers in the shells of some cephalopods.
parole.testo: From Latin sīphunculus (“little tube”), from sīphō (“tube, pipe”) + -culus (diminutive suffix), from Ancient Greek σίφων (síphōn), of uncertain and possibly non-Indo-European Mediterranean substrate origin.

parole.significato: sunstroke
parole.testo: From Latin sīriāsis, from Ancient Greek σειρίᾱσις (seiríāsis, “heatstroke”)

parole.significato: An ancient Egyptian musical instrument, to be shaken, consisting of a metal frame holding percussive metal beads.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sīstrum, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek σεῖστρον (seîstron), from σείω (seíō, “shake”).

parole.significato: An emerald.
parole.testo: From Latin smaragdus, from Ancient Greek σμάραγδος (smáragdos), μάραγδος (máragdos), from a Semitic language.

parole.significato: Emerald.
parole.testo: From Latin smaragdinus, from Ancient Greek σμάραγδινος (smáragdinos), from σμάραγδος (smáragdos). See emerald for more.

parole.significato: Cleansing.
parole.testo: From Latin smecticus, from Ancient Greek σμηκτικός (smēktikós), from σμήχειν (smḗkhein, “to wipe, to cleanse”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic”).

parole.significato: A whitish sebaceous secretion that collects between the glans penis and foreskin or in the vulva.
parole.testo: From Latin, borrowed from Ancient Greek σμῆγμα (smêgma), alternative form of σμῆμα (smêma, “soap, detergent”), from σμάω (smáō, “to wipe, clean”).

parole.significato: The lack of aspiration on a vowel or semivowel in Ancient Greek.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin spīritus lēnis, from Ancient Greek ψιλὸν πνεῦμα (psilòn pneûma).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or characteristic of the philosopher Socrates or his philosophy or methods.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Sōcratic(us). By surface analysis, Socrat(es) + -ic.

parole.significato: A person of unusual wisdom.
parole.testo: From Latin Solomōn (variant of Salomon), from Ancient Greek Σολομών (Solomṓn), from Biblical Hebrew שְׁלֹמֹה (šĕlōmōʰ), from שָׁלוֹם (šālōm, “peace”). Doublet of Shlomo and Suleiman.

parole.significato: Wise men; sages.
parole.testo: From the Latin sophī, the nominative plural form of sophus, from the Ancient Greek σοφός (sophós).

parole.significato: Synonym of sophistical, of or related to the ancient Sophists, characterized by fallacious reasoning.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin sophisticus, borrowing of Ancient Greek σοφιστικός (sophistikós). Equivalent to sophist + -ic and sophism + -istic.

parole.significato: wisdom, knowledge, learning
parole.testo: From the Middle English sophie, from the Latin sophia, from the Ancient Greek σοφῐ́ᾱ (sophĭ́ā, “high knowledge”: “learning”, “wisdom”); compare Sophia.

parole.significato: The awkward or humorous use of different languages mixed together, often using a foreign term incorrectly or in an inap…
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: A series of propositions whereby each conclusion is taken as the subject of the next.
parole.testo: From the Latin sōrītēs, from the Ancient Greek σωρῑ́της (sōrī́tēs, “fallacy of the heap”), from σωρός (sōrós, “heap”).

parole.significato: iron(II) sulfate, or some earth impregnated with it
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sory, from Ancient Greek σῶρυ (sôru, “a kind of ore”).

parole.significato: A fleshy spike (inflorescence) with reduced flowers, usually enclosed by a spathe, characteristic of aroids.
parole.testo: Via Latin spādīx from Ancient Greek σπᾱ́δῑξ (spā́dīx, “palm branch”).

parole.significato: Someone who has been castrated; a eunuch or castrato.
parole.testo: From Latin spadō, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: A Spartan, especially a full citizen.
parole.testo: From Middle English Sparciate, from Latin Spartiātēs, from Ancient Greek Σπᾰρτῐᾱ́της (Spărtĭā́tēs), from Σπᾰ́ρτη (Spắrtē) + -ᾱ́της (-ā́tēs).

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or affected by spasm.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin spasticus, from Ancient Greek σπαστικός (spastikós, “drawing in”). By surface analysis, spasm + -tic. Cf. French spastique and see also spasm.

parole.significato: A type of straight sword originating from the first-century Roman Empire. It was worn typically by cavalry officers and…
parole.testo: From Latin spatha, from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē, “any broad blade, of wood or metal”). Doublet of spade, spathe, and epee.

parole.significato: A large bract that envelops or subtends a whole inflorescence, typically a spadix.
parole.testo: From Latin spatha, from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē, “blade”). Doublet of epee, spatha, and spade.

parole.significato: A kitchen utensil consisting of a flat surface attached to a long handle, used for turning, lifting, or stirring food.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin spatula (“a flat piece”), the diminutive form of spatha (“broad or flat tool”), from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē, “a broad wood or metal blade”). Doublet of spauld; compare spatha and spathe.

parole.significato: The reproductive cell or gamete of the male; a spermatozoon.
parole.testo: From Middle English sperme, from Latin sperma, from Ancient Greek σπέρμα (spérma, “seed, semen”). Compare also Old French esperme, sparme.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or resembling sperm.
parole.testo: From Middle English spermatik, from Latin spermaticus, from Ancient Greek σπερματικός (spermatikós). By surface analysis, spermat- + -ic.

parole.significato: A spherical aggregation of raphides in a plant cell
parole.testo: Derived from Latin sphaera + Ancient Greek ῥαφίς (rhaphís).

parole.significato: Shaped as a sphere; being a sphere.
parole.testo: English spheric [from Latin sphaericus, from Ancient Greek σφαιρικός (sphairikós)] + -al.

parole.significato: An aluminous earth of a grayish yellow color; a medicinal clay.
parole.testo: From Latin sphragis, sphragidis (“Lemnian earth”), from Ancient Greek σφραγίς (sphragís, “a seal”), so called because sold in sealed packets.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the circulatory pulse.
parole.testo: From Latin sphygmicus, from Ancient Greek σφυγμικός (sphugmikós), from σφυγμός (sphugmós, “pulse”), whence sphygm-.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to sex or fornication (especially homosexual) between three or more people.
parole.testo: From Latin spintria (“male prostitute”), from Ancient Greek σφιγκτήρ (sphinktḗr, “something which binds”), referring to the anal sphincter.

parole.significato: Synonym of rough breathing.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin spīritus asper, from Ancient Greek δασὺ πνεῦμα (dasù pneûma).

parole.significato: Synonym of smooth breathing.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin spīritus lēnis, from Ancient Greek ψιλὸν πνεῦμα (psilòn pneûma).

parole.significato: Resembling or having the form of a spiral or helix.
parole.testo: From Latin spiroïdes, from Ancient Greek Ancient Greek σπειροειδής (speiroeidḗs). By surface analysis, spire + -oid.

parole.significato: Of, related to, or located near the spleen.
parole.testo: From Latin splēnicus, from Ancient Greek σπληνικός (splēnikós, “of the spleen”). By surface analysis, splen- + -ic.

parole.significato: The thick posterior part of the corpus callosum of the brain.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin splēnium (“plaster, patch”), from Ancient Greek σπληνῐ́ον (splēnĭ́on, “pad or compress of linen”).

parole.significato: Having or relating to spondees.
parole.testo: From Latin spondaicus, spondiacus, from Ancient Greek σπονδειακός (spondeiakós, “(music) used at a libation”).

parole.significato: A word or metrical foot of two syllables, either both long or both stressed.
parole.testo: From Latin spondēus (“spondee”), from Ancient Greek σπονδεῖος (spondeîos, “associated with a libation”) from σπονδή (spondḗ, “libation”): spondees were often used in melodies sung at libations.

parole.significato: A joint of the backbone; a vertebra.
parole.testo: From Middle English spondile, spondyle, from Latin spondylus, from Ancient Greek σφόνδῠλος (sphóndŭlos, “vertebra”).

parole.significato: Any of various marine invertebrates of the phylum Porifera, that have a porous skeleton often of silica.
parole.testo: From Middle English sponge, from Old English spunge, taken from Latin spongia, from Ancient Greek σπογγιά (spongiá), from σπόγγος (spóngos). Displaced native Old English swamm (“fungus, sponge”).

parole.significato: A dinner bell, (historical) a shrill little bell used to signal dinner for medieval monks.
parole.testo: From Latin squilla, from Ancient Greek σκίλλα (skílla).

parole.significato: One of the sweet spices used by the Jews in Biblical times for preparing incense; it is thought to have been an oil or…
parole.testo: From Latin stactē, from Ancient Greek στακτή (staktḗ, “oil of myrrh”) from στακτός (staktós, “oozing out in drops”).

parole.significato: Synonym of stadion (“former Greek unit of distance”).
parole.testo: From Latin stadium, from Ancient Greek στάδιον (stádion), a 600-foot racetrack, a distance of 600 Greek feet. Cognate with French stade. Doublet of stadium, stadion, and estadio.

parole.significato: A venue where sporting events are held.
parole.testo: From Latin stadium (“a measure of length, a race course”) (commonly one-eighth of a Roman mile; translated in early English Bibles by furlong), from Ancient Greek στάδιον (stádion, “a measure of length, a running track”), especially the track at Olympia, which was one stadium in length. The Greek wo

parole.significato: Someone from Stagira.
parole.testo: From the Latin Stagirites, from the Ancient Greek Σταγιριτης (Stagiritēs, “natives of Stagira”), from Σταγειρος (Stageiros, “Stagira”).

parole.significato: The uvula of the soft palate.
parole.testo: From Latin staphylē, from Ancient Greek σταφυλή (staphulḗ).

parole.significato: An abnormal protrusion of the uveal tissue through the eyeball.
parole.testo: Latin, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: A gold, silver or electrum coin of ancient Greece.
parole.testo: From Latin statēr, from Ancient Greek στατήρ (statḗr).

parole.significato: Unchanging; that cannot or does not change.
parole.testo: Modern Latin staticus, from Ancient Greek στατικός (statikós), from ἵστημι (hístēmi, “to make stand”). By surface analysis, stasis + -tic.

parole.significato: Plants of the genus Limonium having spikes of white or mauve flowers.
parole.testo: From Latin staticē, from Ancient Greek στατικός (statikós, “standing still”).

parole.significato: A highly toxic, perennial plant with purple flowers (Staphisagria macrosperma, syn. Delphinium staphisagria).
parole.testo: Late Middle English, from Latin staphisagria, from Ancient Greek σταφίς (staphís, “grape”) (from σταφυλή (staphulḗ, “bunch of grapes”)) + ἀγρία (agría, “wild”) (literally "living in the fields," from ἀγρός (agrós, “field”)).

parole.significato: Soapstone. (often synonymous; more information at soapstone § Terminology).
parole.testo: From Latin steatītis, from Ancient Greek στέαρ (stéar, “tallow”). By surface analysis, steat(o)- (“fat”) + -ite (“stone”).

parole.significato: An obelisk or upright stone pillar, usually as a primitive commemoration or gravestone.
parole.testo: From Latin stēla, from Ancient Greek στήλη (stḗlē). Doublet of stele.

parole.significato: A family tree or recorded genealogy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin stemma, from Ancient Greek στέμμα (stémma).

parole.significato: A person with a powerful or stentorian voice.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Stentōr, from Ancient Greek Στέντωρ (Sténtōr), the name of a herald in the Iliad who had a loud voice.

parole.significato: Synonym of fecaloma.
parole.testo: From Latin stercus (“dung”) + -oma, from Ancient Greek -ωμα (-ōma, “tumor, mass”). See fecaloma.

parole.significato: antimony
parole.testo: From Latin stibium (“antimony”), which was imported from Ancient Greek στίβι (stíbi), a variant of στίμμι (stímmi), itself originating from Egyptian s-d-m-N33C:Z2ss (sdm).

parole.significato: A grey mineral, Sb₂S₃, that is the main ore of antimony; in powdered form, used as the cosmetic called kohl.
parole.testo: From Latin stibium, from Ancient Greek στίβι (stíbi), a variant of στίμμι (stímmi).

parole.significato: A technique in drama or poetry, in which alternating lines, or half-lines, are given to alternating characters, voices,…
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek στιχομυθία (stikhomuthía), from στίχος (stíkhos, “line of verse”) (see sticho-) + μῦθος (mûthos, “speech”).

parole.significato: An indication of infamy or disgrace.
parole.testo: From Latin stigma, from Ancient Greek στίγμα (stígma, “mark of slavery or disgrace”), from στίζω (stízō, “to mark”). Closely related to stigme, and distantly related to stick.

parole.significato: A garment consisting of a decorated band worn on the back of the neck, each end hanging over the chest, worn in ecclesi…
parole.testo: From Old English stole, from Latin stola, from Ancient Greek στολή (stolḗ, “stole, garment, equipment”); akin to stall. Doublet of stola.

parole.significato: Any member of the genus Styrax of about 130 species of large shrubs or small trees, mostly native to temperate or tropi…
parole.testo: From Middle English storace, storage, storax, storaxe, storrax, from Latin storax, styrax, from Ancient Greek στύραξ (stúrax). Doublet of styrax.

parole.significato: A painful, frequent need to urinate, when the bladder is largely empty or with little urine production.
parole.testo: From Middle English strangury, from Latin stranguria, from Ancient Greek στραγγουρία (strangouría).

parole.significato: The leader or commander of an army; a general.
parole.testo: From Latin strategus, from Ancient Greek στρατηγός (stratēgós, “general”). See stratagem.

parole.significato: The science and art of military command as applied to the overall planning and conduct of warfare.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin stratēgia, from Ancient Greek στρατηγία (stratēgía, “office of general, command, generalship”), from στρατηγός (stratēgós, “the leader or commander of an army, a general”), from στρατός (stratós, “army”) + ἄγω (ágō, “to lead, conduct”).

parole.significato: A bird-like demon feeding on human flesh and blood.
parole.testo: From Latin strix, from Ancient Greek στρίξ (stríx, “screecher”).

parole.significato: A scaly multiple fruit resulting from the ripening of an ament in certain plants, such as the hop or pine.
parole.testo: From Latin strobilus (“a pinecone”) and Latin strobila, from Ancient Greek στρόβιλος (stróbilos). All senses refer to things that look like, or somewhat like (via fancied resemblance), a pinecone.

parole.significato: The tissue structure of an organ, etc., that serves to support it.
parole.testo: From Latin strōma (“mattress, bed covering”), from Ancient Greek στρῶμα (strôma, “bed”), from στόρνυμι (stórnumi, “to stretch out”).

parole.significato: A turn in verse, as from one metrical foot to another, or from one side of a chorus to the other.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin stropha, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek στροφή (strophḗ, “a turn, bend, twist”). Compare strap and strop. Compare typologically rehearsal, rehearse (related to French herser (“to harrow”) << Latin hirpex, another meaning shift from the idea of turning).

parole.significato: A band worn around the breasts, serving as a form of bra in ancient times.
parole.testo: From Latin strophium, from Ancient Greek στρόφιον (stróphion).

parole.significato: The fear of Hell.
parole.testo: From Latin stygius, from Ancient Greek Στύγιος (Stúgios, “relating to Styx”), and -phobia.

parole.significato: The top step of the crepidoma, i.e. the platform upon which the superstructure of the building is erected.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin stylobata, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek στυλοβάτης (stulobátēs), from στῦλος (stûlos, “pillar”) + βαίνω (baínō, “to go, to walk”).

parole.significato: In Greek mythology, a flock of metallic man-eating birds that haunted Lake Stymphalis in Arkadia. They were slain by He…
parole.testo: From Latin Stymphālides, from Ancient Greek Στυμφαλίδες ὄρνιθες (Stumphalídes órnithes, “birds of Stymphalus”).

parole.significato: Bringing about contraction of tissues; harsh, raw, austere.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin stypticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek στυπτικός (stuptikós), from στύφω (stúphō, “to contract”).

parole.significato: To use an angle to delimit (mark off, enclose) part of a straight or curved line, for example an arc or the opposite si…
parole.testo: From Latin subtendere, from sub (“under”) + tendere (“to stretch, extend”), itself a semantic loan from Ancient Greek ὑποτείνω (hupoteínō, “to subtend”), from which hypotenuse also derives. See tend.

parole.significato: A person devoted to luxury and pleasure; a hedonist.
parole.testo: The noun is a learned borrowing from Latin Sybarīta + English -ite (suffix forming demonyms). Sybarīta is derived from Ancient Greek Σῠβᾰρῑ́της (Sŭbărī́tēs, “(noun) inhabitant of Sybaris; (adjective) decadent; self-indulgent”), from Σῠ́βᾰρῐς (Sŭ́bărĭs, “Sybaris”) + -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs, suffix forming dem

parole.significato: Of or having the qualities of a sybarite (“a person devoted to luxury and pleasure”); dedicated to excessive comfort an…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Sybarīticus (“of or pertaining to Sybaris or its inhabitants”) + English -ic (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’, forming adjectives from nouns). Sybarīticus is derived from Ancient Greek Συβαρῑτικός (Subarītikós), from Σῠβᾰρῑ́της (Sŭbărī́tēs, “(noun) inhabitant of Syb

parole.significato: A tree, mentioned in Luke's Gospel, and thought to be the black mulberry.
parole.testo: From Latin sȳcamīnus, from Ancient Greek σῡκάμῑνος (sūkámīnos), from Hebrew שִׁקְמָה (shikmá, “sycamore”) (with assimilation to σῦκον (sûkon, “fig”)).

parole.significato: The fawning behavior of a sycophant; servile flattery; fawningness.
parole.testo: From Latin sȳcophantia, from Ancient Greek σῡκοφᾰντῐ́ᾱ (sūkophăntĭ́ā), equivalent to sycophant + -cy.

parole.significato: One who uses obsequious compliments to gain self-serving favour or advantage from another; a servile flatterer.
parole.testo: First attested in 1537. From Latin sȳcophanta (“informer, trickster”), from Ancient Greek συκοφάντης (sukophántēs), itself from σῦκον (sûkon, “fig”) + φαίνω (phaínō, “to show, demonstrate”). The gesture of "showing the fig" was a vulgar one, which was made by sticking the thumb between two fingers,

parole.significato: A figure of speech in which one word simultaneously modifies two or more other words such that the modification must be…
parole.testo: From Latin syllepsis, from Ancient Greek σύλληψις (súllēpsis), from συλλαμβάνω (sullambánō).

parole.significato: Omission of the conclusion of a syllogistic argument.
parole.testo: From Latin syllogismus (“syllogism”), from Ancient Greek συλλογισμός (sullogismós). Doublet of syllogism.

parole.significato: commensurable; symmetrical
parole.testo: Partly from Latin symmetros and partly from Ancient Greek σύμμετρος (súmmetros), + -al.

parole.significato: Synonym of symmetrical
parole.testo: From symmetry + -ic, from Latin symmetria, from Ancient Greek συμμετρία (summetría).

parole.significato: Exact correspondence on either side of a dividing line, plane, center or axis.
parole.testo: From Latin symmetria, from Ancient Greek συμμετρία (summetría), from σύμμετρος (súmmetros, “symmetrical”), from σύν (sún, “with”) + μέτρον (métron, “measure”). By surface analysis, sym- + -metry.

parole.significato: A conference or other meeting for discussion of a topic, especially one in which the participants make presentations.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin symposium, from Ancient Greek συμπόσιον (sumpósion, “drinking party”) from συμπίνω (sumpínō, “drink together”), from συν- (sun-, “together-”) + πίνω (pínō, “drink”). Morphologically compare compotation.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Ancient Greek symposium.
parole.testo: From Latin sympoticus or Ancient Greek συμποτικός (sumpotikós).

parole.significato: Synonym of sympotic.
parole.testo: From Latin sympoticus or Ancient Greek συμποτικός (sumpotikós) + -al.

parole.significato: Piling up of terms, especially adjectives, often as invective.
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek συναθροισμός (sunathroismós, “collection, union, rhetorical grouping of diverse words”).

parole.significato: A congregation.
parole.testo: Latin, from Ancient Greek σύναξις (súnaxis, “gathering”), from συνάγω (sunágō, “to gather”). See synagogue.

parole.significato: One who holds an office in an Eastern Catholic or Orthodox Church roughly equivalent to that of an episcopal vicar in t…
parole.testo: From Latin syncellus, from Ancient Greek σύγκελλος (súnkellos).

parole.significato: A complicated, interlocking word-order pattern in early Latin verse, demonstrated by Virgil and his contemporaries.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin synchysis, from Ancient Greek σύγχυσις (súnkhusis, “a mixing”).

parole.significato: The elision or loss of a sound from the interior of a word, especially of a vowel sound with loss of a syllable.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin syncopē, from Ancient Greek συγκοπή (sunkopḗ), from συγκόπτω (sunkóptō, “cut up”) + -η (-ē, nominalization suffix), from σύν (sún, “beside, with”) + κόπτω (kóptō, “strike, cut off”). Partly continues the (near-)doublets syncopis and sincopin, both from the Old Frenc

parole.significato: The reconciliation or fusion of different systems or beliefs (religious, cultural, or otherwise cosmologic or ontologic…
parole.testo: From Latin syncretismus, from Ancient Greek συγκρητισμός (sunkrētismós, “federation of Cretan cities”), from συγκρητίζω (sunkrētízō, “to unite against a common enemy”), from σύν (sún, “together”) (see English syn-) + Κρῆτες (Krêtes, “Cretans”). By surface analysis, syn- + Crete + -ism (“Crete joinin

parole.significato: Of or related to syndeton, the use of a conjunction.
parole.testo: From Latin syndeticus, from Ancient Greek συνδετικός (sundetikós), from σύνδεσις (súndesis, “binding”) + -κός (-kós, “-ic: forming adjectives”), from συνδεῖν (sundeîn, “to join, to bind”), from σῠν- (sŭn-, “together”) + δεῖν (deîn, “to bind, to tie”).

parole.significato: A figure of speech that uses the name of a part of something to represent the whole, or the whole to represent a part,…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin synecdochē, from Ancient Greek συνεκδοχή (sunekdokhḗ, “receiving together”) from σύν (sún, “with”) + ἐκ (ek, “out of”) + δέχεσθαι (dékhesthai, “to accept”), this last element related to δοκέω (dokéō, “to think, suppose, seem”).

parole.significato: Of, related to or produced by a synod; synodal.
parole.testo: From Latin synodicus, from Ancient Greek συνοδικός (sunodikós, “of or related to an assembly or meeting”). Equivalent to synod + -ic.

parole.significato: A term (word or phrase) which is synonymous with others.
parole.testo: From Middle English sinonyme, from Latin synōnymum, from Ancient Greek συνώνυμον (sunṓnumon), neuter singular form of συνώνυμος (sunṓnumos, “synonymous”), from σύν (sún, “with”) + ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”). By surface analysis, syn- + -onym.

parole.significato: The use of two or more synonyms together to amplify or explain a given subject or term. A kind of repetition that adds…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin synōnymia, from Ancient Greek συνωνυμία (sunōnumía). Doublet of synonymy.

parole.significato: A square formation of 256 soldiers arranged into sixteen files, sixteen ranks deep, led by a syntagmatarch; a syntagma.
parole.testo: First attested in 1670–1 and then once per century since; from the Latin syntagmatarchia, from the Ancient Greek συνταγματαρχία (suntagmatarkhía), from σύνταγμα (súntagma), whence the English syntagma.

parole.significato: The formation of something complex or coherent by combining simpler things.
parole.testo: From Latin synthesis, from Ancient Greek σύνθεσις (súnthesis, “a putting together; composition”), from συντίθημι (suntíthēmi, “put together, combine”), from συν- (sun-, “together”) + τίθημι (títhēmi, “set, place”). Doublet of sandhi.

parole.significato: A speaker of the Syriac language (see above).
parole.testo: From Latin Syriacus (“Syrian”), from Ancient Greek Συριακός (Suriakós, “Syrian”, adjective), from Συρία (Suría) [the Greek name for Aram, and probably based on the name Ἀσσυρία (Assuría, “Assyria”)] + -ακός (-akós).

parole.significato: The chief priest in the Roman province of Syria.
parole.testo: From Latin Syriarcha, from Ancient Greek Συριάρχης (Suriárkhēs).

parole.significato: syrinx: Of or pertaining to a tube or tuboid structure, such as a fistula.
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from Latin sȳrinx, from Ancient Greek σῦριγξ (sûrinx, “pipe, tube, channel, fistula”). More at syrinx § Etymology.

parole.significato: A set of panpipes.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin sȳrinx (“reed; reed pipe, panpipes”), from Ancient Greek σῦριγξ (sûrinx, “panpipes; pipe-shaped object”), from Pre-Greek. Doublet of syringe. The plural form syringes is a learned borrowing from Latin sȳringes.

parole.significato: A long dress that trailed on the floor, worn by tragic actors.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin syrma, from Ancient Greek σύρμα (súrma), from σύρω (súrō, “to drag”).

parole.significato: Synonym of quicksand.
parole.testo: From Latin syrtis, from Syrtis (“Sirte, Gulf of Syrtis”), from Ancient Greek Σύρτις (Súrtis), an area of Libya proverbially treacherous for sailing owing to the effect of wind and waves on its quicksand. Doublet of Sirte.

parole.significato: Capable of, or taking place by, alternate contraction and dilatation.
parole.testo: From Latin systalticus (“drawing together”), from Ancient Greek συσταλτικός (sustaltikós), from συστέλλω (sustéllō). Compare systole.

parole.significato: The combination of different elements; synthesis.
parole.testo: From post-classical Latin systasis, and its source, Ancient Greek σύστασις (sústasis, “composition, construction”), from συν- (sun-, “syn-”) + στάσις (stásis, “stasis”).

parole.significato: Having a space equal to two diameters or four modules between two columns; said of a portico or building.
parole.testo: From Latin systȳlos, from Ancient Greek σύστῡλος (sústūlos, “with columns standing close”) from σύν (sún, “with”) + στῦλος (stûlos, “column”): compare French systyle. By surface analysis, sy- + -style.

parole.significato: A ribbon worn in the hair in ancient Greece.
parole.testo: From Latin taenia, from Ancient Greek ταινία (tainía, “ribbon, tape”).

parole.significato: An infection of tapeworms of the genus Taenia that does not usually cause any disease.
parole.testo: From Latin taen(ia) (from Ancient Greek ταινία (tainía, “band, ribbon, tapeworm”)) + -iasis (““pathological or morbid condition””)

parole.significato: A marked natural ability or skill.
parole.testo: From Middle English talent, from Old English talente, borrowed from the plural of Latin talentum (“a Grecian weight; a talent of money”), from Ancient Greek τάλαντον (tálanton, “balance, a particular weight, especially of gold, sum of money, a talent”). Compare Old High German talenta (“talent”). La

parole.significato: A stork of the genus Mycteria (formerly Tantalus), especially the American wood stork, Mycteria americana.
parole.testo: From Latin Tantalus, from Ancient Greek Τάνταλος (Tántalos, “Tantalus”), a Phrygian king in Greek mythology who was condemned to stand in a pool of water which receded every time he tried to drink, and with overhanging branches of fruit which pulled back whenever he tried to eat. Doublet of Tantalus

parole.significato: A membranous layer of tissue.
parole.testo: From Latin tapētum. Further from Ancient Greek τάπης (tápēs). Doublet of tapet.

parole.significato: A figure of speech whereby something is given less importance by the name given it than it merits.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tapīnōsis (“depreciation”), itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ταπείνωσις (tapeínōsis, “lowering”), from ταπεινός (tapeinós, “low”).

parole.significato: Any primate in the family Tarsiidae; a tarsier.
parole.testo: From French tarsi(er) + -id, from Latin tarsus, from Ancient Greek ταρσός (tarsós, “wickerwork mat"; "broad, flat surface"”).

parole.significato: A tarsier or extinct relative; any member of the infraorder Tarsiiformes
parole.testo: From French tarsi(er) + -oid, from Latin tarsus, from Ancient Greek ταρσός (tarsós, “wickerwork mat"; "broad, flat surface"”).

parole.significato: An ancient people who inhabited the Crimean Mountains.
parole.testo: From Latin Taurī, from Ancient Greek Ταῦροι (Taûroi).

parole.significato: The ritual slaughter of a bull.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin taurobolium, from Ancient Greek ταυροβόλιον (taurobólion).

parole.significato: Someone with a Taurus star sign.
parole.testo: From Latin Taurus (from taurus (“bull”)), from Ancient Greek Ταῦρος (Taûros) (compare Aramaic תּוֹר (tor), Arabic ثَوْر (ṯawr)), ultimately originating with Sumerian 𒄞𒀭𒈾 (GU₄.AN.NA, “Bull of Heaven; constellation Taurus”) . Latin taurus (“bull”) is a doublet of steer, tur, Tavros, and Tarvos.

parole.significato: Tautology.
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Technique.
parole.testo: Partly from Latin technicus and partly from Ancient Greek τεχνικός (tekhnikós); probably modelled on German Technik. Doublet of technique.

parole.significato: A figure of a man (often Atlas) used as a pillar for support.
parole.testo: From Latin telamon, from Ancient Greek τελαμών (telamṓn, “pillar shaped as a male figure, strap used for carrying”).

parole.significato: A tribe of Acarnania descending from Teleboas.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Tēleboae, from Ancient Greek Τηλεβόαι (Tēlebóai), plural of Τηλεβόᾱς (Tēlebóās).

parole.significato: A monocular optical instrument that magnifies distant objects, especially in astronomy.
parole.testo: From tele- + -scope. From Latin tēlescopium, from Ancient Greek τηλεσκόπος (tēleskópos, “far-seeing”), from τῆλε (têle, “afar”) + σκοπέω (skopéō, “to look at”). Coined in 1611 by the Greek mathematician Giovanni Demisiani for one of Galileo Galilei's instruments presented at a banquet at the Accadem

parole.significato: An igneous rock consisting essentially of plagioclase and either leucite or nephelite, or both.
parole.testo: From Latin tephrītis and Ancient Greek τεφρῖτις (tephrîtis). By surface analysis, tephro- + -ite.

parole.significato: Synonym of teraph.
parole.testo: From ecclesiastical Latin theraphim, from Ancient Greek θεραφίν (theraphín), from Hebrew תְּרָפִים (t'rafím, “household gods”).

parole.significato: A mollusc of the genus Teredo, especially of species Teredo navalis.
parole.testo: From Latin terēdō (“woodworm”), from Ancient Greek τερηδών (terēdṓn, “wood-worm”). Compare Ancient Greek: τέρην (térēn, “smooth, gentle”).

parole.significato: A small square piece of stone, wood, ivory or glass used for making a mosaic.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tessera (“a cube, a die with numbers on all six sides”), from Ancient Greek τέσσαρες (téssares, “four”).

parole.significato: A serious and often fatal disease caused by the infection of an open wound with the anaerobic bacterium Clostridium tet…
parole.testo: From Latin tetanus, from Ancient Greek τέτανος (tétanos), from τείνω (teínō, “to stretch”).

parole.significato: A bird belonging to the tribe Tetraonini, of which the genus Tetrao is the type.
parole.testo: Latin tetrao (“a heath cock, grouse”), from Ancient Greek. Compare French tétraonide.

parole.significato: In or of four identical experiments.
parole.testo: From Latin plicō (“to fold”) + Ancient Greek τετράς (tetrás, “four”).

parole.significato: A noun that has four cases.
parole.testo: From Latin tetraptōtum, from Ancient Greek τετράπτωτος (tetráptōtos).

parole.significato: A governor or ruler of a quarter of a country, especially of a fourth part of a province in or client state of Ancient…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tetrarchēs, from Ancient Greek τετράρχης (tetrárkhēs), from τετρα- (tetra-, “four”) + -άρχης (-árkhēs, “ruler, leader”).

parole.significato: A four-line stanza.
parole.testo: From Latin tetrastichon, from neuter of Ancient Greek τετράστιχον (tetrástikhon, “having four rows”), from τετρα- (tetra-, “four”) + στίχος (stíkhos, “row”).

parole.significato: Either of two large, ovoid structures of grey matter within the forebrain that relay sensory impulses to the cerebral c…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin thalamus, from Ancient Greek θάλαμος (thálamos, “an inner chamber, a bedroom, a bed”).

parole.significato: The presentation of something as a marvel rather than in a neutrally descriptive way.
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek θαυμασμός (thaumasmós, “a wondering”).

parole.significato: god or deity
parole.testo: From Latin theo- (“god”), combining form of theos (“god”); from Ancient Greek θεο- (theo-, “god”), combining form of θεός (theós, “god”).

parole.significato: Theban; of or pertaining to Thebes, especially in the context of the Coptic scriptures.
parole.testo: From Latin Thēbaicus, from Ancient Greek Θηϐαϊκός (Thēbaïkós).

parole.significato: Any of several external cases or sheaths.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Latin thēca, from Ancient Greek θήκη (thḗkē, “a case, box, receptacle”), from τίθημι (títhēmi, “put, set, place”). Doublet of tay.

parole.significato: A toll or custom required from travelling merchants as a tax on doing business.
parole.testo: From Latin telōnium, from Ancient Greek τελώνῐον (telṓnĭon, “custom house”), from τέλος (télos, “due, tax, toll”).

parole.significato: god; deity
parole.testo: From Latin theo- (“god”), combining form of theos (“god”); from Ancient Greek θεο- (theo-, “god”), combining form of θεός (theós, “god”).

parole.significato: A fiador.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Theodōrus, borrowed from Ancient Greek Θεόδωρος (Theódōros), from θεός (theós, “god”) + δῶρον (dôron, “gift”). The name was popularized in reference to the prominent St Theodore of Amasea. Unrelated to Theodoric.

parole.significato: A student of theology
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin theologus, from Ancient Greek θεολόγος (theológos). Equivalent to theo- + -logue.

parole.significato: Concerned with theories or hypotheses rather than with practical matters.
parole.testo: English theory + -etic, from Latin theōrēticus, from Ancient Greek θεωρητικός (theōrētikós).

parole.significato: A Jewish sect which flourished in Alexandria and other parts of the Diaspora of Hellenistic Judaism in the final years…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin [Term?], from Ancient Greek θερᾰπευταί (therăpeutaí), plural of θερᾰπευτής (therăpeutḗs, “one who serves the gods, worshipper”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the city of Therma.
parole.testo: From Therma + -ean, modelled after Latin Thermaeus, from Ancient Greek Θερμαῖος (Thermaîos).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the city of Therma.
parole.testo: From Latin Thermaicus, from Ancient Greek Θερμαϊκός (Thermaïkós).

parole.significato: A publication that provides synonyms (and sometimes antonyms and other semantic relations) for the words of a given lan…
parole.testo: 16th century, borrowed from Latin thēsaurus, from Ancient Greek θησαυρός (thēsaurós, “storehouse, treasure”); its current English usage/meaning was established soon after the publication of Peter Roget's Thesaurus of English Words and Phrases in 1852. Doublet of treasure.

parole.significato: Senses relating to logic, rhetoric, etc.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English thesis (“lowering of the voice”) and also borrowed directly from its etymon Latin thesis (“proposition, thesis; lowering of the voice”), from Ancient Greek θέσῐς (thésĭs, “arrangement, placement, setting; conclusion, position, thesis; lowering of the voice”), from τῐ́θημῐ (t

parole.significato: Of, or relating to drama and acting; dramatic, theatrical.
parole.testo: From Latin Thespis, from the name of the Ancient Greek actor Thespis (fl. 6th century BCE), from Θέσπις (Théspis) + -ian.

parole.significato: A group of singers and dancers assembled to celebrate the festival of one of the gods.
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek θίασος (thíasos).

parole.significato: A cupola, a dome, a rotunda; a tholus.
parole.testo: Anglicization of Latin tholus (“cupola, dome, rotunda”), from Ancient Greek θόλος (thólos, “dome, vault”), further etymology uncertain but possibly cognate with θᾰ́λᾰμος (thắlămos, “bedroom; inner chamber”) and/or English dale. Doublet of tholus and tholos.

parole.significato: An infidel or doubter.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English Thomas, from Latin Thōmās m (as in the Vulgate), from Ancient Greek Θωμᾶς m (Thōmâs), the Biblical Greek transcription of Aramaic תאומא or תאמא (“twin”), the nickname of one of the Twelve Apostles. In the gospel of John (11:16, 20:24), the Aramaic nickname is also trans

parole.significato: The region of the mammalian body between the neck and abdomen as well as the cavity containing the heart and lungs.
parole.testo: From Latin thorax, from Ancient Greek θώραξ (thṓrax, “a breastplate, cuirass, corslet”).

parole.significato: Boastful, bragging, vainglorious.
parole.testo: From Latin Thrasō, Thrason-, the name of a boastful soldier in the play Eunuchus by Terence. The name is derived from Ancient Greek θρασύς (thrasús, “bold, audacious”).

parole.significato: a dirge or lamentation
parole.testo: From Latin threnus, from Ancient Greek θρῆνος (thrênos, “funeral lament”).

parole.significato: A spot in the wing veins of Neuroptera, Hymenoptera and Trichoptera.
parole.testo: From Latin thyridium, from Ancient Greek θυρίδιον (thurídion), diminutive of θύρᾱ (thúrā, “door”).

parole.significato: A staff topped with a conical ornament, carried by Bacchus or his followers.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin thyrsus, from Ancient Greek θύρσος (thúrsos). Doublet of thyrse, torse, and torso.

parole.significato: The three-tiered papal crown.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tiāra, from Ancient Greek τιάρα (tiára), of unknown ultimate origin.

parole.significato: Any one of Uranus and Gaia's daughters; a female Titan.
parole.testo: From Latin Titanis, from Ancient Greek Τιτανίς (Titanís). By surface analysis, Titan + -id.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or denoting those rays of light which produce chemical effects; actinic.
parole.testo: Latin Tithonius (“belonging to Tithonus, the consort of Aurora”), from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: An ancient people of Bactria.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Tocharī pl, from Ancient Greek Τόχαροι pl (Tókharoi).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Tochari (people of Bactria).
parole.testo: From Latin Tocharī + -ian, the first element deriving from Ancient Greek Τόχαροι (Tókharoi, “Tochari/Tukharas (an ancient people of Bactria)”), plural of Τόχαρος (Tókharos), probably from an Indo-Iranian source (Old Persian [script needed] (tuxāri-), Khotanese [script needed] (ttahvāra)); compare Sa

parole.significato: A small state, consisting of a few cities or towns; a petty country governed by a toparch.
parole.testo: From Latin toparchia, from Ancient Greek τοπαρχία (toparkhía), from τόπος (tópos, “place”) + ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “rule”).

parole.significato: A kind of mural decoration common in Ancient Roman houses, usually featuring landscapes.
parole.testo: From Latin topia, from Ancient Greek τόπια (tópia), ultimately from Ancient Greek τόπος (tópos, “place”).

parole.significato: Of, or relating to art of topiaries.
parole.testo: From Latin topiarius (“of or relating to ornamental gardening; an ornamental garden, an ornamental gardener”), from Latin topia (“ornamental gardening, landscape painting”), from Ancient Greek τόπια (tópia, “artistic representation in which natural or artificial features of a place are used as the m

parole.significato: topical
parole.testo: From Latin topica, from Ancient Greek τοπικός (topikós, “pertaining to a place, local, pertaining to a common place, or topic, topical”), from τόπος (tópos, “a place”).

parole.significato: A precise description of a place.
parole.testo: First attested in 1432. From Middle English topographye, from Latin topographia, from Ancient Greek τοπογραφία (topographía), from τόπος (tópos, “place”) + γράφω (gráphō, “to write”).

parole.significato: The description of an imaginable or nonexistent place.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin topothesia.

parole.significato: Synonym of confluence of sinuses.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin torcular Hērophilī (“Herophilos' winepress”), named after Greek physician Herophilos, while torcular was the Latin calque of Ancient Greek ληνός (lēnós, “anything shaped like a tub or trough; wine vat”), originally described by Herophilos.

parole.significato: A protein which is toxic (i.e. organic and poisonous)
parole.testo: From toxin 'organic poison' (from Middle Latin toxicus 'poisonous', from Latin toxicum 'poison (for arrows)', from Ancient Greek (toxikon), from (toxa) 'arrows', from (toxon) 'bow') + albumin 'protein' (from French albumine, from Latin albumen 'egg white', from albus 'white'). The term was first use

parole.significato: Any of several species of Asian pheasant of the genus Tragopan.
parole.testo: From Latin tragopān (“bird found in Ethiopia”), from Ancient Greek τράγος (trágos, “he-goat”) + Πάν (Pán, “Pan”).

parole.significato: Of, caused by, or causing trauma.
parole.testo: From the Latin traumaticus, from the Ancient Greek τραυματικός (traumatikós), from τραῦμα (traûma). By surface analysis, trauma + -tic.

parole.significato: A grouping of three.
parole.testo: PIE word  *tréyes From Latin triad-, stem of trias (“three, triad”), from Ancient Greek τριάς (triás). By surface analysis, tri- + -ad. parole.significato: A metrical foot consisting of three short syllables.
parole.testo: PIE word  *tréyes From the Latin tribrachys, from the Ancient Greek τρῐ́βρᾰχῠς (trĭ́brăkhŭs), from τρῐ- (trĭ-, “tri-”) + βρᾰχῠ́ς (brăkhŭ́s, “short”). Compare the French tribraque.

parole.significato: A couch for reclining at mealtimes, extending round three sides of a table, and usually in three parts.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin trīclīnium, from Ancient Greek τρικλίνιον (triklínion).

parole.significato: Triennial: occurring once in three years.
parole.testo: From Latin trietericus, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: trigonal; triangular
parole.testo: Latin trigonus, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: A set of three connected works—usually dramas, literary pieces, films, or musical compositions—all related by theme, ch…
parole.testo: PIE word  *tréyes Learned borrowing from Latin trilogia, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek τριλογία (trilogía, “trilogy”). Morphologically from tri- + -logy.

parole.significato: A three-legged stand or mount.

parole.testo: PIE word  *tréyes Borrowed from Latin tripod- (stem of tripūs, tripodis), from Ancient Greek τρίποδ- (trípod-, stem of τρίπους, τρίποδος (trípous, trípodos), literally “three-footed”); equivalent to tri- + -pod. Doublet of tripus, tripos, and teapoy.

parole.significato: A noun which has three cases.
parole.testo: From Latin triptōtum, from Ancient Greek τρίπτωτος (tríptōtos), from τρι- (tri-, “three”) + πίπτω (píptō, “to fall”) + -τος (-tos, verbal adjective–forming suffix), influenced by the verbal noun πτῶσις (ptôsis, “inflection”).

parole.significato: A vessel (usually a pot or cauldron) resting on three legs, often given as an ornament, a prize, or as an offering at a…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin tripūs, from Ancient Greek τρίπους (trípous); doublet of tripod, tripos, and teapoy. In the sense associated with Cambridge University, the Tripus is named after the three-legged stool on which he sat during the degree-awarding ceremony.

parole.significato: In Ancient Greek musical theory, the lower-pitched of the two movable notes in the farther tetrachord on a lyre, pitche…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin tritē, from Ancient Greek τρίτη (trítē, literally “third [string]”).

parole.significato: Any member of the hummingbird genus Trochilus.
parole.testo: From Latin trochilus (“a kind of small bird”), from Ancient Greek τροχίλος (trokhílos), from τρέχω (trékhō, “to run”).

parole.significato: A kind of tablet or lozenge
parole.testo: From Latin trochiscus, from Ancient Greek τρόχισκος (trókhiskos, “a small ball”). See troche.

parole.significato: A member of a supposed prehistoric race that lived in caves or holes, a caveman.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Trōglodytae (“cave-dwelling people”), from Ancient Greek τρωγλοδύτης (trōglodútēs, “one who dwells in holes”), from τρώγλη (trṓglē, “hole”) + δύω (dúō, “to get into”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to troglodytes, or dwellers in caves.
parole.testo: From Latin troglodyticus, Ancient Greek τρωγλοδυτικός (trōglodutikós, “of cave-/hole-dwellers”) from τρωγλοδύτης (trōglodútēs, “cave-/hole-dweller”) from τρώγλη (trṓglē, “hole”) + δύω (dúō, “enter, go into”), equivalent to troglodyte + -ic.

parole.significato: Pertaining to Troy; Trojan.
parole.testo: Latin Troicus, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Something recurring across a genre or type of art or literature; a motif.
parole.testo: From Latin tropus, from Ancient Greek τρόπος (trópos, “a manner, style, turn, way; a trope or figure of speech; a mode in music; a mode or mood in logic”), related to τροπή (tropḗ, “solstice; trope; turn”) and τρέπειν (trépein, “to turn”); compare turn of phrase. The verb is derived from the noun.

parole.significato: Mouthpart of certain types of organism such as an insect or a member of the Rotifera.
parole.testo: From Latin trophus, from Ancient Greek τροφός (trophós, “feeder”).

parole.significato: The turning of an organism (chiefly a plant) or part of an organism either towards or away from a stimulus; (countable)…
parole.testo: From -tropism (suffix meaning ‘growth towards; movement, turning’) (possibly based on geotropism and heliotropism), from Latin tropus + English -ism (suffix forming nouns of action, process, or result). parole.significato: Blowing from sea to land.
parole.testo: From Latin tropae(us) (“turning back”, “returning”, adjective) + -an; from the Plinian phrase ventī tropaeī (“sea-breezes”, literally “winds blowing from the sea towards the land”), from Ancient Greek τροπαῖος (tropaîos, adjective) (also used in the noun phrase πνοή τροπαία (pnoḗ tropaía, “an altern

parole.significato: To drive a truck.
parole.testo: Perhaps a shortening of truckle, related to Latin trochus (“iron hoop, wheel”) from Ancient Greek τροχός (trokhós).

parole.significato: Someone with turriphilia.
parole.testo: Coined by Theodore Ziolkowski in 1998. Equivalent to Latin turris (“tower”) + -philia, from Ancient Greek φιλία (philía).

parole.significato: An (often manic) affection for, love of, or attraction (in any form) towards towers or similarly shaped or designed obj…
parole.testo: Coined by Theodore Ziolkowski in 1998. From Latin turris (“tower”), from Ancient Greek τύρρις (túrrhis) + -philia, from Ancient Greek φιλία (philía, “love, affection”).

parole.significato: Relating to callused and swollen things.
parole.testo: From Latin tylo-, from Ancient Greek τύλη (túlē, “swelling”) and τύλος (túlos, “lump, knot”).

parole.significato: Relating to callused and swollen things.
parole.testo: From Latin tylo-, from Ancient Greek τύλη (túlē, “swelling”) and τύλος (túlos, “lump, knot”). By surface analysis, tyl- + -o-.

parole.significato: A grouping based on shared characteristics; a class.
parole.testo: From Middle English type (“symbol, figure, emblem”), from Latin typus, from Ancient Greek τύπος (túpos, “mark, impression, type”), from τύπτω (túptō, “to strike, beat”).

parole.significato: Forming terms relating to typing or typography.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin typo-, from Ancient Greek τύπος (túpos).

parole.significato: Of, or relating to tyranny or a tyrant.
parole.testo: From Latin tyrannicus + -al; ultimately from Ancient Greek τύραννος (túrannos) (absolute ruler, despot).

parole.significato: Synonym of Tyrrhenian.
parole.testo: From Latin Tyrrhēnus, from Ancient Greek Τυρρηνός (Turrhēnós).

parole.significato: A neighbor whose house is on fire or has burned down.
parole.testo: From Latin Ūcalegōn, from Ancient Greek Οὐκαλέγων (Oukalégōn). He was one of the Elders of Troy, whose house was set on fire by the Achaeans when they sacked the city. He is one of Priam's friends in the Iliad (3.148) and the destruction of his house is referred to in the Aeneid (2.312).

parole.significato: A place beyond the borders of the known world.
parole.testo: From Latin ultima Thūlē, nominative feminine singular of ultimus (“furthest”) + Thule, from mediaeval geography; originally from the Ancient Greek Θούλη (Thoúlē), a (possibly mythical) island to the north of Britain.

parole.significato: Magical control over shadows.
parole.testo: From Latin umbra (“shadow”) + -mancy (“divination of”), from Latin -mantia, ultimately from Ancient Greek μᾰντείᾱ (mănteíā, “divination”).

parole.significato: A representation of the sacred asp, symbolising supreme power in ancient Egypt.
parole.testo: From Latin uraeus, from Ancient Greek οὐραῖος (ouraîos). parole.significato: Celestial, heavenly; uranic.
parole.testo: From Latin Ūrania (“muse of astronomy in Greek mythology”) + -an (suffix forming agent nouns). Ūrania is derived from Ancient Greek Οὐρᾰνῐ́ᾱ (Ourănĭ́ā, “muse of astronomy”), from οὐράνιος (ouránios, “of or relating to the sky, celestial, heavenly”) (from οὐρανός (ouranós, “the sky; heaven, home of t

parole.significato: Of or relating to The Urantia Book, a spiritual and philosophical book of unknown authorship in the early 20th century.
parole.testo: From Urantia + -an, from Latin Ūranus, from Ancient Greek Οὐρανός (Ouranós), from οὐρανός (ouranós, “sky, heaven”).

parole.significato: An abnormal or irrational fear of worms or being infected by worms.
parole.testo: From Latin vermis (“worm”) + -phobia: Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos, “fear”).

parole.significato: The way an organism responds to mechanical (physical) vibrations.
parole.testo: From vibro-, from Latin vibrāre (“vibrate”) + Ancient Greek τάξις (táxis, “arrangement”)

parole.significato: The condition or disease of having a virus in the bloodstream.
parole.testo: From Latin virus (“poison”), in conjunction with Ancient Greek αἷμα (“blood”).

parole.significato: Someone with a Virgo star sign.
parole.testo: From Latin virgō (“maiden, virgin; name of constellation”), calque of Ancient Greek παρθένος (parthénos, “virgin; name of constellation”), ultimately derived through mythic reinterpretation from ancient Mesopotamian constellations, as Akkadian absinnu (“seed furrow; name of constellation”) and Sumer

parole.testo: From wisdom + tooth, calque of Latin dēns sapientiae, which is itself a calque of Ancient Greek σωφρονιστῆρες (sōphronistêres, “prudent or self-controlled ones (i.e. teeth)”), because they arrive approximately when one has reached the age of prudence or wisdom. parole.significato: An ill-tempered woman.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Xanthippē or its etymon Ancient Greek Ξανθίππη (Xanthíppē), the name of Socrates’ wife, from ξανθός (xanthós, “blond; golden, yellow”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱas- (“blond; grey; white”)) + ἵππος (híppos, “horse”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eḱ- (“horse;

parole.significato: A gift or offering.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin xenium, from Ancient Greek ξένιον (xénion), neuter accusative of ξένῐος (xénĭos, “pertaining to a guest”, adjective), ultimately from ξένος (xénos, “guest, stranger”). First attested in the 1700s.

parole.significato: A room (or separate guesthouse) in a monastery for the temporary accommodation of guests or pilgrims.
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek ξενοδοχεῖον (xenodokheîon, “place for strangers, inn”) from ξένος (xénos, “guest, stranger, foreigner”) + δέχομαι (dékhomai, “receive, accept”).

parole.significato: A Greek and Roman utensil consisting of a sea sponge fixed to the end of a wooden stick, typically thought to have been…
parole.testo: From Latin xylospongium, from Ancient Greek ξῠλοσπόγγῐον (xŭlospóngĭon), diminutive of ξῠλόσπογγος (xŭlóspongos). By surface analysis, xylo- (“wood”) + sponge.

parole.significato: The officer in charge of a xystus in Ancient Greece.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin xystarchēs, from Ancient Greek ξυστάρχης (xustárkhēs).

parole.significato: One who is zealous, one who is full of zeal for their own specific beliefs or objectives, usually in the negative sense…
parole.testo: Initially only found as Middle English zelote, an epithet of Simon the Zealot, acquiring its current senses in the 16th and 17th centuries. The Middle English derives from Latin zēlōtēs, from Ancient Greek ζηλωτής (zēlōtḗs, “emulator, zealous admirer, follower”), from ζηλόω (zēlóō, “to emulate, to b

parole.significato: Characteristic of zealots, especially those that were part of rebellious movements in biblical times.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin zēlōticus, from Ancient Greek ζηλωτικός (zēlōtikós). Equivalent to zealot + -ic.

parole.significato: Requiring or involving an infinite number of intervals within a finite time.
parole.testo: Via Latin Zēnō, from Ancient Greek Ζήνων (Zḗnōn), an ancient derivative of Ζεύς (Zeús), from Proto-Hellenic *dzéus, from Proto-Indo-European *dyḗws. Modern scientific and philosophical use derives from Zeno of Elea, poser of Zeno's paradoxes.

parole.significato: Pertaining to any of various people named Zeno or Zenon, or to their philosophies.
parole.testo: From Latin Zēnōn (also Zēnō) or its etymon Ancient Greek Ζήνων (Zḗnōn) + -ian. By surface analysis, Zenon + -ian.

parole.significato: A light wind from the west.
parole.testo: From Latin zephyrus (“west wind”), from Ancient Greek Ζέφυρος (Zéphuros). Doublet of zefir, zéphire, Zephyr, and Zephyrus. The confectionery sense is a semantic loan from Russian зефи́р (zefír).

parole.significato: An on-board hostess on the California Zephyr train, which originally operated between 1949 and 1970.
parole.testo: From zephyr (“light wind from the west”) + -ette (suffix forming nouns meaning the female equivalent of something). parole.significato: Each of the five regions of the earth's surface into which it was divided by climatic differences, namely the torrid zo…
parole.testo: From Latin zōna, from Ancient Greek ζώνη (zṓnē, “girdle, belt”). Doublet of zona.

parole.significato: The frieze of a column, especially one decorated with animals.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin zōophorus, from Ancient Greek ζωοφόρος (zōophóros).

parole.significato: An ancient Greek waist-belt for men.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin zōstēr (“shingles”), from Ancient Greek ζωστήρ (zōstḗr, “girdle”).

parole.significato: An unfermented kind of Egyptian malt beer.
parole.testo: From Latin zȳthum, from Ancient Greek ζῦθος (zûthos).
